docs.title: kb-core
docs.text:
The library between the Kokeb Labs chip drivers and a board HAL. Five parts, each its own CMake target and package, one version:

Part Target Holds Used by utils kb::utils Error model, time units, containers, CRCs Everyone rtos kb::rtos Sleeps, locks, queues, threads (FreeRTOS, ThreadX or none) Everyone dma kb::dma DMA buffers, leases, cache-policy regions, copy-out streams Ports, handlers interfaces kb::interfaces Bus and pin contracts (C++20 concepts), host test port HAL, handlers, MCU ports handlers kb::handlers Driver bindings, handlers, start-up pipeline, thread models HAL

MCU ports (components/ports/esp32/ first) are separate CMake projects in this repository until they move to their own repositories (MCU ports and repositories).

Status: release candidate. v0.1.0-rc.1 is the first release candidate: the parts, 23 pinned chip drivers and the ESP32 and host ports, tested in CI. APIs may still change before 0.1.0.

docs.title: In 30 seconds
docs.text:
Configure a project in the browser: pick an MCU, an RTOS and chip drivers, and download a pinned project with its SBOMs, licence report and build files (how it works). Or build kb-core itself:

cmake -S . -B build                     # host: every part, no driver
cmake -S . -B build -DKB_PARTS=utils    # one part alone

Start with the architecture, then the layering rules and the plan.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Where kb-core sits, what each part holds, and the path one call takes from a HAL to a chip.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
The layer stack Figure description and sources

From top to bottom. The product application (control, protocols, safety layer) calls the board HAL: its facade and managers built on kb-hal-common, the board config (bus table, thread model per bus, chip list, pins) and the platform bind, which builds the port objects and sets the start-up order. The board HAL uses kb::handlers and picks one MCU port. In kb-core, kb::handlers (bindings, handler core, start-up pipeline, owner and guarded access) uses the driver of each chip and the interface contracts; kb::interfaces (C++20 concepts only, plus the host test port) rests on kb::rtos (the API, with the backends none, FreeRTOS and ThreadX), and kb::rtos rests on kb::utils (Status/Result, units, containers, CRC, seqlock). Each driver- is brand-free, has its own CI at level high and is pinned at release tags. The MCU port (port-esp32 in components/ports/esp32, its own CMake project; port-stm32 planned in its own repository) satisfies the interface contracts and touches the vendor SDK in its boundary files only; the RTOS backends touch the kernel in theirs. The vendor SDK, kernels and mbedTLS (ESP-IDF, STM32 HAL, FreeRTOS, ThreadX, mbedTLS) are SOUP: never analysed, never edited.

Drawn from: docs/model/layer-stack.graph.yml.

docs.title: One call through the layers
docs.text:
A HAL reads a register of a PF1550 power IC. Only the last step knows it runs on an ESP32.

One call through the layers Figure description and sources

A HAL reads a register of a PF1550 power IC; solid arrows are calls, going down, and dashed arrows are returns, going up. The HAL calls the guarded handler with Call(timeout, ReadRegister) (its bus is declared guarded), which takes the handler lock and then the bus lock, both bounded, and calls the driver. The driver calls its own WriteRead hook, WriteRead(addr, tx, n, rx, m), implemented by the kb binding (Pf1550Port), which calls WriteRead(addr, span, span) on the ESP32 I2cDevice of the port. The port answers ok or an I2cFailure (AddressNack, DataNack, Bus, Timeout, BusStuck); the binding returns a bool and keeps the failure for GetLastFailure; the driver returns its Result; the handler returns a kb::Result carrying the driver's error in detail. Only the last step knows it runs on an ESP32.

Drawn from: docs/model/call-sequence.graph.yml.

docs.title: Build selection
docs.text: cmake/kb_build_settings.cmake selects everything kb-core builds: KB_MCU picks the MCU gate and the default RTOS, KB_RTOS the one backend, KB_PARTS the parts (dependencies added), KB_ENABLE_<DRIVER> the drivers, and the MCU gate table (cmake/kb_mcu_gates.cmake) stops a configure that enables a driver its MCU cannot run (the WS2812 driver needs the ESP32 RMT peripheral). kb-core compiles no MCU source: the MCU port is its own project. No platform macro is produced: code never tests the MCU.

docs.title: Configurator checks
docs.text:
The configurator runs two sets of rules on every change. The shared rules are the resolver specification (Assembler and resolver, codes KB-RES-NNN): configurator/resolver.mjs implements them exactly as the kb tool does, proven by the shared vectors in tests/resolver/vectors/, and it writes the lock, the CMake files and kb-fetch.sh. The site checks below (codes CFG-<area>-NNN, configurator/js/resolver.js) explain the same problems in plain words and add what only the site knows from its catalogue: bus instances of the target, point-to-point lines, I2C addresses, the pin budget, handler bindings, tested version sets and known vulnerabilities. Where a site check covers a shared rule, the page shows one finding with both codes.

A selection is offered for download only when both sets find no error.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• Site catalogue (configurator/data/catalog.json, schema configurator/schemas-draft/catalog.schema.json): a superset of kb-core's catalogue (catalog/schemas/catalog.schema.json) with labels, targets and their bus instance counts, boards and their free GPIO (where known), bus kinds, chip cards, scans and tested sets. configurator/js/shared.js derives kb-core's catalogue from it for the shared rules.
  • Selection (schema configurator/schemas-draft/kb-image.schema.json): image name, kb-core version, port version (null for an in-tree port), MCU family, target and board, RTOS, the drivers (name, version, the bus value used via, the bus bus) and the thread model of each bus. shared.js turns it into kb-image.yml.

docs.title: Bus instances
docs.text: A bus is named <instance><index>: i2c0, spi1, uart1, can0, pio0, adc0. Each driver bus value maps to an instance kind and a pin cost (bus_kinds in the catalogue): i2c to i2c (2 shared pins), spi to spi (3 shared pins and a chip select per device), uart to uart (2 pins, one driver), modbus to uart (an RS-485 line shared by Modbus devices, 3 pins), can and canopen to can (2 pins), adc to adc (one channel and pin per device), pio to pio (one RMT channel and pin per driver on ESP32). A target lists how many instances of each kind it has. In kb-image.yml a bus whose name does not give the bus value (Modbus on uart1, CANopen on can0) carries an explicit kind.

docs.title: Thread models
docs.text: Every bus has exactly one model, owner or guarded (ADR-0009). The site's default is owner, except guarded for I2C and ADC buses without a chip that needs an owner task.

docs.title: Tested sets
docs.text: A selection belongs to a tested set when kb-core, the port and every driver are at that set's versions (a subset of the set is allowed) and the set has a passing configuration for the same MCU family, target and RTOS. A selection with a driver that did not resolve belongs to none.

docs.title: Vectors
docs.text: One JSON file per case (schema configurator/schemas-draft/resolver-vector.schema.json) in configurator/tests/vectors/resolver/: catalog (a path relative to the vector), image, and expect with ok, errors, warnings, optionally infos and a partial resolved compared key by key. They run against configurator/tests/vectors/catalog-fixture.json. The configurator's tests also run every shared vector of tests/resolver/vectors/ through configurator/resolver.mjs, and check on every site vector that the site never accepts a selection the shared rules refuse.

docs.title: Exports
docs.text:
The downloads are tested end to end, as a user gets them. configurator/tools/export-matrix.json lists the selections:

Row Platform Drivers Build host-only host, no RTOS none host: app, every header, run host-shared-i2c host, std::thread five on one guarded I2C bus, three on an owner SPI bus host esp32c6-freertos ESP32-C6, FreeRTOS bmp581 and pcal9555 on one I2C bus ESP-IDF v5.5 esp32s3-freertos ESP32-S3, FreeRTOS bno08x (SPI, owner), ws2812_rmt (RMT), tmc9660 (UART) ESP-IDF v5.5 stm32-few STM32H7, FreeRTOS three refused: the family has no port yet (KB-RES-004) cortexm-few host family, cross-compiled the same three Cortex-M4 with arm-none-eabi-g++ esp32s3-every-driver ESP32-S3, FreeRTOS every driver of the catalogue ESP-IDF v5.5 host-every-driver host, std::thread every driver that runs off ESP32 host
  1. node configurator/tools/export_matrix.mjs OUT --chrome makes each selection with the page's own code and, in headless Chrome, clicks every Download button of the Files panel, the ZIP button and the offline copy; each download must equal the Node result byte for byte. A refused row must fail with its code.
  2. python3 configurator/tools/validate_exports.py OUT validates the SPDX 2.3 SBOM with the SPDX project's spdx-tools and the CycloneDX 1.6 SBOM against the official schema (CycloneDX's cyclonedx-python-lib, strict), kb-image.yml and the lock against kb's schemas, the licence report against the lock and both SBOMs, and checks that kb resolve writes the same lock and build files as the page.
  3. configurator/tools/export_build.sh OUT/<row>/project host|cortex-m|esp-idf [KB_CORE_DIR] runs the project's kb-fetch.sh (every submodule at its locked tag and commit) and builds it as its README says. The board file includes the handler binding of every selected driver, so the build compiles each one. With KB_CORE_DIR, kb-core inside the project is moved to that checkout first.

CI (.github/workflows/ci-exports.yml) runs the rows marked ci on every change to the configurator, the kb tool, the libraries or the build files, with kb-core at the commit under test: export through Chrome, validate, then the host, Cortex-M and ESP-IDF builds.

docs.title: Using the configurator
docs.text:
The configurator is a page that turns a few choices into a pinned, repeatable kb-core project with its evidence (ADR-0013, ADR-0014). It runs entirely in the browser: nothing is sent anywhere, no cookie is set, and the selection lives in the address bar, so a copied link reproduces it exactly. To use it without a network, take the offline copy (the link in its footer, or configurator/offline.html in the repository) and open it from disk.

Open the configurator: pick a platform, add drivers, download the project. The defaults already resolve, so a first project takes four choices and one click.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
1. Platform. Pick the MCU family (ESP32, STM32, host), the target and the board. The target fixes how many I2C, SPI, UART, CAN and RMT instances exist; a named development board also gives the number of free pins. A family marked planned has no port yet and cannot be built.
  2. RTOS and versions. Pick the RTOS backend the family allows (ESP-IDF runs FreeRTOS only; ThreadX on the families that list it), the kb-core version and, once the port has its own repository, the port version. Until kb-core has a release, the catalogue offers its development revision, pinned by commit and flagged with a warning. C++ standard declares what your toolchain builds with (language: in kb-image.yml, x= in the link); a part that needs a newer standard is then refused with the newest version that fits, and a driver added afterwards gets that version (Language floor). Left at Not declared, nothing is checked.
  3. Drivers. Search the catalogue by chip, bus or capability, or filter by bus. Each card shows the chip, its package, the buses it speaks, its capabilities, its licence, its status and a pinout or block diagram (click it for every figure). Each driver has a version selector with its published releases; the default is kb-core's pin, else the newest release. Release candidates (marked rc) are hidden by default: turn on Show release candidates to list them and to add a driver that has only release candidates. The switch is kept in the link (c=1) and turns on by itself when a link or an opened project already uses an rc, and while kb-core itself has only release candidates (the page then starts on the newest one instead of an empty selection). A search with no match offers request it: a link to the driver request form of kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-requests, prefilled with the search text reduced to letters, digits, ., _ and -; the footer links to the request forms for a driver and for a port or target. The page itself sends nothing.

  4. Buses and thread models. Each driver goes on a bus (i2c0, spi1, uart1, pio0, ...). Give each bus one thread model (ADR-0009): an owner task that serves every device on it, or a guarded facade that locks around each call. Chips that must be serviced continuously (bno08x) need an owner task. The pin meter adds up the bus pins and the optional control pins.

  5. Inside and tested. For the kb-core version of the selection: the Architecture map (the parts, the port and your drivers; pick one for what it holds, needs and how it was tested), the Evidence of that release (the test protocol and its results, read from the release's CI artifacts, each chart with its table; also on Test evidence) and Versions (every kb-core version with its headline evidence).

docs.title: Open an existing project
docs.text:
Open an existing project, folded above step 1, takes your project's kb-image.yml and its kb-image.lock.yml (pick both at once; a lock alone also works). The page reads them in the browser with the file picker: nothing is uploaded or stored. The address bar gets only catalogue identifiers: the project's own image name stays out of it while the project is open, and drivers this catalogue does not list are left out of the selection (and named under the file picker). The project becomes the selection of the four steps, with every version taken from the lock, and Available upgrades lists one row per component (kb-core, an extracted port, each driver):

  • the current version and the version it can move to: the newest final release that passes the gates against the new kb-core (MCU family, kb_core_min, the owner-task rule, the bus kind in use); tick Offer release candidates (the same switch as in step 3) to include rcs, or pick a version per row (the same as kb upgrade --to); versions that are held back are listed but cannot be picked, and Clear chosen versions undoes the picks;
  • the change (major, minor, patch, prerelease, or commit when the lock pins another commit than the catalogue for the same version), marked breaking by SemVer (a new major; before 1.0 a new minor; before 0.1 a new patch), with a link to the new tag's release notes;
  • the newest release and a newer release candidate, the versions held back and why;
  • known vulnerabilities of both versions (or not scanned) and the ones the upgrade fixes.

Use the upgraded versions moves the selection to the plan; the Check panel then shows the usual findings for it, including the tested-set status. Download kb-upgrade.md, kb-image.yml and kb-image.lock.yml give the same bytes as kb upgrade kb-image.yml --catalog data/catalog.json -o . run on the page's own catalogue (configurator/data/catalog.json, which kb reads as it is; the kb tool). Both run the upgrade rules of the shared specification, pass the same vectors, and a test plans every driver of the shipped catalogue in both and compares the files. With a different catalogue (a kb release's catalog.json built later, with other versions or scans) the answers differ as the catalogues do.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
Every change runs two rule sets and lists their findings in plain words, each with its code:

  • the shared rules of the kb tool (KB-RES-*, Assembler and resolver): MCU gates, RTOS per family, kb_core_min, one thread model per bus, kRequiresOwner, versions that exist;
  • the site checks (CFG-*, Configurator checks): bus instances of the target, a point-to-point UART shared by two drivers, Modbus and plain serial on one line, I2C address clashes, the pin budget, handler bindings, tested version sets and known vulnerabilities.

Errors block the downloads; warnings (a release candidate, an untested combination, a development revision) do not.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
File What it is kb-image.yml The selection (schema 1); kb resolve kb-image.yml gives the same lock kb-image.lock.yml Every pin by tag and commit, with the MCU, RTOS, parts, buses and CMake values CMakePresets.json, kb_image.cmake KB_MCU, KB_RTOS, KB_PARTS, KB_ENABLE_* and each KB_DRIVER_<NAME>_DIR (external/drivers/) for kb-core's build kb-fetch.sh Adds kb-core, the port and every driver to your repository as git submodules under external/ at their tags, checks every commit, refuses a moved tag, records no branch, never recurses; --verify re-checks them in CI (layout) evidence/sbom.cdx.json, evidence/sbom.spdx.json CycloneDX 1.6 and SPDX 2.3 SBOMs of exactly the selection, identifiers derived from the lock, plus the SDK and RTOS as SOUP evidence/licences.md Each component's SPDX licence and copyright holder evidence/status.md The tested version set or an untested combination warning, the known-vulnerability scan of each component (or not scanned), the compatibility rows and the findings Starter project (.zip) All of the above plus an ESP-IDF or CMake project skeleton with a board layer

The lock, the presets, kb_image.cmake and kb-fetch.sh are written by the same resolver code as kb resolve, so they match byte for byte. Every file is repeatable: the same selection gives the same bytes, in any time zone; the timestamp is the newest commit date of the selected components.

docs.title: Where the facts come from
docs.text:
The catalogue (configurator/data/catalog.json) is generated by configurator/tools/build_catalog.py from the driver repositories: for every vX.Y.Z and vX.Y.Z-rc.N tag it reads driver.yml, the README's summary and At a glance table, LICENSE, docs/hardware.yml and the chip figures at that tag's commit, never from a working tree. A tag whose commit differs between a local clone and GitHub stops the build. Known-vulnerability results come from the scan in CI (osv-scanner); a component without a scan shows not scanned. Bus counts and free pins of targets and boards are approximate where the catalogue says so; check the board's schematic.

Contact: kokeblabs@gmail.com

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
The organisation's rules apply (.github/CONTRIBUTING.md). What is particular to kb-core:

  • Fresh code under the pipeline. Each unit goes through design, build, self-review, the local gate, independent review and fixes before it is merged (ADR-0005).
  • C++20 and concepts only. No virtual functions; a new base class needs a row in the register of ADR-0006.
  • Layering. A change never adds an include or a link across the rules in Layering rules; a change to a boundary file, a deviation record or the rules themselves needs a second reviewer.
  • The port seam. Code in components/ports/<mcu>/ uses only installed kb-core headers; nothing in components/lib/ reaches into components/ports/.
  • One part per pull request where possible; the CHANGELOG entry goes under that part.
  • Driver pins change only to a release or release-candidate tag whose CI passed; never a branch, never an edit inside components/drivers/.
  • Tests with the change: unit tests in the part, an integration test for a binding, a docs test for every new code block.
  • Sign off every commit (git commit -s). No attribution lines.

docs.title: Deviations
docs.text:
kb-core follows MISRA C++:2023 and the KB-CPP20 profile at the handbook's high level (ADR-0011). The handbook's project-wide records (MD-CPP-001 onwards) apply as everywhere. kb-core's own records are in deviations/deviations.yml, and only the boundary files in deviations/boundary-files.yml may need them. Each MCU port keeps its own two files in components/ports/<mcu>/deviations/.

Boundary file (planned) Records Why components/lib/rtos/backends/freertos/freertos_boundary.cpp kb-core (DEV-KBC-NNN) FreeRTOS C API: macros used as calls, void* task arguments, opaque handles components/lib/rtos/backends/freertos/freertos_isr.cpp kb-core (DEV-KBC-NNN) ...FromISR calls and the yield macro components/ports/esp32/src/esp32_bus_boundary.cpp ESP32 port (DEV-KBP-ESP32-NNN) ESP-IDF I2C, SPI and UART C API components/ports/esp32/src/esp32_io_boundary.cpp ESP32 port (DEV-KBP-ESP32-NNN) ESP-IDF GPIO, ADC, TWAI and RMT C API and callbacks with void* user data components/ports/esp32/src/esp32_time_boundary.cpp ESP32 port (DEV-KBP-ESP32-NNN) esp_timer and ROM delay

The record format is in deviations/README.md. The guidelines each file needs are confirmed against the first MISRA scan of real code, not guessed in advance; a record lists exact files, the justification, the mitigation and a review date, and lapses unless renewed. Every change to a boundary file or a record needs a second reviewer.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Examples are first-class in kb-core. Each one is a real program or project that CI builds; the documentation shows its source through snippet includes, never a pasted copy, so a page cannot drift from code that compiles; and each is listed in one index, examples/examples.yml, which the build, the README table, the documentation and the configurator catalogue are checked against (tools/examples/examples.py check).

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• A host example is a folder under examples/host/ with main.cpp, CMakeLists.txt and README.md. It is built with -DKB_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON (the host job of CI does so on every pull request) and runs as the ctest test example_<id>. It uses the strict flags of the library, needs no hardware and prints one line.
  • An ESP-IDF example is an app of the ESP32 port's example project (ADR-0007), listed in that port's app_config.yml and built by its own CI job with ESP-IDF v5.5. It stays with the port so that it moves out with it.
  • The code a page shows sits between // --8<-- [start:<name>] and // --8<-- [end:<name>] in the example's main.cpp, and the page includes it with a snippet include of that file and section.

docs.title: Figures
docs.text: Every diagram of this site is a committed SVG pair, light and dark, drawn from a small model file by the documentation toolchain (figkit, shipped in the shared kokeb-mkdocs-theme). There is no script in the reader's browser: the pages load no Mermaid, stay fast on a phone and print. The figure catalogue lists every figure with its description.

docs.title: What every figure has
docs.text:
• One source. docs/model/<id>.<kind>.yml is the only place a figure is edited. The kind is one of the shared figkit kinds: state, graph, seq, timeline, matrix, bytes or pipeline. A figure that shows facts of the repository (the components) is a small module docs/diagrams/figures/<id>.py instead: its data() reads the facts and its build() turns them into the same model and draws it with from_model, so it cannot drift from the code.
  • A phone-first layout. About 640 px wide, read top to bottom, with short labels on the cards and arrows. Long text goes to the reads paragraph under the figure, not onto the figure.
  • A light and a dark file. <id>.svg and <id>.dark.svg, laid out once, so the two cannot differ, plus <id>.adaptive.svg, one file for both themes. Pages embed the pair with a marker pair and the site follows the theme toggle.
  • Accessible text. The one-sentence alt becomes the <title> and the alt of every embed; the reads paragraph becomes the <desc> and the long description under the figure. Colour is never the only carrier of meaning: forbidden or faulty edges are dashed and labelled, states and matrix cells carry a word, and a matrix also gets a table twin, <id>.table.html.
  • Checks. Text contrast of at least 4.5:1 and shape contrast of at least 3:1 in both themes, text that fits its card, no arrow under a card, text of at least 7 pt when printed on A4, and SVG and alt lint, all from kokeb-docs figures --lint. kokeb-docs figures --check fails CI when a committed SVG differs from a fresh build, and tools/docs/check_figures.py rejects Mermaid fences, .mmd files, a missing light or dark file or source, a module that does not draw with figkit, and an SVG with a script or an external reference.

docs.title: The palette
docs.text:
Colours are tokens, never hex values: the Kokeb copper (gold in dark) for kb-core itself, and one tone for each kind of thing, the same in every figure, so a reader learns it once. Write the tone in the model (tone: violet).

Role Tone Used for core brand, copper (gold in dark) kb-core as a whole, kb::utils contract blue kb::interfaces, port contracts, shared state, inputs handler violet kb::handlers, bindings, the start-up pipeline rtos amber kb::rtos and its backends, timing port teal MCU ports, the host port, bus domains driver green driver-<chip> (and "ok", "allowed", outputs) product magenta the application and the board HAL soup slate SOUP and things not built yet (a card without the accent tint) bad rose forbidden edges, failures, fault paths tool brown generators, the kb tool, tasks and tests

A matrix uses the status tones instead: ok, warn, fail, na and planned, each drawn with a mark and a word. Solid arrows are calls or "depends on"; dashed arrows are optional, returns or forbidden, always with a label that says which. Every figure has a legend that names each tone it uses.

docs.title: Choosing a kind
docs.text:
Kind For Examples here graph Layers, flows and call chains: cards and arrows in ranks, top to bottom layer-stack, ci-flow, call-sequence state A state machine: states, transitions, a start disc, self loops handler-health, dma-lease seq Messages between three or four participants over time async-poll matrix A verdict per row, with a word and a mark in every cell dependency-rules, misra-scope pipeline Columns of stacked items handler-startup timeline Lanes against a time axis none yet bytes A record laid out byte by byte none yet

Keep a graph or state figure to about two cards per rank: a rank of three cards makes the figure wider than 640 px. A seq figure with five participants is too wide for a phone; draw the call chain as a graph with solid calls going down and dashed returns going up instead (see call-sequence). One figure, handler-threading, stays a module of plain figkit calls, because it stacks two small graphs one above the other, which the graph kind would put side by side.

docs.title: Add a figure
docs.text:
1. Scaffold it: kokeb-docs figkit new --kind graph --id <id> --page docs/<page>.md (from the repository root, with KOKEB_DOCS_CONFIG=_config/mkdocs.yml). This writes docs/model/<id>.graph.yml and adds the embed marker to the page.
  2. Edit the model. Write the one-sentence alt (40 to 300 characters) and the reads paragraph first: at least two sentences, naming every state, participant, lane or column. Then the cards, the edges and the legend. Quote a list item that holds a comma or a colon (lines: ["MCU, RTOS"]), or YAML splits it.
  3. For a state or graph figure, run kokeb-docs figkit layout <id> and commit docs/diagrams/<id>.layout.json. This is the only step that needs Graphviz; run it again whenever the cards, edges or text change.
  4. Build and look at it: kokeb-docs figures writes the SVGs, figures.json and the catalogue, and fills the embed markers. The build refuses low contrast, text that does not fit, overlapping cards, an arrow under a card or a label on a card; fix the model rather than the check. rsvg-convert -w 360 docs/diagrams/<id>.svg -o /tmp/<id>.png shows it at phone width.
  5. Run kokeb-docs figures --lint, kokeb-docs check, python3 tools/docs/check_figures.py and the strict site build, or tools/preflight.sh, which runs them. Commit the model, the layout lock and everything under docs/diagrams/ together.

Rules of thumb: at most about ten cards per figure (split a bigger story in two), labels of a few words, the same tone for the same thing as everywhere else, and a figure that shows repository facts reads them in data() and names its sources. Never edit an SVG or a layout lock by hand, write a hex colour, or put a time stamp in a model.

docs.title: The kb tool
docs.text:
kb builds the catalogue, resolves a kb-image.yml into a lock and the files a build needs, lists and applies upgrades to newer catalogued versions, and writes SBOMs from a lock. It implements the resolver specification of ADR-0014; the configurator site implements the same rules and passes the same vectors.

Python 3.10 or newer and the standard library; PyYAML only to read YAML files (JSON input, and a lock, which is JSON after one comment line, need nothing else).

python3 tools/kb/kb.py --help          # from the kb-core root
cd tools && python3 -m kb --help       # or as a module

docs.title: Build a catalogue
docs.text:
# Offline, from local clones: a driver clone or a folder of driver-* clones, plus kb-core's own tags and pins
python3 tools/kb/kb.py catalog build --drivers-dir ../drivers --kb-core-dir . -o catalog.json

# The working revision of kb-core as an unreleased version (warned as KB-RES-W03 when used)
python3 tools/kb/kb.py catalog build --drivers-dir ../drivers --kb-core-dir . --include-head -o catalog.json

# Online, with gh (logged in): every driver-* repository of the organisation, or some of them
python3 tools/kb/kb.py catalog build --online --org kokeb-labs-drivers --repo driver-pcal9555 -o catalog.json

# Binding facts (requires_owner) from the configurator's platform file, until a kb-core release records them
python3 tools/kb/kb.py catalog build --drivers-dir ../drivers --platforms configurator/data/platforms.json -o catalog.json

Only vX.Y.Z and vX.Y.Z-rc.N tags are read. A driver.yml that disagrees with its tag (name, version) or has an invalid field is reported and left out; the command then exits 1.

docs.title: Resolve an image
docs.text:
python3 tools/kb/kb.py resolve kb-image.yml --catalog catalog.json -o out/
Exit Meaning 0 Resolved; out/ holds kb-image.lock.yml, CMakePresets.json, kb_image.cmake, kb-fetch.sh 1 The image does not resolve: one line per error, error KB-RES-NNN <subject>: <message> 2 Bad arguments, or a file that cannot be read or parsed

Warnings (warning KB-RES-WNN ...) go to standard error and do not change the exit code. Without -o the lock is written to standard output. Copy the files to the root of your project's git repository and run sh kb-fetch.sh: it adds kb-core, the port and every driver as submodules under external/ at their tags, checks each commit against the lock and refuses a moved tag. sh kb-fetch.sh --verify (in CI, for example) only checks that every submodule is still at its pinned commit. kb_image.cmake and the presets point each KB_DRIVER_<NAME>_DIR at external/drivers/.

docs.title: Find and apply upgrades
docs.text:
The update path Figure description and sources

From the top. kb outdated (exit 3 when a component can move), kb upgrade, or the configurator's Open an existing project view plan from the current lock, the catalogue and the image; the current versions come from the lock. kb-core moves first, then an extracted port, then each driver in name order. Each candidate must pass the driver gates in order (MCU family, kb_core_min, owner-task rule, bus kind in use); a newer version that fails is held back with the code of its first failing gate. The plan lists one row per component with the SemVer change, whether it breaks, and known vulnerabilities fixed and remaining. kb upgrade writes a new image and lock, the CMake files, the fetch script and kb-upgrade.md; the user then reviews the diff, runs sh kb-fetch.sh, builds and tests.

Drawn from: docs/model/update-path.graph.yml.

# What can move: one row per component (kb-core, an extracted port, each driver)
python3 tools/kb/kb.py outdated kb-image.yml --catalog catalog.json
python3 tools/kb/kb.py outdated kb-image.yml --catalog catalog.json --allow-rc --json

# Write the upgraded project: kb-image.yml, its lock, CMake files, kb-fetch.sh and kb-upgrade.md
python3 tools/kb/kb.py upgrade kb-image.yml --catalog catalog.json -o .
python3 tools/kb/kb.py upgrade kb-image.yml --catalog catalog.json --to kb-core=0.4.1 --to bmp581=0.2.0 -o .

--catalog takes kb's catalogue (kb catalog build, or a kb-core release's catalog.json) or the configurator's configurator/data/catalog.json, which kb converts exactly as the page does, so both plan the same thing; any other file is refused with exit 2. Both read the project's current versions from kb-image.lock.yml beside the image (or --lock FILE; --no-lock ignores it): an image may leave versions out, and without its lock "current" would mean today's newest. kb-core moves first, then an extracted port, then every driver to its newest release (--allow-rc also takes release candidates) that passes the gates against the new kb-core: MCU family, kb_core_min, the owner-task rule and the bus kind in use. A newer version that fails a gate is listed as held back with the gate's code. --to NAME=VERSION (repeatable; kb-core, port-<family> or a driver) moves one component to exactly that version, a release candidate or a kb-core development revision included; a downgrade is refused. A lock whose commit (or kind) for a version differs from the catalogue's, such as a kb-core development revision whose version has since been tagged or a moved tag, is shown as a change (prerelease or commit) and warned with KB-UPG-W04. The rules are the upgrade section of the resolver specification, and the configurator's Open an existing project view applies the same rules and, given the same catalogue, writes the same bytes.

kb-upgrade.md lists each component's change (major, minor, patch, prerelease), whether it is breaking by SemVer (a new major; before 1.0 a new minor; before 0.1 a new patch) with a link to the new tag's release page, the held-back versions, the known vulnerabilities fixed and still present (from the catalogue's osv scans, or not scanned), the warnings and the next steps. -o . rewrites the project's kb-image.yml in one fixed style (comments and layout are not kept). Review the diff, run sh kb-fetch.sh to move every submodule, then build and test.

Exit kb outdated kb upgrade 0 every component is at its newest selectable version the files are written (or the report printed) 1 the plan fails: error KB-UPG-NNN or KB-RES-NNN lines the same 2 bad arguments, or a file that cannot be read the same 3 at least one component can move not used

docs.title: Write an SBOM
docs.text:
python3 tools/kb/kb.py sbom out/kb-image.lock.yml --format cyclonedx -o image.cdx.json
python3 tools/kb/kb.py sbom out/kb-image.lock.yml --format spdx -o image.spdx.json

The same lock always gives the same bytes: the CycloneDX serial number and the SPDX namespace derive from the lock's SHA-256, and no clock is read. --created (or SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH) adds a creation time; SPDX, which requires one, otherwise uses 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. The SDK and RTOS (ESP-IDF, FreeRTOS, ThreadX when selected) are listed as SOUP. Every top-level component carries a kb:osv property (CycloneDX) or comment (SPDX) with its known-vulnerability scan: from --catalog catalog.json when its versions carry scans, else not scanned.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
python3 tools/kb/tests/run.py              # unit tests and every vector (exit 77 without PyYAML; 1 in CI)
node tests/resolver/run_js_vectors.mjs     # the same and the upgrade vectors through configurator/resolver.mjs

Both run under CTest with -DKB_BUILD_TESTS=ON (kb_cli_unit, kb_resolver_js_vectors).

docs.title: Language floor
docs.text: Every part of a kb project says which C++ standard it needs at least: kb-core itself, its in-tree ports and every driver version. This page says where that is written, how a project declares the standard it builds with, and what the resolver, the configurator and CMake do with both.

docs.title: In 30 seconds
docs.text:
• kb-core needs C++20, GCC 10 or Clang 13 or newer. So does every driver published today.
  • A project may declare its own standard in kb-image.yml. Then a part that needs more is refused, with the newest version that fits, before anything is downloaded.
  • Without that declaration nothing changes: every part is taken at its default version, and CMake builds C++20.

docs.title: Where the floor is written
docs.text:
Part File Read by A driver, per release driver.yml language: at the tag kb catalog build, the configurator's catalogue builder kb-core and its in-tree ports kb.yml language: CMake (cmake/kb_language.cmake), both catalogue builders A project kb-image.yml language: (optional) kb resolve, kb upgrade, the configurator

The block is the same everywhere; it follows the organisation's standards registry (profiles such as KB-CPP20 with their compiler floors):

language:
  standard: 20              # the minimum ISO C++ standard
  profile: KB-CPP20         # the handbook profile of that standard
  compilers: {gcc: "10", clang: "13"}   # the oldest compilers it promises to build with (quoted)
  tested: [20]              # every standard CI compiles it under

The catalogue copies standard, profile, compilers and tested into each version, with source saying where they came from. A tag published before its driver had the block is recorded with the registry default, C++20 and the KB-CPP20 compiler floors (GCC 10, Clang 13, MSVC 19.30, Arm GCC 10, ESP-IDF 5.0), and source: default.

docs.title: Declaring the project's standard
docs.text:
# kb-image.yml
schema: 1
kb_core: {version: 0.1.0-rc.1}
mcu: {family: esp32, target: esp32c6}
language: {standard: 20, compilers: {gcc: "12"}}   # compilers are optional
drivers: [tmc9660]

standard is one of 17, 20, 23 and 26; compilers may name gcc, clang, msvc, arm_gcc and esp_idf. In the configurator, step 2 has a C++ standard choice that writes the same block; the version lists of step 3 show what each version needs (0.5.2, C++20).

docs.title: What the resolver does
docs.text:
The same rules in kb resolve, kb upgrade and the configurator (docs/design/assembler.md, rule 7), held to the shared vectors 027 to 032 in tests/resolver/vectors/:

Situation Result A driver named with a version whose floor is above the project's KB-RES-024, with the newest version that fits A driver named without a version, its default above the project's The newest version that fits is used, warning KB-RES-W04 The same, and no version fits KB-RES-024, no alternative: raise the project's standard kb-core's floor above the project's KB-RES-024, subject kb-core, with the newest kb-core that fits A compiler the project names is older than the part's floor for it KB-RES-025, with the newest version that fits kb upgrade A newer version above the project's floor is held back with the same code

An example. The catalogue has tmc9660 0.6.0 (C++23, GCC 13), 0.5.2 (C++20) and 0.5.0 (no block, so C++20). A project that declares C++20 and names 0.6.0 gets:

KB-RES-024 tmc9660: tmc9660 0.6.0 needs C++23; the project builds with C++20. tmc9660 0.5.2 is the newest
version that builds with C++20, or raise language.standard to 23

The finding carries alternative: "0.5.2", which the configurator shows. The same project naming tmc9660 without a version resolves to 0.5.2 with KB-RES-W04. A project that declares C++23 and GCC 12 and names 0.6.0 gets KB-RES-025 (gcc 13 or newer), again with 0.5.2.

The project's standard is what the build uses; a part's tested list is evidence that a newer standard also works, never permission to build a part at a standard below its floor.

docs.title: What CMake does
docs.text:
cmake/kb_language.cmake reads the floor from kb.yml:

  • KB_CPP_STANDARD (cache) is the standard kb-core builds with. It defaults to the floor and may be 20, 23 or 26. A value below the floor stops the configure step with a message that names both (-DKB_CPP_STANDARD=17 fails; the CTest kb_language_floor proves it).
  • Every kb target requires the floor of its consumers (cxx_std_20 today); kb-core's own tests, header checks and boundary files build at KB_CPP_STANDARD, and each header check asserts the matching __cplusplus.
  • A project whose image declares a language gets KB_CPP_STANDARD from its kb_image.cmake and its presets.

Raising kb-core's floor is a breaking change and one edit: standard in kb.yml (CMake, the catalogue and the resolver follow), plus the changelog entry under Breaking.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• tools/kb/tests/test_language.py: the block reader, the default, a bad block naming every problem, the catalogue field, kb.yml and CMake reading the same number, and that no library target hard-codes a standard.
  • The shared vectors through both resolvers (kb_cli_unit, kb_resolver_js_vectors).
  • The catalogue check (build_catalog.py --check) fails when a driver's block at a tag is malformed.

The compiler floors themselves are tested by the organisation's weekly floor-compiler job (GCC 10, Clang 13) in each driver repository.

docs.title: Layering rules
docs.text:
What may depend on and include what, and the checks that enforce it (ADR-0001, ADR-0007).

Which layer may depend on which Figure description and sources

The twelve allowed dependencies come first: the application uses the board HAL, kb::rtos and kb::utils; the board HAL uses kb::handlers, kb::interfaces and one MCU port; the MCU port uses the installed kb::interfaces headers only and the vendor SDK headers in boundary files only; kb::handlers uses the drivers and kb::interfaces; kb::interfaces uses kb::rtos; kb::rtos uses kb::utils. The seven forbidden dependencies follow, each with the check that catches it: the application using kb::interfaces or the SDK directly (the include checker and the symbol lint), kb::handlers using the SDK (the poison build and the include checker) or an MCU port (the CMake DAG check), kb::interfaces using an MCU port (the include checker, LAY-010), a driver using kb::utils (the driver CI and the include checker), and kb::utils using kb::rtos (the CMake target graph). Each cell carries a word and a mark, so the meaning does not rest on colour alone.

Drawn from: docs/model/dependency-rules.matrix.yml.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. Dependencies point down only: utils <- rtos <- interfaces <- handlers.
  2. Applications reach hardware only through their HAL: they never include kb/interfaces/... or kb/handlers/... and never link kb::interfaces or kb::handlers. They may use kb::utils and kb::rtos.
  3. SDK and RTOS headers appear only in the .cpp files listed in a boundary-files.yml: kb-core's own (deviations/boundary-files.yml, RTOS backends) and each port's (components/ports/<mcu>/deviations/boundary-files.yml). No public header includes one.
  4. An MCU port uses kb-core only through its public, installed headers; nothing in components/lib/ includes anything from components/ports/.
  5. No #if on a platform macro above those files. The build selects folders; code does not select itself.
  6. No board or product value in kb-core: pins, addresses, rail tables and timeouts arrive as configuration.
  7. Drivers include nothing from kb-core, and kb-core never modifies a driver.

docs.title: Enforcement
docs.text:
Check Catches Where CMake visibility A consumer that did not link a part cannot find its headers; backends are PRIVATE; a port sees only the installed package cmake/kb_part.cmake, each components/lib/<part>/CMakeLists.txt, components/ports/<mcu>/CMakeLists.txt Include and dependency checker An include across a forbidden boundary, an SDK include outside a boundary file, an include across the port seam, a target link against the DAG, an application including interfaces or handlers tools/include_checker/ (spec), CI ci-layering.yml Poison build An #if on an MCU or SDK macro in platform-free code tests/poison/ Symbol lint An application or platform-free object referencing an SDK or native RTOS symbol tools/include_checker/ (spec)

A HAL runs the same checker with its own zone file, which adds its private, public and application zones.

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text: Where things live is decided once, in tools/layout/paths.yml. CMake, the tools, tools/preflight.sh and the tests read that file; none of them spells out a location, so another grouping is a change of one line there. Prose, workflow files and YAML cannot read it and carry the literal path; a check fails when one still names a retired location.

docs.title: Top level
docs.text:
Parts, ports and drivers Figure description and sources

Read from the folders of the repository, so the figure cannot drift. The folder components/lib holds the parts: kb::utils at the bottom, kb::rtos on it, kb::interfaces on that, and kb::handlers on top; kb::dma, the chip-neutral DMA vocabulary, also rests on kb::utils. The folder components/ports holds the MCU ports, which satisfy the interface contracts (the host port is for tests only). The folder components/drivers holds the pinned drivers, each a submodule at a release tag, listed by name; kb::handlers binds them and nothing else may use them.

Drawn from: components/lib; components/ports; components/drivers; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/components-map.py.

Folder Holds components/lib/ The four parts: utils, rtos, interfaces, handlers (one CMake target and package each) components/ports/ esp32 (own CMake project, moves to port-esp32) and host (the std::thread RTOS backend, built in kb-core's project) components/drivers/ Driver submodules pinned to release or rc tags, and drivers.lock.yml examples/ Programs built in CI and shown in these pages; the example index catalog/ compat.yml (generated) and the JSON schemas in catalog/schemas/ tests/, tools/, docs/, configurator/ Repository tests, tools, this site, the hosted configurator third_party/ Pinned third-party sources used for tests and cross builds (SOUP): the Eclipse ThreadX submodule _config/, deviations/, cmake/, .kokeb/, .github/ Organisation-wide conventions, kept at the root

components/ groups the three kinds of component that sit next to each other: libraries, ports and drivers. Files at the root are README.md, AGENTS.md, CHANGELOG.md, LICENSE, CMakeLists.txt, .gitignore and .gitmodules; nothing else is allowed there.

docs.title: One file, three readers
docs.text:
tools/layout/paths.yml has four sections, all flat key: value and - item lines so that CMake, Python and Node can each read it with a few lines of code:

  • layout: name to path (lib, ports, drivers, host_port, schemas, examples, ...).
  • retired: former paths and the name they became, so a stale reference can be found and rewritten.
  • vendor: the files a consumer that keeps a pinned copy of kb-core needs (see below).
  • root_dirs, root_files: the allowlist of top-level entries.
Reader How CMake include(cmake/kb_layout.cmake), then kb_layout(lib VAR) or the variables KB_LIB_DIR, KB_PORTS_DIR, KB_DRIVERS_DIR, KB_HOST_PORT_DIR, KB_TESTS_DIR, ... (and KB_<NAME>_REL) Scripts python3 tools/layout/layout.py get lib (--abs for an absolute path), layout.py list Python tools tools/layout/layout.py as a module; the kb tool through tools/kb/repolayout.py Tests the same module; tools/layout/tests/ checks that CMake and Python read the same values

Checks, run by tools/preflight.sh, by ctest (kb_layout_*, kb_examples_*) and by ci-layout.yml:

  • layout.py root: fails on a top-level entry that is not in root_dirs or root_files.
  • layout.py stale: fails when a tracked file still names a retired location; stale --fix rewrites it.

docs.title: Changing the grouping
docs.text:
1. git mv the folders (submodules included) and edit the values under layout.
  2. Add the old values under retired, then python3 tools/layout/layout.py stale --fix and review the diff.
  3. Update root_dirs if a top-level folder appeared or went, and vendor if the set of copied files changed.
  4. Run tools/preflight.sh.

docs.title: Where things moved
docs.text:
Old New lib/ components/lib/ ports/ components/ports/ drivers/ (the submodules drivers/driver-<chip> and drivers/drivers.lock.yml) components/drivers/ host/rtos/CMakeLists.txt components/ports/host/CMakeLists.txt host/rtos/README.md components/ports/host/README.md host/rtos/host_backend.cpp components/ports/host/src/host_backend.cpp schemas/ catalog/schemas/

Unchanged: .github/, .kokeb/, _config/, catalog/ (its files), cmake/, configurator/, deviations/, docs/, examples/, tests/, tools/. New: components/ (the parent of the moved folders), cmake/kb_layout.cmake, tools/layout/, tools/examples/, tools/kb/repolayout.py, examples/CMakeLists.txt, examples/examples.yml, examples/host/*, docs/examples.md, .github/workflows/ci-layout.yml.

The JSON schema $id URLs (https://kokeb-labs.github.io/kb-core/schemas/...) are published addresses, not repository paths, and did not change.

docs.title: If you keep a copy of kb-core
docs.text:
The MCU port repositories (port-esp32, port-stm32) keep an unchanged copy of the kb-core files they build against in third_party/kb-core, recorded in third_party/kb-core.lock (a repo, commit and ref line, then one <sha256> <path> line per file) and re-hashed by CMake at configure time ("kb-core copy: N files equal the lock"). The lock format does not change. What changes is the set of paths the snapshot tool (tools/kb_core_snapshot.py, its PATHS) copies, and therefore the paths inside the lock:

PATHS entry before After lib/<part>/... (utils, rtos, interfaces: CMakeLists.txt, inc, backends/none, backends/freertos, host) components/lib/<part>/... host/rtos components/ports/host cmake (esp32 port) or the listed cmake/*.cmake files (stm32 port) the same, plus cmake/kb_layout.cmake (and cmake/kb_tool_tests.cmake for a list that names files) (none) tools/layout/paths.yml, which cmake/kb_layout.cmake reads LICENSE, CMakeLists.txt, tests/harness unchanged

The count rises by two files (cmake/kb_layout.cmake, tools/layout/paths.yml); the host RTOS backend is two files before and after. The authoritative list is python3 tools/layout/layout.py vendor in the kb-core checkout, and the test kb_layout_unit copies exactly that list into an empty folder and configures it, so the list cannot go stale unnoticed. A copy without tools/layout/paths.yml stops at configure time and says so.

Other places in a consumer that name kb-core paths change the same way: layering rules that match third_party/kb-core/lib/<part>/inc/... become third_party/kb-core/components/lib/<part>/inc/... (the harness tests/harness stays), and the comment pointing at kb-core's drivers/drivers.lock.yml is now components/drivers/drivers.lock.yml. An installed kb-core package (find_package(kb)) is unaffected: install paths, targets (kb::utils, ...), headers and kbConfig.cmake did not change.

A kb-image.lock.yml written before the move records an in-tree port as ports/esp32 or lib/interfaces/host; those path values are now components/ports/esp32 and components/lib/interfaces/host. The resolver and kb upgrade write the new ones; the old values are informational only.

docs.title: Existing checkouts of kb-core
docs.text:
Driver submodules moved with git mv, so their commits and URLs are unchanged and their .gitmodules section names are kept. In a checkout that has them populated, deinitialise them before switching to a commit after the move, then initialise again:

git submodule deinit --all
git checkout <branch after the move>
git submodule update --init

docs.title: Port contracts
docs.text: kb contracts are C++20 concepts on the kb side, and only concepts (ADR-0006). Each driver keeps its own port concept, and a binding in kb::handlers satisfies the driver's port over kb contracts. MCU ports (components/ports/<mcu>/) and the host test port satisfy the kb contracts.

docs.title: What the drivers ask for
docs.text:
Every driver port is a CRTP base <chip>::<Bus>Interface<Derived> plus a concept that checks each hook's exact signature. All hooks are noexcept; every driver requires bool EnsureInitialized().

docs.title: kb contracts
docs.text:
The concepts, their members and their *Ref values are listed on the interfaces page, with the adapters that prove they serve the drivers' ports.

Concept Requires kb::iface::I2cBus EnsureReady, Write, WriteRead, Read (spans), LastFailure (None, AddressNack, DataNack, Bus, Timeout, BusStuck) kb::iface::SpiDevice EnsureReady, Transfer(tx, rx) with CS held; optional SpiClockControl kb::iface::UartPort EnsureReady, Write, Read(span, timeout) returning a count, FlushInput; optional UartBaudControl, UartTxDrain kb::iface::GpioOutput, GpioInput, GpioInterrupt Set(Level), Toggle(); Get(Level&); edge interrupts with a callback kb::iface::AdcChannel ReadRaw, ReadMillivolts, FullScale kb::iface::PwmOutput SetFrequencyHz, SetDuty(Duty), Enable kb::iface::CanBus EnsureReady, Send(frame, timeout), Receive(frame, timeout) kb::iface::MonotonicClock Now() as the 64-bit kb::Instant; bindings narrow with wrap-safe arithmetic kb::iface::BusyWait WaitUs below 1 ms; longer waits use kb::rtos::SleepFor kb::iface::LogSink Write(level, text), bounded, no allocation

The asynchronous forms I2cAsync and SpiAsync (async.hpp, ADR-0016) are the sync contracts plus Start...(deadline), Poll(now) and Cancel(); a port without a native form serves them through AsyncFromSync. Planned: PulseTx (ws2812-rmt).

docs.title: Interface rules
docs.text:
Rule Detail Concepts only No base class carries a contract; each port has static_assert(Concept<Port>) beside it; compile-fail tests reject incomplete types Run-time choice Through a type-erased *Ref (context pointer plus a constant table of function pointers), itself checked against the concept; added per contract when a HAL needs one Bus and device are separate A controller per peripheral (owns recovery and statistics) and a small device value (controller reference, address, clock, timeout) that satisfies the contract; no container of owned devices, no integer handles Every call is bounded Blocking calls take a timeout or use the device's; RecoverBus() (nine clocks and a STOP) is explicit Results kb::Result<std::size_t> for transfers, kb::Status for the rest; detail holds the vendor code Held transaction BusDomain::Hold(timeout) returns an RAII BusHold; a driver call, or a sequence of calls through Guarded::Hold() or OwnerAccess::Held(), runs inside it (two-frame reads, EEPROM ranges, se05x T=1); see bus access Asynchronous form I2cAsync, SpiAsync: Start(..., deadline), Poll(now) never waits, Cancel(); completion from the ISR by an event flag; a late completion is Timeout Buffers std::span in kb contracts; bindings adapt to the drivers' pointer-plus-length hooks

The bindings bridge the drivers' differences: start-up names (the start-up pipeline), read results (bool, size_t, BusRead{status,count}, BusStatus, RxStatus), four clock shapes, three I2C shapes, pin hooks and two log shapes. The hook bases absorb the common cases; bno08x and se05x get hand-written bindings. No driver has or needs a lock hook: locking is the access facade's job (thread models).

The se05x driver also needs host cryptography (random, hash, AES, ECDH, ECDSA); the HAL supplies the driver's crypto port directly, and kb-core defines no crypto contract.

docs.title: RTOS and SDK boundary
docs.text:
Where kb-core and its MCU ports touch a scheduler or an MCU SDK, and the rules for those files.

Folder Selected by May include components/lib/rtos/backends/none/ KB_RTOS=NONE nothing beyond the C++ subset components/lib/rtos/backends/freertos/ KB_RTOS=FREERTOS FreeRTOS headers, in its boundary .cpp files components/lib/rtos/backends/threadx/ KB_RTOS=THREADX ThreadX headers, in threadx_boundary.cpp only components/lib/interfaces/host/ always (tests, host examples) nothing beyond the C++ subset components/ports/esp32/src/ the ESP32 port project (its own CMake project) ESP-IDF headers, in its boundary .cpp files

Rules:

  • Public headers declare kb types only; backend and SDK handles live in opaque storage sized and aligned by the header.
  • A boundary file converts types and maps errors; it holds no logic that needs its own test beyond that.
  • Delays wait at least the time asked: milliseconds to ticks rounded up, plus one tick, uint32_t inputs.
  • FreeRTOS objects use the static allocation API only, ThreadX objects tx_*_create on kb-owned control blocks and stacks; no heap.
  • Calls safe from an interrupt are the ...FromIsr functions only, and each says so in its documentation.
  • FreeRTOS, ThreadX and ESP-IDF are SOUP: versions and known anomalies are recorded in the SOUP list (the port keeps its own rows when it moves out).

kb-core's boundary files are listed in deviations/boundary-files.yml and their MISRA deviations in deviations/deviations.yml; each port has the same two files in components/ports/<mcu>/deviations/ (Deviations).

docs.title: Coverage and mutation
docs.text:
• Coverage: 100 % of lines and branches of the library code (components/lib/<part>/inc, the RTOS backends) is the target and the current state. Tests pass their inputs through kb_test::Rt() (a volatile copy), so a constexpr function runs at run time and is measured, instead of being folded by the compiler.
  • Mutation: level high, enforced: every scored mutant is killed. A mutant that cannot change behaviour (an initial value every path overwrites, a comparison whose two forms agree at the only value where they differ, a compile-time margin) is listed in docs/assurance/equivalent-mutants.yml with its reason; never deleted.
  • Locally: tools/preflight.sh --container runs coverage, sanitizers and fuzzing in the CI image.
  • Hung tests: every kb-core CTest test has a TIMEOUT of KB_TEST_TIMEOUT seconds (120 by default, about ten times the slowest suite's normal run), and the preflight and container gates pass ctest --timeout 300 for the rest, so a hang fails in minutes instead of holding a runner.

docs.title: CI
docs.text:
The CI flow Figure description and sources

From the top. Every change first passes tools/preflight.sh on a workstation, then reaches CI as a pull request or push. Always run: repository checks (DCO, lint, handbook, drift), layering (include checker, CMake DAG, poison build, symbol lint), layout and examples (root allowlist, retired locations, example index), own parts (host build and tests on GCC and Clang, clang-tidy, cppcheck), MISRA at level high (CodeQL pack plus kokeb-cpp20, host and Cortex-M) and pin hygiene (gitlink, lock and a release or rc tag with a green gate, never a branch). Run when the paths under components/drivers, handlers, interfaces, ports or cmake match, and on main and tags: quality (coverage, sanitizers, fuzz, mutation kill-rate gate), integration (the binding, port, MCU and RTOS matrix from catalog/compat.yml), the ESP-IDF v5.5 build of the port and the catalogue (regenerate compat.yml, fail on drift). Never re-run for components/drivers: the drivers' own tests, fuzz, mutation, MISRA, tidy and docs, which each driver runs in its own repository and which are trusted through pin hygiene. Everything ends in one required gate, ru-ci-gate; a tag vX.Y.Z adds the release assets (per-part packages, SHA256SUMS, compat.yml, release lock, SBOM, CVE scan, licence report, provenance), and a schedule re-scans releases for known vulnerabilities and records the tested version set kb YYYY.N.

Drawn from: docs/model/ci-flow.graph.yml.

Check Workflow ci-tools reusable workflow Host build, tests, clang-tidy, cppcheck ci-host.yml ru-host-ci Coverage, sanitizers, fuzz, complexity (level high) ci-quality.yml ru-host-quality MISRA C++:2023 and KB-CPP20 (level high) ci-misra.yml ru-misra Cortex-M cross build ci-cross-build.yml ru-cross-build ESP32 port and its examples ci-esp32.yml ru-build Docs ci-docs.yml ru-mkdocs-publish DCO, org standard, lint, handbook, drift ci-repo-checks.yml ru-repo-checks Each part alone, install consumers ci-standalone.yml ru-cmake-matrix Integration of pinned drivers ci-integration.yml ru-cmake-matrix, ru-host-ci Mutation ci-mutation.yml ru-mutation Pin hygiene ci-pins.yml ru-pin-hygiene Layering and poison build ci-layering.yml ru-layering compat.yml ci-catalog.yml ru-catalog Layout allowlist, retired locations, example index ci-layout.yml - (tools/layout, tools/examples) Release lock, SBOM, CVE scan, licence report release.yml ru-release-evidence

Not re-run for driver content: unit tests, coverage, mutation, fuzzing, MISRA, clang-tidy, cppcheck, complexity and handbook checks of the drivers. Each pinned driver passed them in its own CI at its release tag; pin hygiene proves the pin is that tag (ADR-0004).

docs.title: Versioning and release
docs.text:
• One version for all of kb-core, set only in cmake/kb_version.cmake and carried by every part's package (find_package(kb 0.1 COMPONENTS utils rtos)). Semantic Versioning over the union of the parts: a breaking change in any part is a major (before 1.0: a minor) for all. While components/ports/esp32/ lives here it is released with kb-core; after it moves out it has its own version (ADR-0007).
  • CHANGELOG.md keeps one [Unreleased] with a section per part, one for the ESP32 port and one for driver pins.
  • Driver pins (ADR-0002, ADR-0012): every pin is the commit of a vX.Y.Z or vX.Y.Z-rc.N tag whose CI passed, never a branch. A bump is one pull request with the gitlink, the components/drivers/drivers.lock.yml entry, binding and test changes, the regenerated catalog/compat.yml and a CHANGELOG line.
  • Release: tag vX.Y.Z (release candidates vX.Y.Z-rc.N first) on a green main. The release carries one package per part, SHA256SUMS, compat.yml, signed build provenance and the release evidence:
File What kb-core-<version>.lock.yml kb-core's own tag and commit SHA, every pin (tag, commit, release or rc), the toolchain and SOUP versions CI used, the SHA-256 of every release file kb-core-<version>.spdx.json, kb-core-<version>.cdx.json SBOM in SPDX 2.3 and CycloneDX 1.6 kb-core-<version>.cve.json Known-CVE scan of the SBOM, with scan date and database version (re-scanned on a schedule) kb-core-<version>.licences.md Licence report: each component's SPDX licence and copyright holder
  • A driver states the oldest kb-core it needs in its driver.yml (kb_core_min); a pin whose kb_core_min is above the kb-core being built fails CI.
  • Later: tested version sets kb YYYY.N, the kb tool with kb-image.yml, and the hosted configurator, all reading the catalogue, the release lock and the evidence (Configurator).

docs.title: Architecture decision records
docs.text:
Decisions of kb-core, one file each, numbered in order and never reused. A decision is changed by a new record that supersedes or amends the old one; the old record stays. Handbook decisions are cited as "handbook ADR-NNNN".

ADR Decision Status ADR-0001 Layering rule and its enforcement Accepted; rule 2 amended by ADR-0007 ADR-0002 Drivers are consumed as submodules pinned to release tags Accepted; sharpened by ADR-0012, amended by ADR-0014 ADR-0003 Concepts for contracts, CRTP only for shared behaviour Superseded by ADR-0006 ADR-0004 CI: what kb-core runs and what it trusts from driver CI Accepted; level set by ADR-0011 ADR-0005 No code is ported from older stacks Accepted ADR-0006 Interface contracts are C++20 concepts only; a register of permitted bases Accepted ADR-0007 MCU ports start isolated in components/ports/<mcu>/, ready to move out Accepted ADR-0008 Repository names of the kb family Accepted; amended 2026-11-14 (brandless port-<family>) ADR-0009 Handler thread models, declared per bus Accepted ADR-0010 Handler start-up is a pipeline of declared stages Accepted ADR-0011 Assurance level high; drivers and handlers are not the safety layer Accepted ADR-0012 Pins to release or rc tags only; release lock with its own SHA Accepted; amended by ADR-0014 ADR-0013 Hosted configurator with repeatable, pinned projects and evidence Accepted; amended by ADR-0014 ADR-0014 kb-core is the assembler: own libraries plus a manifest and lock of pinned parts, one resolver Accepted ADR-0015 Eclipse ThreadX is a supported kb::rtos backend, its kernel a pinned SOUP submodule Accepted ADR-0016 Non-blocking bus access (Start/Poll) and held bus transactions (BusHold) Proposed ADR-0017 A kb::rtos object's destructor deletes its native object (one delete call per kind in the backend seam) Accepted ADR-0030 DMA buffers are owned by the CPU or the device and move by a lease; a cancel that cannot be confirmed quarantines (number provisional) Accepted ADR-0031 Streams copy frames out of the DMA ring and say what they lost (number provisional) Accepted ADR-0032 A region states its cache policy; the default is non-cacheable (number provisional) Accepted

Format: Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives considered.

docs.title: ADR-0001: Layering rule and enforcement
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-14). Rule 2 amended by ADR-0007 (MCU ports in components/ports/<mcu>/).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Layered embedded stacks often state a platform-free rule without checking it. In one earlier stack an audit found more than twenty places where platform or product code had leaked into handlers and libraries, and none was caught because every MCU branch compiled out in the host build. Applications could also include interface headers directly, so the HAL was not the only way to hardware.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Dependencies point down only: kb::utils <- kb::rtos <- kb::interfaces <- kb::handlers. Applications may use kb::utils and kb::rtos; kb::interfaces and kb::handlers are for the HAL only.
  2. SDK and RTOS headers are allowed only in the .cpp boundary files listed in a boundary-files.yml: kb-core's own list (deviations/boundary-files.yml, RTOS backends in components/lib/rtos/backends/<rtos>/) and each MCU port's list (components/ports/<mcu>/deviations/boundary-files.yml). No #if on a platform macro elsewhere.
  3. Independent checks, each able to fail CI: CMake visibility (backends PRIVATE; HALs link interfaces and handlers PRIVATE; a port sees kb-core only through its installed package), the include and dependency checker (tools/include_checker/), the poison build (tests/poison/) and a symbol lint on linked objects.
  4. Board and product values reach kb-core only as configuration.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A leak is a CI failure, not a review comment. HALs reuse the same checker with their own zone file.
  • The few boundary files concentrate every SDK call and every MISRA deviation, so review effort goes there.
  • Some convenience is lost: a HAL cannot re-export interface headers to its applications.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Review only: failed before. CMake visibility only: does not stop include-by-path or a public header leak.
  • One target for all of kb-core: simpler to consume, but cannot express "applications may use utils and rtos only".

docs.title: ADR-0002: Driver consumption
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-14). Pin rules sharpened by ADR-0012; the pins are part of the assembler manifest of ADR-0014.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Drivers are separate repositories with their own CI and release tags. Pinning them through an aggregate repository that is itself a submodule of the core makes one driver change take two or three pull requests with a merge order and a re-pin after merge. kb-core must also serve ESP-IDF, host and later STM32 builds, and its configuration must be reproducible and archivable.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Drivers are git submodules under components/drivers/driver-<chip>/, each pinned to the commit of a release tag or release-candidate tag whose CI passed, never a branch (ADR-0012). components/drivers/drivers.lock.yml records repository, tag and commit; CI checks it against the gitlink and the driver's driver.yml (ADR-0004). KB_DRIVER_<CHIP>_DIR lets a consumer supply a driver from elsewhere (its own checkout, a FetchContent result, an ESP-IDF managed component). Only enabled drivers are initialised, without --recursive.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A driver bump is one kb-core pull request. The pin is a commit in kb-core's own history, auditable and buildable offline.
  • Consumers run one more command (git submodule update --init ...); the configurator writes it for them (ADR-0013).
  • Registry publication (ESP-IDF component manager) remains possible on top, without changing kb-core.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Option Why not the default Pinned FetchContent Network at configure time, cache handling inside ESP-IDF, pin in CMake text instead of git history ESP-IDF component manifest ESP-IDF only; host and STM32 need another path; every driver must publish first Vendored copies A driver fix would be made twice, and the copy drifts from the released driver

docs.title: ADR-0003: Concepts for contracts, CRTP only for shared behaviour
docs.text:
Status: Superseded by ADR-0006.

This record is kept as written so the history of the decision stays readable. ADR-0006 keeps its core (concepts for every contract, no virtual functions, CRTP only where a base adds shared behaviour), makes it C++20 only, adds a register of the permitted base classes with the reason for each, names how a HAL makes a run-time choice without a virtual function, and records how kb-core relates to handbook ADR-0016.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The drivers define their ports as a CRTP base plus a concept that checks exact hook signatures, with no virtual functions (handbook ADR-0003). Earlier layered stacks used abstract base classes with virtual functions for buses and CRTP adapter bases for driver hooks. kb-core needs contracts for buses and pins that cost nothing at run time and fail at compile time when a port is incomplete.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Every kb contract (kb::iface::I2cBus, SpiDevice, UartPort, ...) is a concept only, with no base class. A port satisfies it; a conformance static_assert per port proves it.
  • CRTP is used only where the base adds shared behaviour: the per-bus hook bases in kb::handlers, the kb::rtos thread base and the handler base. A base that would only forward calls is not written.
  • No virtual functions in any part. Where type erasure is unavoidable it is a function pointer plus a context pointer, at one named place.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Static dispatch everywhere; errors in a port show at compile time with the concept's name.
  • Generic code over contracts is templated; build times are watched, and headers stay small.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Abstract base classes (virtual dispatch, a vtable per port, against the profile); CRTP everywhere (forwarding boilerplate with no behaviour, and harder diagnostics than concepts).

docs.title: ADR-0004: CI strategy, what kb-core runs and what it trusts
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-14). Assurance level set by ADR-0011 (high).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Each driver passes its own full CI before a release tag: host tests, coverage, sanitizers, fuzzing, MISRA, clang-tidy, cppcheck, complexity, handbook check, cross and ESP32 builds, plus mutation runs and independent review in its pipeline. Re-running all of that in kb-core for every driver would cost CI minutes and add no evidence about the same commit.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
kb-core runs:

  1. Its own parts at full rigor for level high (ADR-0011): host tests with two compilers, clang-tidy and cppcheck, coverage gates, sanitizers, fuzzing, complexity, mutation testing, MISRA C++:2023 with KB-CPP20 on host and Cortex-M, standalone build of each part and install consumers.
  2. Integration: compile and link of every binding over every port and allowed MCU/RTOS configuration; host tests that drive each driver through its kb binding with the driver's chip model; the ESP-IDF build of the ESP32 port and its examples, as the port's own job (ADR-0007).
  3. Pin hygiene: each pin equals a release or release-candidate tag whose CI gate passed, and that tag's driver.yml agrees with the lock file, the MCU gate table and this kb-core version (ADR-0012).
  4. The include and dependency checker, the poison build and the symbol lint; catalog/compat.yml generation; docs; DCO and org standard checks.
  5. Release evidence on every tag: the release lock, the SBOM, the known-CVE scan and the licence report (ADR-0012, ADR-0013).

kb-core does not re-run for driver content: driver unit tests, coverage, mutation, fuzzing, MISRA, clang-tidy, cppcheck, complexity, handbook and docs checks. kb-core's analysers restrict their reported paths to components/lib/ (and each port's job to its own folder). The trust is conditional: pin hygiene is the proof that the pinned commit is the one that passed.

Every check is a thin caller of a kokeb-labs/ci-tools reusable workflow. New reusable workflows needed in ci-tools: ru-mutation, ru-cmake-matrix, ru-pin-hygiene, ru-layering, ru-catalog, ru-release-evidence.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• CI time is spent on kb-core's own code and on the joints between kb-core and drivers, where new defects live.
  • A pin to an untested commit or a branch cannot pass. A driver whose CI was weaker than required at its tag is caught by the handbook level check of pin hygiene.
  • Until the pending reusable workflows exist, those checks run locally only; their caller files are present but not called from ci.yml.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Re-running driver CI inside kb-core (double cost, same evidence); trusting pins without checking (an untested or retagged commit could slip in).

docs.title: ADR-0005: No code is ported from older stacks
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-14).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Older embedded stacks exist that hold useful ideas (one build entry point with an MCU gate table, adapter bases for driver hooks, lazy initialisation, compiled documentation snippets) and known defect classes (platform leaks, round-down delays, heap use, several handler shapes, untested ports). Their code was not written under the current pipeline, standard or licence.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: kb-core code is written fresh under the driver pipeline: design, build with tests and fuzz targets, self-review against the defect catalogue, the local gate, independent review, fixes. Older code is at most a source of ideas and requirements; its defect classes become test cases. No file, function or block is copied from it, and nothing that identifies it, its products or its people appears in kb-core.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every line of kb-core has the same provenance, licence (MIT, "The kb-core authors") and evidence trail, which configuration management and independent review need.
  • Delivery is slower than a port; the migration order (utils, rtos, interfaces, bindings, handlers) delivers usable parts early.
  • Hardware evidence from older code is used as requirements (timings, failure modes), not as proof for new code; new code needs its own bench runs.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: A scripted rename port (fast, but carries every known defect and an unclear provenance); a partial port of "good" files (no clean line between good and bad, and review would have to treat every file as new anyway).

docs.title: ADR-0006: Interface contracts are C++20 concepts only
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-13). Supersedes ADR-0003.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
kb-core needs contracts for buses, pins, clocks and logs that cost nothing at run time, fail at compile time with a readable message when a port is incomplete, and match the drivers, whose ports are a CRTP base plus a concept that checks every hook's exact signature (handbook ADR-0003).

Two facts pulled the other way. Handbook ADR-0016 allows virtual functions at three run-time boundaries and names two of them inside kb-core: Base* peripheral interfaces in interfaces/base/ and a virtual BaseThread with a threads manager. And a real board can mix two implementations of one contract, such as a GpioOutput that is an MCU pin for one chip and an I/O-expander pin for another. A design revision therefore proposed a concept plus a small abstract Base* class for every contract. The owner decided against it: one contract per bus, written once, in modern C++20.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. C++20, and only C++20. kb-core is written for C++20 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20, required, no extensions). There is no fallback for an older standard and no test of __cplusplus to select one.
  2. Every contract is a concept in kb::iface (I2cBus, SpiDevice, UartPort, GpioOutput, GpioInput, AdcChannel, CanBus, PulseTx, MonotonicClock, BusyWait, LogSink, ...). No base class carries a contract. Every port proves conformance with a static_assert(kb::iface::I2cBus<Port>) beside its definition, and compile-fail tests prove that incomplete types are rejected.
  3. No virtual functions in kb-core. kb-core uses none of the virtual boundaries handbook ADR-0016 permits: there are no Base* interface classes, and kb::rtos threads are a CRTP base, not a virtual BaseThread. A registry of threads holds non-virtual control blocks (stack statistics, liveness, a stop flag), never pointers to a polymorphic base.
  4. A base class exists only where shared behaviour truly needs it, and each one is a row of the register below with its reason. A base that would only forward calls is never written. Adding a row needs a new ADR or an amendment of this one.
Base class Kind Why it needs a base kb::handlers::I2cHooks<Derived, Bus>, SpiHooks, UartHooks, AdcHooks, GpioHooks CRTP They implement a driver's hooks once for every chip on that bus: failure recording, counters, the at-least delay split (busy-wait below 1 ms, kb::rtos::SleepFor from 1 ms) and clock narrowing with wrap-safe arithmetic. Without them every binding repeats four pieces of correctness-critical code kb::rtos::Thread<Derived, StackBytes> CRTP The run loop, fixed-rate waiting with overrun counting, stop handling, step-time statistics and the liveness beat are written once; a derived thread supplies only Setup, Step and Cleanup kb::handlers::HandlerCore<Derived, Driver> CRTP The lifecycle state machine, the health record and the start-up pipeline runner (ADR-0010) are written once for every handler
  1. Run-time choice without virtual functions. Where a HAL must choose an implementation at run time, it uses a type-erased reference from kb::iface (GpioOutputRef, I2cBusRef, LogSinkRef, ...): a non-owning value holding a context pointer and a pointer to a constant table of function pointers, produced from any type that satisfies the concept by one template, and itself checked with static_assert against the same concept. A *Ref is added for a contract only when a HAL needs one; each is listed in the contract's documentation as a type-erasure point.

docs.title: Relation to handbook ADR-0016
docs.text: Handbook ADR-0016 permits virtual functions at its three boundaries; it does not require them. kb-core is stricter, which the handbook check accepts: .kokeb/handbook.yml lists no virtual-boundary folder, so the virtual-outside-interfaces check rejects any virtual anywhere in kb-core. Two statements of the handbook no longer describe kb-core and are proposed for amendment: boundary 1 (Base* interfaces in kb-core's interfaces/base/) and the kb-core half of boundary 3 (BaseThread, BaseThreadsManager). Boundary 2 (kb-hal-common's managers and sinks) is outside kb-core and unchanged. The layout of handbook ADR-0013 (interfaces/base/, interfaces/mcu/<family>/) is amended by ADR-0007.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
