• One contract per bus, written once; nothing can drift between a concept and a parallel class.
  • Static dispatch everywhere; an incomplete port fails at compile time with the concept's name.
  • A run-time choice costs one indirect call per operation and is visible in the code as a *Ref.
  • The MISRA C++:2023 rules on virtual functions and hierarchies never apply to kb-core code.
  • Generic code over contracts is templated; build times are watched and headers stay small.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Option Why not Concept plus a small abstract Base* per contract Two forms of each contract to keep in step; a vtable per port; rejected by the owner Abstract base classes only Virtual dispatch on every transfer and no compile-time check of the hook signatures CRTP base for every contract Forwarding boilerplate with no behaviour, and harder diagnostics than concepts std::function or a virtual adapter for run-time choice Allocation or a vtable; the *Ref gives the same choice without either

docs.title: ADR-0007: MCU ports start isolated in components/ports/<mcu>/, ready to move to their own repositories
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-13). Amends ADR-0001 rule 2 and the layout of handbook ADR-0013 (interfaces/mcu/<family>/).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: An MCU port implements kb-core's contracts over one vendor SDK. It has a different toolchain, SDK container, CI, SOUP list and MISRA deviation posture from the platform-free parts, and its release cadence follows the SDK, not kb-core. Keeping ports inside components/lib/interfaces/ couples all of that to kb-core: every SDK container in kb-core's CI, an SDK bump forcing a kb-core release, every family's deviations in kb-core's records. Moving a port out later is cheap only if the seam exists from the first commit. While the contracts are still changing, a separate repository would turn every contract change into two pull requests.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Each MCU family port lives in components/ports/<mcu>/ in kb-core, starting with components/ports/esp32/. It is built as its own CMake project (project(kb_port_<mcu>)) that uses kb-core only through the installed package (find_package(kb CONFIG REQUIRED COMPONENTS interfaces rtos utils)), and under ESP-IDF as its own component (kb_port_esp32). It never uses a kb-core source path, a private header or a kb-core CMake variable.
  2. Everything a separate repository would need is already per port: README.md, CMakeLists.txt, inc/kb/port/<mcu>/ (namespace kb::port::<mcu>, target kb::port_<mcu>), src/ with the boundary files, deviations/ (its own boundary-files.yml and deviations.yml, ids DEV-KBP-<MCU>-NNN), examples/, its own CI caller and its own SOUP rows.
  3. The include checker refuses an include from components/lib/ into components/ports/ and from components/ports/ into anything of kb-core but the public kb/<part>/ headers (LAY-010, LAY-011). kb-core's own CMake never adds an MCU port as a subdirectory.
  4. The host port is not an MCU port: it is platform-free test doubles with fault injection that every test needs, so it stays in kb-core as components/lib/interfaces/host/ (target kb::interfaces_host), and its std::thread RTOS backend is components/ports/host/ (target kb_rtos_backend_host), the one folder of the ports tree that kb-core's own CMake adds (amended by the repository layout, layout). RTOS backends stay in kb-core (components/lib/rtos/backends/<rtos>/): the RTOS API does not depend on the MCU.
  5. Extraction: when the contracts are stable (M4 exit: interfaces at v0.4 and the first bindings proven on the bench), components/ports/esp32/ moves with its history (git filter-repo --subdirectory-filter components/ports/esp32) to port-esp32 (ADR-0008), which then versions on its own; kb-core drops the folder and catalog/compat.yml gains a kb-core x port compatibility row. New families (STM32) start directly in their own repository. The decision to extract, or to wait, is recorded when M4 ends.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• kb-core's assurance scope ends at the SDK seam; each port carries its own SDK, toolchain, CI, deviations and SOUP list.
  • Until extraction, one pull request can change a contract and its ESP32 port together.
  • After extraction a contract change is a kb-core release plus a port pull request, and the board HAL pins one kb-core and one port.
  • KB_MCU in kb-core still selects the MCU gate and the default RTOS, but no MCU source is compiled by kb-core.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Option Why not Ports inside components/lib/interfaces/ports/<mcu>/ (the first skeleton, handbook ADR-0013) SDK containers, SDK-driven releases and every family's deviations inside kb-core One kb-ports repository for all families The same coupling between families, moved one repository over A repository per family from day one Two pull requests for every contract change while the contracts are still moving

docs.title: ADR-0008: Repository names of the kb family
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-13); amended 2026-11-14 (port repositories are brandless and live in kokeb-labs-drivers, see Amendment). Proposed names only: this record creates no repository.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: kb-core will be surrounded by MCU port repositories (ADR-0007), reference board HALs, a hosted configurator (ADR-0013) and possibly a home for tested version sets. The drivers already have a scheme (kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-<chip>, brand-free, handbook ADR-0012). Names chosen one at a time drift; a name also fixes the namespace, CMake target, package and include root that users type.

docs.title: Names
docs.text: Repository Organisation Holds Examples kb-core kokeb-labs kb::utils, kb::rtos, kb::interfaces (contracts and host port), kb::handlers, driver pins, catalogue kb-core port-<family> kokeb-labs-drivers One MCU family port: the contracts implemented over that SDK, its boundary files, examples, SOUP list port-esp32, port-stm32 kb-hal-common kokeb-labs Shared HAL bases (handbook ADR-0005) kb-hal-common kb-board-<board> kokeb-labs A reference board HAL for a public development or evaluation board kb-board-esp32s3-devkitc kb-configurator kokeb-labs The hosted configurator site and its resolver kb-configurator kb-app-template kokeb-labs The starter project the configurator fills kb-app-template kb-trains kokeb-labs Tested version sets (kb YYYY.N) and their evidence, only if they outgrow the configurator repository kb-trains driver-<chip> kokeb-labs-drivers Brand-free chip drivers (unchanged) driver-bno08x board-<name> a product organisation A product's own board HAL; not part of the kb family, so no kb- prefix board-<name>

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. Lower case, words separated by -, ASCII only. No product, customer or person name in any repository name.
  2. The kb- prefix is reserved for repositories the kb family releases from kokeb-labs; nothing else uses it. Repositories in kokeb-labs-drivers (drivers and MCU ports) are brandless and carry no kb- prefix.
  3. <family> is the lower-case KB_MCU value and names an SDK family, not a chip: port-esp32 serves every ESP32 target (esp32, esp32s3, esp32c6, ...) as targets inside one repository.
  4. <board> is the vendor's board name, lower case, without the vendor's punctuation.
  5. Each repository's name fixes its code names:
Repository Namespace CMake target Package Include root ESP-IDF component kb-core kb, kb::utils, kb::rtos, kb::iface, kb::handlers kb::utils, kb::rtos, kb::interfaces, kb::handlers kb (components) kb/<part>/ kb port-<family> kb::port::<family> kb::port_<family> kb_port_<family> kb/port/<family>/ kb_port_<family> kb-board-<board> kb::board::<board_with_underscores> kb::board_<board> kb_board_<board> kb/board/<board>/ kb_board_<board>
  1. Every repository tags vX.Y.Z and vX.Y.Z-rc.N only, publishes its site at https://kokeb-labs.github.io/<repository>/, is MIT with copyright "The <repository> authors", and uses kokeblabs@gmail.com as its only public address.

Figure: repository family.

docs.title: Amendment (2026-11-14)
docs.text:
Owner decision: less branding on the repositories that sit beside the drivers.

  1. MCU port repositories are brandless and live in the kokeb-labs-drivers organisation, next to the drivers they serve: kokeb-labs-drivers/port-<family> (port-esp32, port-stm32). The earlier name kb-port-<family> in kokeb-labs is withdrawn.
  2. Their code names do not change: namespace kb::port::<family>, CMake target kb::port_<family>, package kb_port_<family>, include root kb/port/<family>/, ESP-IDF component kb_port_<family>. The code says which contracts it implements; the repository name says what it is. The in-repository port (components/ports/esp32/) already uses these code names, so extraction still renames nothing.
  3. kb-core keeps its name and stays in kokeb-labs, with the other kb- repositories of the table.
  4. Pins of an extracted port follow the driver rules (ADR-0012): a vX.Y.Z or vX.Y.Z-rc.N tag, recorded by repository, tag and commit in the lock (ADR-0014).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A user can tell from a name what a repository holds and which code names it brings.
  • The in-repository port already uses its future code names (kb::port::esp32, kb::port_esp32), so extraction renames nothing; only the repository is named port-esp32.
  • Creating any of these repositories is a separate owner decision; until then only kb-core exists.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Option Why not kb-esp32, kb-stm32 Does not say it is a port; collides with a later board or example repository One repository per chip variant (port-esp32s3) Duplicates the SDK seam per variant; the SDK already abstracts the variants kb-hal-<board> for reference boards "HAL" is already the name of the layer every board has; board says what it is Configurator inside kb-core permanently Its release cadence and web toolchain differ; it starts there only as a skeleton

docs.title: ADR-0009: Handler thread models, declared per bus
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-13).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Drivers are not thread-safe and take no lock; the layer that owns a driver owns its lock and the bus lock (every driver contract says so). Two ways of sharing a bus work in practice. One owner task per bus that serves every device on it and publishes snapshots removes most locks and priority inversion, and suits high-rate or timing-critical devices. A lock taken around each call suits slow, sporadic devices (an EEPROM, an I/O expander, a power IC) used from several tasks. Mixing the two on one bus is where trouble starts: a lock-free owner and a locking caller on the same wires. Some chips also need continuous servicing (bno08x streams reports and completes commands asynchronously), so they cannot be served by occasional locked calls. Callers on other tasks should not have to change their code when a bus moves from one model to the other.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. The handler core (kb::handlers::HandlerCore<Derived, Driver>) is single-threaded by construction: it holds no lock and must only be called from one context at a time. Thread safety is added around it by exactly one of two access facades, chosen by the thread model of its bus.
  2. Each bus declares its thread model in the board configuration, and the type says it: kb::handlers::BusDomain<Bus, ThreadModel::Owner> or BusDomain<Bus, ThreadModel::Guarded>. A handler's facade must match its bus's model; a mismatch is a compile error, and the image check refuses a bus declared with both.
  3. Model O, owner task (the default for real-time buses): one kb::rtos::Thread owns the bus and calls Service(now) on each of its handlers every step. Service runs any pending start-up stage, drains the handler's command queue (a bounded number per step), runs the periodic work and publishes a SeqlockSnapshot. Other tasks use OwnerAccess<H>: Latest() returns a lock-free copy of the newest snapshot with its sequence number and age; Request(command, timeout) posts to the bounded queue and waits for the owner's completion, returning Busy when the queue is full and Timeout when the owner does not finish in time. A debug-build check asserts that Service runs on the owner task. LockPolicy is None: the bus has no mutex.
  4. Model G, guarded facade (slow, sporadic devices used by several tasks): Guarded<H> owns the handler and is the only way to reach it. Every operation Call(timeout, operation, args...) takes the handler's mutex, then the BusDomain mutex, both with bounded TryLockFor, runs the single-threaded call and releases both. The lock order is fixed (handler, then bus), a lock is never held across another handler or a user callback, and a call that cannot get both locks in time returns Timeout and sends nothing. This lets several tasks use a handler safely without any of them owning the bus.
  5. One caller API. OwnerAccess<H> and Guarded<H> expose the same typed operations to callers (each a kb::Result with a timeout), so HAL managers and application code do not change when a bus changes model. Health() is lock-free (a seqlock snapshot) in both models.
  6. A chip that must be serviced continuously declares it in its binding (kRequiresOwner = true, bno08x); its handler cannot be wrapped in Guarded<H> (compile error).
  7. Interrupts never call handlers: an ISR sets an event flag or notifies the owner task.

Figure: handler thread models.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A bus has one locking story, visible in its type; mixing models on one bus cannot compile.
  • Real-time buses carry no mutex and no priority inversion; slow devices stay simple to call from anywhere.
  • Request on an owner bus costs one queue round trip; callers that only need data read Latest().
  • The handler core is tested once, single-threaded; the two facades are tested separately (TSan on the FreeRTOS POSIX port, lock-order and timeout tests).

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Option Why not Shared mutex only Priority inversion and lock traffic on real-time buses; cannot serve chips that need continuous polling Owner task only Forces a task per bus for a single EEPROM read now and then Handler with a built-in recursive lock Hides the locking model; recursive locks mask lock-order defects A raw bus-mutex pointer passed to each handler No owner for recovery and statistics; replaced by BusDomain

docs.title: ADR-0010: Handler start-up is a pipeline of declared stages
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-13).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Handbook ADR-0021 makes EnsureInitialized() the one start-up entry point of drivers and handlers: idempotent, retried from scratch after a failure, and never hidden inside a read. Twenty-one drivers follow it directly. Two chips start differently, for reasons in the chips themselves:

  • bno08x (sensor hub, SHTP): Begin(config) validates the configuration, brings the port up and starts the reset (an NRST pulse when the port has the SetReset hook) and returns at once. Poll(now_us) then runs the reset wait, the hub's advertisement and the initialise handshake; Ready() turns true when the session is up, and each wait is bounded by Config::startup_timeout_ms (the driver enters Faulted when one expires). Every command afterwards completes asynchronously as an OpDone event. Begin() called again starts a new session.
  • se05x (secure element, T=1 over I2C): Open() validates the configuration, opens the link, reads the card identification data, selects the IoT applet, reads its feature bits, runs the capability probes, reads the lifecycle state and opens platform SCP03 when the policy or the chip requires it, each wait bounded by the link. The platform SCP03 key handles are given before, without I/O (SetPlatformKeys()). Open() on an open device returns WrongState; Close() ends it; Recover() climbs the driver's own recovery ladder; PowerCycle() is available with a reset port.

A handler that special-cases these two in code would grow a third and fourth shape with the next chip. The pipeline should be one runner over a declared plan, with a waiver only where a chip truly cannot fit.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Every handler's EnsureInitialized() runs its chip's start-up plan, a constexpr list of stages declared in the binding (kStartupPlan). The runner is written once, in HandlerCore.
  2. Stage kinds, in this order (a plan lists only the ones its chip needs):
Kind Does Typical driver call Power Enable a rail or an enable pin, wait its settle time HAL pin through the binding HostReset Host-driven reset: pulse, hold, release the driver's reset hook, or Begin() Boot Wait the boot time or a ready condition (ready pin, advertisement) Poll() until ready Link Bring up a transport session (T=1, SHTP) inside Open() or Poll() Identify Read the ID, select an applet, probe capabilities EnsureInitialized(), Open() Secure Open a secure channel needed for normal use (platform SCP03) inside Open() Configure Apply the configuration EnsureInitialized(), SetFeature() ops Verify Read back, check the lifecycle state a read
  1. Each stage declares: its kind (one or more), the driver call, sync (one call) or polled (repeated until done), its deadline (a configuration field, never a constant inside kb-core), and whether it is optional (skipped when the HAL supplies no pin, rail or key for it). One driver call may cover several kinds; the plan says which.
  2. The runner records a StartupReport (the stage reached, kb::Status, the driver's error in detail, the time each stage took). On a failure it runs the plan's abort call (if any), destroys the driver and stays Constructed, so the next EnsureInitialized() starts again from the first stage (handbook ADR-0021).
  3. Both thread models use the same plan (ADR-0009). StartStep(now) runs at most one step of the current stage and returns Pending, Ok or the failure, so an owner task never blocks on a start-up. EnsureInitialized() is the loop over StartStep(), waiting with kb::rtos::SleepFor between polls, bounded by the sum of the stage deadlines; under Guarded<H> it holds the guarded locks for that bound.
  4. The plans:
Chip Plan 21 drivers Identify + Configure = driver.EnsureInitialized() (sync); optional Power and HostReset when the HAL supplies the pin and the driver does not drive it itself bno08x HostReset (or Link without NRST) = Begin(cfg) (sync); Boot + Link = Poll(now) until Ready() (polled, deadline from startup_timeout_ms, fails on Faulted); Configure = one SetFeature per configured sensor, polled until each OpDone (deadline from op_timeout_ms) se05x Secure keys = SetPlatformKeys() (sync, no I/O, optional); Link + Identify + Secure = Open() (sync, bounded by the link), skipped when IsOpen(); Verify = lifecycle state against the HAL's expectation (optional)
  1. Recovery is per plan too: the generic plan recovers with Deinitialize() then the plan; se05x calls the driver's Recover() (its ladder) before Close() and a full plan; bno08x reports a hub restart as a Reset event (health Degraded, the driver restores its sensors) and re-runs the plan only after Faulted.

docs.title: What does not fit, and the waivers
docs.text:
Both chips fit the handler pipeline; no handler-level waiver is needed. Two things stay outside it:

  • Applet sessions of se05x (UserID, AESKey, ECKey) are not a start-up stage: they need credentials per use and the chip allows one at a time, so the handler opens them per transaction, inside a held bus transaction.
  • The driver APIs themselves differ from handbook ADR-0021, and changing them would break what the chips need:
Waiver Driver Differs from handbook ADR-0021 Why it cannot change Absorbed by W-01 driver-bno08x Start is Begin(config) plus Poll(now), not EnsureInitialized(); Begin() again restarts a running session The hub starts asynchronously and must be polled; a blocking start would hold the bus for the whole reset and handshake The handler's plan; EnsureInitialized() is idempotent at the handler W-02 driver-se05x Start is Open(), stop Close(); Open() on an open device returns WrongState Open and close are session operations of the secure element (link, applet, secure channel), not a chip configuration The handler's plan skips Open() when IsOpen()

The waivers are recorded here for kb-core; each driver repository records its own in its next release.

docs.title: Amendment 1 (2026-11-14): one stage per kind
docs.text:
A plan lists each kind once, in kind order, and HandlerCore checks that at compile time. Two plan rows above name a kind twice, so they are written as follows; the calls and their order are unchanged:

  • se05x: SetPlatformKeys() (no I/O, only when the HAL supplies key handles) is the first call of the Link + Identify + Secure stage, before Open().
  • bno08x without NRST: Link = Begin(cfg) (sync), Identify = Poll(now) until Ready() (polled), then Configure. With NRST the plan is as in the table.

Figures: start-up pipeline and lifecycle.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One start-up runner, tested once; a new chip with a different start adds a plan, not a handler shape.
  • Every start-up failure names its stage, which is what bench debugging needs first.
  • Owner tasks never block on a start-up; guarded callers get a bounded, blocking EnsureInitialized().
  • bno08x requires an owner bus (ADR-0009, kRequiresOwner).

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Option Why not Hand-written start-up per special chip A new handler shape per special chip; nothing shared to test Change bno08x and se05x to a blocking EnsureInitialized() Breaks released drivers and blocks a bus for a whole handshake Waivers only, no pipeline Leaves the two chips outside the uniform handler API

docs.title: ADR-0011: Assurance level high; drivers and handlers are not the safety layer
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-13). Sets the level used by ADR-0004.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The first skeleton declared kb-core at the handbook's safety level. That level asks for a commercial MISRA checker run, requirements traced to code and tests, every reachable branch covered and a signed evidence package per release, and the handbook allows it only per component, by a decision record, when a product team intends to qualify that component. The handbook puts drivers and kb-core at high from their first release. No commercial checker is available today. More importantly, a safety function must not depend on a bus transfer succeeding: a driver or a handler can fail, block until its timeout or report stale data, so neither can be the layer that keeps a product safe.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. kb-core declares level high (.kokeb/handbook.yml), and every reusable workflow it calls runs at high.
  2. Drivers and handlers are not the safety layer. Safety functions (reaching the safe state, independent monitoring, the decision to kick a watchdog) belong to the product's safety layer, which must reach its safe state without any driver or handler call succeeding (it cuts outputs first and never waits on a bus). kb-core provides building blocks with documented, bounded behaviour (bounded waits, health states, liveness beats) that a safety layer may use as inputs, at the evidence level of high.
  3. MISRA C++:2023 evidence at high: the CodeQL MISRA C++:2023 pack and the org's kokeb-cpp20 profile pack on host and Cortex-M builds, plus kb-core's compliance matrix (handbook misra_matrix.py) that states, for every guideline, how it is met: CodeQL, the profile pack, compiler warnings, sanitizers, coverage, fuzzing, mutation testing, or review. One recorded library deviation above the boundary files, DEV-KBC-004 (see the amendment below); each boundary file's findings are recorded deviations.
  4. safety stays a later option, to be taken per component by a new ADR when a product intends to qualify it and a MISRA checker accepted for that purpose has been obtained. Candidates to price (the owner decides): a commercial MISRA C++:2023 checker with a perpetual or low-cost licence, run locally before a release and reconciled with the CodeQL results in the compliance matrix. Until then nothing in kb-core claims the safety level or a safety class.
  5. Drivers stay at high; pin hygiene requires high or above at every pinned tag.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The CI configuration is level: high in ci-misra.yml, ci-quality.yml and ci-mutation.yml; the coverage, complexity and fuzz limits are the handbook's for high. kb-core's own exit criteria per part may be stricter (see the plan), as goals, not as a level claim.
  • The assurance records (docs/assurance/) are kept as good practice: SOUP list, traceability per part, review records, equivalent mutants, problem reports.
  • A product that needs a qualified component later starts from complete high evidence rather than from scratch.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Option Why not safety from v0.1.0 Needs a checker the project does not have, and claims more than the code's role justifies standard until v1.0 Below the handbook's floor for code others build products on Make handlers part of a safety function A bus-backed call cannot guarantee reaching a safe state

docs.title: Amendment (2026-11-14, owner decision)
docs.text: The claim of zero repository deviations above the boundary files becomes: one recorded library deviation, DEV-KBC-004, confined to the *Ref adapters in one header (components/lib/interfaces/inc/kb/interfaces/refs.hpp), with a compile-time check that the context type matches. ADR-0006 rule 5 makes run-time choice a type-erased *Ref (a context pointer and a constant table of function pointers, no virtual function); erasing the type needs the context as void*, and getting it back is a conversion that MISRA C++:2023 Rule 8.2.6 forbids. The conversion is one helper (detail::ContextAs<T>), called only from tables generated for T; each *Ref constructor is constrained by the concept and static_asserts it, so a context reaches only the functions of its own type. Every other library file stays deviation-free.

docs.title: ADR-0012: Pins to release or release-candidate tags only; every release records its own SHA and a lock
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-13). Sharpens ADR-0002. Amended by ADR-0014: the release lock is one form of the assembler lock.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A submodule can point at any commit, and .gitmodules can ask for a branch. A pin to a branch tip or to an untagged commit is a pin to code no CI gate ever approved as a release. A kb-core release also has to say exactly what it contains, all the way down, for users who must rebuild it years later and for the configurator's evidence (ADR-0013). A tag name alone is not enough: tags can move.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Every submodule (drivers now, extracted ports later) is pinned to the commit of a tag named vX.Y.Z or vX.Y.Z-rc.N in that repository, whose required CI check passed on that commit. Never main, never a branch, never an untagged commit. .gitmodules carries no branch = entry.
  2. components/drivers/drivers.lock.yml records, per pin: name, repo, tag, commit and kind (release or rc).
  3. A kb-core release may contain release-candidate pins; each is listed in the release notes and in the release lock, and pin hygiene warns on a final kb-core release that contains one.
  4. Each kb-core release records its own commit SHA and a lock file. The release job writes kb-core-<version>.lock.yml, attached to the release, listed in SHA256SUMS and covered by the build provenance:
schema: 1
kb_core: {version: 0.4.0, tag: v0.4.0, commit: <40 hex>}
drivers:
  - {name: pf1550, repo: kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-pf1550, tag: v0.1.0, commit: <40 hex>, kind: release}
ports:
  - {name: esp32, path: components/ports/esp32, commit: <the kb-core commit>}   # after extraction: repo, tag, commit
toolchain: {cmake: <version>, gcc: <version>, clang: <version>, esp_idf: v5.5.x, codeql_misra_pack: <version>}
soup: [{name: freertos-kernel, version: <version>, via: esp-idf}]
files: [{name: kb_utils-0.4.0.tar.gz, sha256: <64 hex>}]

The lock cannot live in the tagged commit (it would change the SHA it records); it is a release file, and the tag's commit is the source of truth it points at. 5. The pin hygiene checks stay and grow: PIN-001 to PIN-010 (tools/pins), plus PIN-011 (no branch = in .gitmodules; the tag matches ^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+(-rc\.\d+)?$; kind agrees with the tag) and PIN-012 (at release: the lock is complete and every commit in it equals the tree being released).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Any kb-core release can be rebuilt from its lock alone, and a moved tag is detected by its SHA.
  • A driver change reaches kb-core only after the driver tagged it and its CI passed.
  • Release candidates can flow through kb-core's own pre-releases without waiting for final driver tags.
  • Consumers' version locks (handbook ADR-0007) reference kb-core by tag and SHA, the same pair the release lock records.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Option Why not Pins to main or a branch No release behind it; the pin changes meaning when the branch moves Final tags only Blocks kb-core pre-releases while drivers are pre-1.0 Lock committed after the release A second commit per release, and the lock would not be in the release's own provenance

docs.title: ADR-0013: A hosted configurator that hands out repeatable, pinned projects with evidence
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-13). Amended by ADR-0014: the site and the kb CLI share one resolver specification and its vectors in tests/resolver/vectors/.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A user of the kb family has to choose an MCU family, an RTOS, a kb-core version, drivers and their handlers, and then get exactly those, pinned, in a form that builds the same way next year. They also need evidence for what they took: what is in it (SBOM), which known vulnerabilities affect it, which licences apply, which combinations were actually tested together. The catalogue (catalog/compat.yml), the release lock (ADR-0012) and tested version sets already hold the facts; what is missing is an easy front end.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. A static configurator website, hosted on GitHub Pages first: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no server, no account, no cookies, no analytics and no third-party script at run time (dependencies are vendored and pinned, a strict Content Security Policy is set). The skeleton lives in kb-core configurator/ now and moves to the kb-configurator repository (ADR-0008) when it needs its own release cadence.
  2. Inputs, all published by kb-core releases and read as static JSON: the catalogue (MCU gates, bindings, kb_core_min, thread-model constraints), the release lock of each kb-core version, the evidence files of each release, and the tested version sets (kb YYYY.N).
  3. The user picks MCU family and target, RTOS backend, kb-core version or a tested set, drivers, the handlers to bind, and the thread model of each bus. The site resolves the selection with the same rules as the kb CLI (drivers to handlers to interfaces to parts, MCU gates, kb_core_min, one thread model per bus, kRequiresOwner); both front ends implement one resolver specification and must pass the same golden test vectors, so they cannot disagree.
  4. Downloads, byte-for-byte repeatable (sorted, no timestamps; the scan date is a separate field):
  5. kb-image.yml, the selection itself;
  6. the git commands: clone kb-core at its tag, check the commit SHA against the release lock, init only the enabled submodules without --recursive, and check each submodule's SHA;
  7. a CMakePresets.json fragment and kb_image.cmake (KB_MCU, KB_RTOS, KB_PARTS, KB_ENABLE_*);
  8. later, an archive of a ready project made from kb-app-template with the same pins.
  9. Evidence for the selection, filtered from the release's evidence to exactly the chosen components:
  10. an SBOM in SPDX 2.3 and CycloneDX 1.6 JSON (kb-core parts, drivers, port, SOUP, with versions, licences, package URLs and SHAs);
  11. known-CVE scan results for those components (scanned in the release job, re-scanned on a schedule so a new CVE shows against an old release; each result carries its scan date and database version);
  12. a licence report (each component's SPDX licence and copyright holder);
  13. the compatibility rows of the selection from the catalogue;
  14. the tested version set the selection belongs to and the configurations that passed, or a clear "untested combination" warning.
  15. kb-core's release job produces the evidence files (pending ci-tools ru-release-evidence); the site never generates evidence itself.
  16. Phases: P0 skeleton page (now); P1 at M4 (catalogue, kb-image.yml, git commands, presets); P2 at M6 (SBOM, CVE results, licence report, tested sets); P3 at M7 (project archive, board.yml pin tables).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One place to get a pinned, explainable project; the same selection always yields the same files.
  • The evidence is release evidence, signed by the release's provenance, not something the site computes.
  • The resolver exists twice (Python CLI, JavaScript site), held together by shared test vectors.
  • A static site cannot fetch sources across origins; P1 and P2 give commands and evidence, and the archive waits for P3.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Option Why not A server-side generator Hosting, accounts and an attack surface for something a static page can do CLI only Harder first contact; the CLI stays for automation ESP-IDF component manifests only ESP-IDF only, and no evidence

docs.title: ADR-0014: kb-core is the assembler
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-14). Amends ADR-0002, ADR-0012 and ADR-0013.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
kb-core holds four libraries of its own and pins the drivers it binds. Around it, MCU ports move into their own repositories (ADR-0008: kokeb-labs-drivers/port-<family>), the configurator site needs the same answers as the command line, and a user wants a driver version that is not the one kb-core happens to pin (a newer release candidate on a bench, or an older release a product qualified). Three questions had no single owner:

  • Which pieces make up one firmware image, and at which exact commits?
  • Which combinations are allowed (MCU gates, RTOS per MCU, kb_core_min, one thread model per bus, kRequiresOwner)?
  • How do two front ends, a Python command line and a static JavaScript site, give the same answer forever?

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. kb-core is the assembler. It is two things:
  2. its own libraries, kb::utils, kb::rtos, kb::interfaces, kb::handlers, with one version;
  3. a manifest and lock of pinned parts: driver repositories at release or rc tags (ADR-0012), port repositories once extracted, and the in-tree ports while they live in kb-core. The manifest is the catalogue (catalog/schemas/catalog.schema.json): every version of every part that may be assembled, with its tag, commit and gates. The lock (catalog/schemas/lock.schema.json) is exactly what one image or one release contains.
  4. Versions are selectable per driver. An image (kb-image.yml, catalog/schemas/kb-image.schema.json) may name a version for each driver and for an extracted port. Without one, the resolver takes kb-core's own pin, else the newest release, else the newest release candidate. Only tags in the catalogue are selectable: never a branch, never an untagged commit. A release candidate is allowed with warning KB-RES-W01.
  5. One resolver specification, one engine per front end. The rules are written once in Assembler and resolver and implemented as a pure function of (catalogue, image): tools/kb/resolver.py for the kb command line and configurator/resolver.mjs for the site. Neither reads a file, a clock or the network while resolving.
  6. Shared vectors prove them identical. tests/resolver/vectors/ holds the golden cases: input catalogue and image, expected error and warning codes with their subjects, and for a valid image the full lock and the bytes of every emitted file. Both implementations run every vector in CI; a seeded property test also feeds the same mutated images to both and compares the results. A rule change changes the specification, both implementations and the vectors in one pull request.
  7. Errors are structured. Every refusal is a stable code KB-RES-NNN with a subject (the field or the part) and a message; warnings are KB-RES-WNN. Front ends may word messages differently; codes and subjects never differ.
  8. Outputs are repeatable. For a valid image the resolver emits the lock (kb-image.lock.yml), a CMakePresets.json fragment, kb_image.cmake (KB_MCU, KB_RTOS, KB_PARTS, KB_ENABLE_*) and kb-fetch.sh. One layout: a user project gets its parts as git submodules under external/ (external/kb-core, external/port-<family> when extracted, external/drivers/driver-<chip>), each checked out at its tag, its commit verified against the lock, no branch in .gitmodules and no recursion; the fetch script creates exactly that, refuses a moved tag, and --verify re-checks an existing tree. kb_image.cmake and the presets point KB_DRIVER_<CHIP>_DIR there. kb sbom turns a lock into CycloneDX 1.6 and SPDX 2.3 JSON whose identifiers derive from the lock's SHA-256, so the same lock gives the same bytes; it lists the SDK and RTOS (ESP-IDF, FreeRTOS, ThreadX when selected) as SOUP and each component's known-vulnerability scan (kb:osv), as the site's downloads do.
  9. The catalogue is built, never edited. kb catalog build reads each driver's driver.yml at each of its vX.Y.Z and vX.Y.Z-rc.N tags, from local clones with git or from GitHub with gh api, plus kb-core's own tags and its platform table. The release job publishes the catalogue next to the release lock; the site reads those files and nothing else.

docs.title: Amended records
docs.text:
• ADR-0002: the submodule pins remain kb-core's defaults; an image may select another catalogued tag of the same driver.
  • ADR-0012: the release lock is one instance of the lock schema; an image lock has the same shape plus the image's MCU, RTOS, parts, buses and CMake values.
  • ADR-0013: "one resolver specification" now names its files: the specification page, the two implementations and tests/resolver/vectors/.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One place answers "what is in this image": its lock, by tag and commit, down to every driver.
  • A driver release reaches users through the catalogue as soon as it is tagged, without waiting for a kb-core pin bump; the bump still decides kb-core's tested default.
  • Two implementations must be kept in step. The vectors make drift a failing test, not a silent disagreement.
  • Combinations outside kb-core's pins are allowed but not necessarily tested; tested version sets (ADR-0013) stay the evidence for that.
  • The JSON schemas are a public contract of kb-core: a change to them is a versioned change (schema: 2).

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Option Why not Only kb-core's submodule pins, no per-driver choice Every driver change waits for a kb-core release; benches cannot try an rc A separate assembler repository A third place for facts kb-core already owns (pins, gates, parts) and another release to coordinate The site calls the Python resolver (a server or WebAssembly) ADR-0013 requires a static site with no server; shipping a Python runtime to the browser is heavier than one small module One implementation generated from the other A generator is a third program to trust; two short hand-written implementations plus shared vectors are easier to review Free-form error text Front ends and tests cannot assert on prose; codes are stable and testable

docs.title: ADR-0015: Eclipse ThreadX is a supported kb::rtos backend
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-11-14). Amends docs/design/plan.md M6 (the ThreadX backend lands before port-stm32).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
kb-core's plan has carried ThreadX as a "later" backend since revision 1, and KB_RTOS=THREADX has been refused with a "not yet" message. Before writing the backend we checked whether ThreadX is still worth supporting in late 2026, against FreeRTOS (and its certified sibling SAFERTOS) and Zephyr. The evidence, as found on 2026-11-14 and checked again in review (rows marked not re-verified could not be loaded the second time):

Question Finding Source Ownership and licence Eclipse Foundation project since the hand-over from Microsoft (announced November 2023); MIT, no royalties threadx.io FAQ, GitHub repository (licence field MIT) Release cadence Seven tagged releases in the last 13 months (publish dates): v6.4.3.202503_rel (2025-10-02), v6.4.5.202504_rel (2026-01-09), v6.5.0.202601_rel (2026-03-06), v6.5.1.202602_rel and ...a (2026-06-08), v6.5.2.202603_rel (2026-10-02, the fixes of nine advisories), v6.5.2.202603b_rel (2026-11-01, latest: eight security fixes, seven in ThreadX Modules and one in the TrustZone-M entry functions) releases, security advisories Community About 3.6k stars, 944 forks, 50 contributors (57 counting anonymous ones), last push 2026-11-09; a small core team that asks members to fund more staff repository, project lead, threadx-dev, 2026-01-09 Safety certificates SGS-TUV Saar certified specific releases to IEC 61508-3:2010 (route 3S, SIL 4), IEC 62304:2015 (class C), ISO 26262-8:2018 (ASIL D) and EN 50128:2011. The certified kernel is ThreadX 6.1.1 (SMP 6.1.3); the certificates were being transferred from Microsoft to the Eclipse Foundation, and 6.4.x was not certified threadx.io FAQ, threadx-dev, 2024-04-04 Access to them Subscribers of the ThreadX Alliance can buy a licence to the safety artefacts package (safety manuals and the documents of each certified release); the code stays MIT. The sources do not say who holds the certificates now; in 2024 their transfer from Microsoft to the Eclipse Foundation was still pending threadx.io FAQ, threadx-dev, 2024-04-04 Certification road map 2026 goal: certify v6.4.1 (IEC 61508, ISO 26262, ...) and finish the SESIP assessment Microsoft started; in April 2026 the project lead said 6.4.1 is "still on track" for this year, with no date threadx-dev, 2026-01-09, threadx, 2026-04-15 STM32 ST ships ThreadX in the STM32Cube firmware packages and the X-CUBE-AZRTOS expansion packages (security bulletin SB0067, April 2026; not re-verified, the PDF did not load in review), and in the STM32CubeMX middleware for newer families (H5, U5); a community answer says STM32CubeMX2 does not offer it yet ST SB0067, ST community, H5, ST community, CubeMX2 NXP, Renesas NXP's MCUXpresso IDE lists ThreadX beside FreeRTOS and Zephyr (the NXP community article on the SDK is not re-verified: it refused automated access); Renesas ships ThreadX in the RA FSP and the RX FSP NXP MCUXpresso IDE, NXP community, Renesas FSP, Renesas RX FSP FreeRTOS and SAFERTOS No certificate for the FreeRTOS kernel itself was found (not sourced: the FreeRTOS page gave no content in review); SAFERTOS (a separate, commercial code base on the FreeRTOS functional model) is pre-certified by TUV SUD to IEC 61508 SIL 3 and ISO 26262 ASIL D FreeRTOS: SAFERTOS, WHIS Zephyr Working toward IEC 61508 SIL 3 (route 3S); no certificate yet in 2026; ISO 26262 to follow Zephyr safety overview, Embedded World 2026 talk

What this means for kb-core:

  • ThreadX is the only RTOS in the field whose source is MIT and whose specific releases hold IEC 61508 SIL 4, IEC 62304 class C and ISO 26262 ASIL D certificates. SAFERTOS is certified but commercial and closed; Zephyr is not certified yet and is a larger, Devicetree-driven system that does not fit a thin seam.
  • It is shipped by the vendors of the MCU families kb-core targets next (STM32 first, then NXP and Renesas), so a board on those families can use the kernel the vendor tooling already configures.
  • The risks are real: a small team, the certified release (6.1.1) is old and the artefacts cost money, the 6.4.1 certificate is promised but not delivered, and ST's newest tooling (CubeMX2) leaves ThreadX out.
  • The cost to kb-core is small: one backend folder of boundary files behind the existing seam (kb/rtos/backend.hpp), the same conformance tests, and one more SOUP entry.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Support Eclipse ThreadX as a kb::rtos backend, KB_RTOS=THREADX, beside NONE, FREERTOS and the host test backend. It implements the same seam with the same contract: static allocation only (tx_*_create on control blocks and stacks that kb objects own), at-least delays, bounded waits, priority-inheriting mutexes, the same ISR rules, and it fails closed when not configured.
  2. ThreadX is SOUP: a git submodule of the official eclipse-threadx/threadx repository at a release tag (third_party/threadx, recorded in docs/assurance/soup.md and the SBOM inputs). No ThreadX source is copied into the tree, edited, or MISRA-scanned; its call sites are boundary files.
  3. kb-core's own tests run the ThreadX backend on the kernel itself: the conformance suite on ThreadX's Linux port (host), and cross-compiles of the backend for Cortex-M0+, M4F and M7F.
  4. kb-core pins the latest release for development and CI. A product that claims the ThreadX certificate must build against a certified release and the Alliance's artefacts; kb-core uses only the long-stable 6.x API (no 6.5-only call), so the backend builds against 6.1.x too: on 2026-11-14 the backend and the kernel at v6.1.1_rel were cross-compiled for Cortex-M0+ and M4F (THREADX_DIR=... PORTS=... tools/preflight/threadx_cross.sh); CI builds only the pinned release. That pin belongs to the product's lock, not to kb-core.
  5. This decision is reviewed when the 6.4.1 certificate is issued or when the project's release cadence stops (no release in 12 months).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The boundary file keeps some bookkeeping that needs the kernel's own types and is a deliberate exception to the "no logic in boundary files" rule of the design (section 20.3): the critical-section nesting count, the timer slot table (a ThreadX expiry gets one ULONG, too narrow for a pointer on a 64-bit host) and the stack fill-pattern scan. The rules that need no kernel type (delay-until, the non-recursive retake, the 64-bit tick extension) are platform-free in kb/rtos/backend_rules.hpp and tested on the host. All of it is under the mutation and coverage gates through the fake kernel.
  • The configurator, kb resolve and CMake stop refusing ThreadX; STM32 is still a planned family until port-stm32 lands, so the RTOS is available but not yet on a released family.
  • One more SOUP item to watch for anomalies (the ThreadX security advisories on GitHub).
  • The seam gains what the design asked for and the ThreadX backend needs anyway (a recursive mutex, a thread's stack free space); the other backends implement it too, so the API stays the same on every RTOS.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Option Why not Drop ThreadX, FreeRTOS only Gives up the only MIT-sourced kernel with SIL 4 / ASIL D / class C certificates, and the kernel ST, NXP and Renesas tooling configures SAFERTOS backend instead Commercial and closed; cannot be a pinned, buildable SOUP in CI. Its API follows FreeRTOS, so the FreeRTOS backend is the starting point if a product needs it Zephyr backend No certificate yet; its kernel objects are configured through Kconfig and Devicetree, a different integration model; revisit when certified CMSIS-RTOS2 as the seam Another layer between kb-core and the kernel, with its own allocation rules; the kb seam already is that layer Copy the ThreadX sources into the tree Breaks the SOUP rule (never edited, pinned, traceable to the official repository)

docs.title: ADR-0016: Non-blocking bus access and held bus transactions
docs.text: Status: Proposed (2026-11-14), for the owner's decision.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Every kb contract call is bounded (ADR-0006), but bounded is not the same as cheap or safe to wait on. Three lessons from earlier work set the requirements:

  • A bus wrapper that busy-polled the peripheral for every transfer cost about 8 % of a core for one sensor read at its control rate. An interrupt-driven start/poll path, added beside it later, removed that cost.
  • A safety task waited inside a vendor I2C call until the watchdog fired. Safety paths must never wait on a bus; the safe-state latch (outputs cut first, no bus touched) is a HAL rule, but the library must make the non-waiting path the easy one.
  • Several drivers need a whole call, or a sequence of calls, held on one bus: as5047u answers a read in the next frame, at25040b writes and reads ranges of several chunks, ads7952 programs a mode and then reads frames, and se05x T=1 exchanges blocks that belong together. A guarded handler already runs each driver call under the bus lock (ADR-0009); a sequence of calls was not covered, and a range of chunks could be interleaved by another task.

The synchronous contracts (I2cBus, SpiDevice) stay as they are: every driver port is synchronous, and start-up and slow paths are fine with a bounded wait.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Asynchronous contract (kb/interfaces/async.hpp). kb::iface::AsyncOperation (Poll(now) returning AsyncPoll, Cancel(), kNonBlocking), I2cAsync (StartWrite, StartWriteRead, StartRead) and SpiAsync (StartTransfer), each also the synchronous contract. Start takes a kb::utils::Deadline and returns at once (Ok, Busy, InvalidArgument, Timeout, NotReady). Poll() never waits: Idle, Pending, or Done with the outcome as a kb::Result<std::size_t> (Completion()), reported exactly once. A transfer not complete by its deadline completes as Timeout, and so does a completion that arrives after the deadline (late data is never Ok). Cancel() is bounded; whether it or a racing completion wins, it returns Ok, the completion is dropped, and nothing touches the caller's buffers afterwards. Completion is signalled from the ISR by the port (an event flag of the owner task, or nothing: the owner polls once per pass).
  2. Ports may adapt now. kb::iface::AsyncFromSync<Bus, Clock> serves the contract from any synchronous port: Start() runs the whole transfer, keeps the deadline rules, and kNonBlocking is false. A hot path does not compile over it: kb::handlers::AsyncPoller<Op, Bytes> requires NonBlocking<Op> unless it is declared AsyncUse::MayBlock. So ports are not forced to implement the native form before a handler needs it, and the type system says where a wait is still hidden.
  3. Owner-task use (kb::handlers::AsyncPoller). It owns the transfer's buffers (they outlive the transfer by construction), starts a transfer with a budget, and Step(now) polls once per pass and reports the completion once; the destructor and Cancel() end a transfer in flight. A hot-path access of an owner bus starts a read in one pass and publishes it in a later one; no pass waits on the bus. Drivers keep their synchronous hooks: a binding uses the poller for reads it frames itself (one register, one frame), and a driver-level async hook is a later template change.
  4. Held transactions. BusDomain::Hold(timeout) returns a [[nodiscard]], move-only RAII BusHold, made only by the domain: on a guarded bus the bus mutex (bounded wait), on an owner bus the pass flag (never waits; a hold and a service pass exclude each other). Bus() is null after Release(), and Bus() on a temporary hold does not compile. For handler calls:
  5. Guarded<H>::Hold(timeout) returns a GuardedHeld: the handler mutex, then the bus, in the order of every call (ADR-0009). It has the facade's Request and Sample, so a binding's app call runs whole under it (at25040b::Write(held, ...)). There is no Held(BusHold&) on a guarded handler: taking the handler lock while holding the bus would invert the lock order.
  6. OwnerAccess<H>::Held(BusHold&) returns an OwnerHeld: the owner task, between passes, runs calls inline under its hold of the bus, several handlers of the bus under one hold. A hold of another bus type does not compile; a hold of another domain object, or a released one, refuses every call.
  7. Every wait is bounded, so a hold taken across two buses in opposite orders by two tasks ends in Timeout, never a hang; the rule is still: never hold two buses.
  8. Safety rule. A safety path never calls a bus: it cuts outputs first and reads only published snapshots (Latest(), Health(), the liveness verdict). The HAL documents its safety latch; kb-core gives no API that lets a safety task wait on a bus without a timeout.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A hot-path read costs one Start() and one Poll() per pass instead of a busy wait; where a port has no native form yet, the wait is visible in the type (MayBlock) and in review.
  • The held calls give multi-chunk and multi-call sequences the same atomicity a single guarded call has, in both thread models, without a recursive lock.
  • BusHold is no longer constructed directly; code that built one with {domain, timeout} uses domain.Hold().
  • An owner-bus hold taken from another task is not refused by a task check (there is none): it excludes the pass and the pass counts a violation, so a misuse shows in the domain's statistics and never races the handler.
  • Ports have work to do before a native hot path exists (below); until then AsyncFromSync keeps every handler building.

docs.title: What each port must add
docs.text: Port Asynchronous contract Held transactions Fault journal store, reset reason components/ports/esp32 (to move to port-esp32) I2cAsync over the i2c_master asynchronous mode (trans_queue_depth > 0, i2c_master_register_event_callbacks, completion sets the owner's event flag from the callback); SpiAsync over spi_device_queue_trans and spi_device_get_trans_result with a zero timeout in Poll(); Cancel() waits at most one queued transaction (the driver cannot abort one) and then drops it; kNonBlocking = true only when both hold Nothing: holds are in kb-core A store in RTC slow memory (RTC_NOINIT_ATTR placement of a RamJournalStore) and one over an NVS blob or a flash partition with one write unit per slot; esp_reset_reason() mapped to kb::utils::ResetReason with the raw value in detail port-stm32 (planned, M6) I2cAsync over HAL_I2C_Master_Transmit_IT/_DMA and the completion callbacks, HAL_I2C_Master_Abort_IT for Cancel(); SpiAsync over HAL_SPI_TransmitReceive_DMA and HAL_SPI_Abort; the known defects of older STM32 bus wrappers as its first tests Nothing Backup SRAM or the RTC backup registers as a store, emulated EEPROM in flash as a second; the RCC_CSR reset flags mapped to ResetReason, then cleared Host (components/lib/interfaces/host) FakeAsyncI2c, FakeAsyncSpi (done) Nothing RamJournalStore (done)

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Option Why not Make every contract call asynchronous (futures or callbacks) Every driver port is synchronous; start-up and slow paths gain nothing and lose simplicity; callbacks from an ISR into handler code break ADR-0009 rule 7 Completion callbacks instead of Poll() A callback runs in the ISR or a port task, outside the handler's one context; the owner pass would need a lock again A Status::Pending value in kb::Status The closed error enum would mean "not an error" for one value; every switch over kb::Status would change; AsyncPoll keeps state and outcome apart Coroutines (C++20) Frame allocation needs a custom allocator per coroutine, debuggers and the MISRA checker handle them poorly, and the owner pass already is the scheduler Require native async in every port now Blocks handler work on port work; AsyncFromSync plus the NonBlocking gate gives the same safety with a visible migration path A recursive bus lock for sequences Hides the lock order and masks lock-order defects (ADR-0009 already rejects it) Held(BusHold&) on guarded handlers Takes the handler lock while holding the bus: the reverse of every other call's order A bus hold that is copyable or a plain scope guard with a public constructor A copy releases twice; a guard built anywhere cannot carry the domain's statistics or the owner-pass exclusion A task-identity check for owner holds The RTOS API has no portable cheap task id at this layer; the pass flag gives mutual exclusion in every build and counts misuse

docs.title: ADR-0017: A kb::rtos object's destructor deletes its native object
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-11-21)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Every kb::rtos object (Mutex, RecursiveMutex, Semaphore, Queue, EventFlags, Timer) builds its native RTOS object in opaque storage inside itself (detail::OpaqueStorage). Until now the backend seam had a create call for each kind but no delete, and every destructor was = default: a native object was never ended. Only Thread had a release hook (ThreadRelease).

That was harmless only while every object had static storage. Tests, and any code that keeps an object on a stack frame or in an object that ends, then build new native objects in bytes whose old native object was never ended:

  • Host backend. A std::mutex and a std::condition_variable were constructed over earlier ones that were never destroyed, so POSIX never saw pthread_mutex_destroy or pthread_cond_destroy before a new init at the same address. On macOS, kb_handlers_threads hung now and then under load, always in the test "recoveries asked by one task while another task's requests run, through the owner task". Five stack samples (three given, one from a local repro, one from a plain preflight with no load generator) show the same state: every thread that uses the channel's event-flag mutex sleeps in __psynch_mutexwait, and no live thread holds that mutex. In the plain-preflight sample the owner task (EventFlags::Set) and the requester (re-locking after its timed wait) both sleep on the mutex and nothing spins. No kb code path can leave that mutex held: every lock is a short RAII scope with no nested lock. The test's teardown hang (~Thread joining for ever) follows from it: Finish() and Stop() time out after 60 s, then the destructor joins a thread that never wakes.
  • Host timers. A HostTimer's thread outlived its Timer, so the callback went on running on storage that had ended (a deterministic failure: a 1 ms timer fired 26 times after its end in the new regression test, then the process aborted).
  • ThreadX. A created object stays on a kernel list; an object on a stack frame left a dangling entry, and a timer kept its slot of the backend's 32-slot table for ever.
  • none. A timer stayed in the fake clock's table, which kept calling into ended storage.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. The backend seam (kb/rtos/backend.hpp) gains one call per kind: MutexDelete, RecursiveMutexDelete, SemaphoreDelete, QueueDelete, EventFlagsDelete, TimerDelete. Each is called once, by the kb object's destructor, only after a successful create, and clears storage.handle. The caller's contract: nothing holds, waits on or uses the object any more (the usual C++ lifetime rule, now stated).
  2. Each destructor calls its delete when the object was created; a never-created object deletes nothing.
  3. Per backend:
Backend Mutex, semaphore, queue Event flags Timer host destructor of the placement-new'd standard-library object destructor destructor, which ends and joins the timer's thread FreeRTOS (and ESP32) vQueueDelete (vSemaphoreDelete is that call) vEventGroupDelete documented no-op ThreadX tx_mutex_delete, tx_semaphore_delete, tx_queue_delete tx_event_flags_delete tx_timer_delete, and its table slot is freed none no-op (plain values) no-op leaves the fake clock's table

The FreeRTOS timer is not deleted: xTimerDelete only queues a command for the timer task, which may still use the control block after the kb object's storage has ended, so a synchronous delete does not exist there. 4. Misuse is defined on the host backend: an object that another thread still holds (mutex) or waits on (semaphore, queue, event flags: a waiter count under the object's own mutex) is left in place, never destroyed under that thread; a timer deleted from its own callback is left running, as its thread cannot join itself. The handle is dropped either way.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• No native object is ever built over one that was not ended, on any backend with a delete.
  • Static objects are unchanged (their destructors run at exit, if at all). Objects on a stack frame or inside an ending object are now correct on ThreadX and the host, and need no slot of the ThreadX timer table after their end.
  • A FreeRTOS Timer still needs static storage, as before; the parts page says so.
  • Regression tests: kb_rtos_tests_* build each kind again and again in the same bytes over every backend; the host suite runs groups and semaphores in shared bytes under contention, checks that a timer never fires after its end, and checks the refusals of item 4. The CTest timeouts (KB_TEST_TIMEOUT) turn any hang left into a failure in minutes.
  • Not proven: the hang has no deterministic reproduction. Before the fix it showed in about 1 run of 100 of the whole suite under load; the evidence that the fix removes it is a run count, recorded in the pull request.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Heap-allocate host objects and never free them (no address is ever reused). Smallest change, but it leaks every object, LeakSanitizer reports it on Linux, and it leaves the ThreadX, none and host-timer problems.
  • Keep the seam; make the host backend detect a re-created address. It cannot tell a new object from an old one at the same address without a delete, so it would guess.
  • Only document "static storage for every object". The rule already existed and tests broke it; nothing checks it, and the host timer and ThreadX table problems show the cost of relying on it.
  • A delete in the FreeRTOS timer via xTimerDelete with a wait. Still asynchronous: the timer task may touch the control block after the command is queued, so it would trade a documented limit for a hidden use-after-end.

docs.title: ADR-0030: DMA buffers are owned by the CPU or the device, and move by a lease
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-15). The number is provisional until the record is merged.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The incidents behind this decision were all one mistake in different clothes: memory that a DMA master writes was also touched by the CPU, or the cache was not told. A transmit buffer read stale because the clean was missing; a receive buffer read stale because the invalidate ran only before the transfer; an invalidate over a range that shared a line with a neighbouring object destroyed the neighbour; a transfer that timed out returned its buffer while the engine was still writing; a synchronous call made the caller's own stack a DMA target. Each was fixed by a comment.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. A DMA buffer is Buffer<Region, Bytes>: static, aligned to the region's unit, padded to a whole number of units. Cache maintenance over it never reaches another object.
  2. A buffer is Cpu, Device or Quarantined. CpuView() returns the data in Cpu only; elsewhere it is empty and counted.
  3. Only the port moves a buffer, through a PortKey<Tag> that only the tag's class can construct. A lease is move-only. Lend runs the maintenance over the owned lines; Complete returns the memory.
  4. Staging copy is the default. A port copies caller data into its own staging buffer and back. Zero-copy is possible only when the application holds a Lease of a buffer in a region the master reaches.
  5. Cancel() returns Fault and quarantines the buffer when a stop cannot be confirmed (the enable bit does not read 0 within its bound). A destroyed active lease quarantines too. Recover returns the buffer only with proof after the peripheral was re-initialised.
  6. A transfer completes once and is reported once (CompletionLatch): a cancel racing the completion produces one outcome and the memory is the CPU's afterwards.
  7. A port reports Capabilities() (mode, ceiling, staging size, alignment) and a DmaHealth record with the mode in use. A fallback to interrupt or polled service is declared and visible, never silent.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A misuse that the incidents show (CPU access during a lease, a forged key, a copied lease) is a build error or a counted refusal, not a comment.
  • Each port writes the register code and the three cache hooks; the rules live once in kb::dma.
  • A cancel can fail, and the caller must handle Fault; a quarantined buffer stays unusable until recovered.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Reference counting leases: hides the one moment that matters (the master stopped) behind a count.
  • Zero-copy by default: the caller's memory becomes a DMA target; rejected after the synchronous-call incident.
  • Returning the buffer at timeout and ignoring a late write: the late write is the incident.

docs.title: ADR-0031: Streams copy frames out of the DMA ring, and say what they lost
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-15). The number is provisional until the record is merged.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A circular DMA ring fills forever. The earlier implementations let the task read the ring in place, overwrote a held frame silently, counted an overflow as data, subtracted two unsigned time stamps taken in different contexts, and let two code paths drain the same flags so a half was delivered twice.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Stream<Frame, Frames, Region> has at least two frames. The interrupt copies each finished hardware frame into a slot (PublishFromDevice: invalidate the frame's lines, copy out) with a sequence number and the completion time; the task takes it with TryTake and holds it in a move-only FrameView.
  2. Three overrun checks: a full ring drops the frame, counts it and flags the next delivered frame Gap(); a hardware overrun or pool overflow is counted by OnOverrun, is never a frame and flags the next one; a copy the hardware lapped is published Torn.
  3. The stall check uses signed elapsed time; a frame stamped after the task read its clock counts as zero elapsed. Each stall episode is counted once.
  4. One interrupt path reads and clears the hardware flags. There is no second drainer.
  5. A content check (Judge) feeds a restart policy: Supervise returns Restart, BackOff or UseFallback, with a new epoch after each. Frames from the declared fallback producer say Fallback().
  6. One producer context and one consumer context; counters are atomics and ring indices are single-writer.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The consumer never sees memory the hardware is writing.
  • Loss is visible in the data (gap, torn, fallback, epoch) and in the counters.
  • A frame costs one copy in the interrupt; the cost is reported (NoteIsrCycles).

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Lending the ring to the task: the held-frame and lapping incidents.
  • A lock between interrupt and task: unbounded interrupt latency.

docs.title: ADR-0032: A region states its cache policy, and the default is non-cacheable
docs.text: Status: Accepted (owner decision, 2026-11-15). The number is provisional until the record is merged.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Which memory a DMA master may use, and what the cache does to it, differs per part: tightly coupled memory that the master cannot reach, cached SRAM that needs maintenance by line, SRAM in a domain next to the peripheral. A buffer placed in the wrong one fails only on the board.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. A Region states its cache policy (Coherent, NonCacheable, Maintained), its line size, its alignment unit and the masters that reach it. The unit is a power of two at least as large as a line; a Maintained region has a real line size.
  2. The default DMA region on a part with a data cache is a non-cacheable block in the memory domain next to the peripheral, set up by the MPU. Maintained regions are for buffers that must live in cached memory.
  3. Compile-time helpers fail the build when a frame exceeds a port's limit, a master cannot reach a region, a size is not a whole number of units, or a stream element differs from the board declaration.
  4. The start-up check Buffer::Verify confirms alignment and placement inside the region's range.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• No cache maintenance in the common path; the maintained path stays tested by the model.
  • A misplaced buffer or oversized frame is a build error, not a field failure.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Cache maintenance everywhere: correct, but every missing call is a silent stale read.
  • One global policy: wrong for parts with more than one memory.

docs.title: Assembler and resolver
docs.text:
kb-core assembles an image from its own libraries and pinned parts (ADR-0014). This page is the resolver specification: the one set of rules that the kb command line (tools/kb/resolver.py) and the configurator site (configurator/resolver.mjs) implement, and that the shared vectors in tests/resolver/vectors/ hold them to. The upgrade planner (tools/kb/upgrade.py, plan in configurator/resolver.mjs) is part of the same specification and has its own vectors in tests/resolver/vectors/upgrade/.

From tags to a project Figure description and sources

From the top. kb catalog build reads each driver's driver.yml at its tags and the kb-core tags with their platform table and pins, and writes catalog.json, every part at every version. The resolver, one specification with a Python and a JavaScript implementation, reads kb-image.yml (what the user selected) and the catalogue, and writes the lock kb-image.lock.yml (every version, tag and SHA) and three project files: CMakePresets.json, kb_image.cmake and kb-fetch.sh. kb sbom turns the lock into CycloneDX 1.6 and SPDX 2.3 documents.

Drawn from: docs/model/assembler-flow.graph.yml.

docs.title: Documents
docs.text:
Document Schema Written by Read by Catalogue catalog/schemas/catalog.schema.json kb catalog build, the release job the resolver Image catalog/schemas/kb-image.schema.json the user, the site the resolver Lock catalog/schemas/lock.schema.json the resolver, the release job kb sbom, the fetch script, people driver.yml catalog/schemas/driver-yml.schema.json each driver repository kb catalog build

All three carry schema: 1. JSON is the exchange format; YAML is accepted where a person writes the file.

docs.title: Catalogue
docs.text:
Every part that may be assembled, at every selectable version:

  • kb_core: repository, licence, authors and its versions (release, rc, or dev for an unreleased revision added with --include-head).
  • parts, rtos (each supported or planned) and mcus: family, status, targets, the RTOS backends it allows, its default RTOS and its port. A port with an empty versions list is inside kb-core (path); an extracted port lists the tags of kokeb-labs-drivers/port-<family>. A family without a port has port: null.
  • drivers: name, repository, folder, kb-core's own pin (pinned), and per tag the version, commit, kind, buses, MCU families ([any] or a list), peripheral, kb_core_min, requires_owner (kRequiresOwner), licence, authors and optional bindings, all read from driver.yml at that tag. Until a kb-core release records its binding facts, kb catalog build --platforms configurator/data/platforms.json adds requires_owner from that file's bindings map.
  • Optional on any version: osv, its known-vulnerability scan (scanned_at, database, findings); on a kb-core version: bindings, the drivers it has a handler binding for. The resolver reads neither; kb sbom and the site report the scans.
  • Optional on a driver or kb-core version: language, its language floor (standard, profile, compilers, tested, source), copied from driver.yml (or kb-core's kb.yml) at that tag; a tag without the block records the registry default, C++20 with profile KB-CPP20 (source: default). An entry without the field is read the same way (Language floor).
