docs.title: Rules
docs.text: Resolution has two phases. Shape checks the image alone; if it finds anything, resolution stops with those errors. Semantics then checks every rule and reports every error it finds, not only the first. Errors and warnings are sorted by code, then subject.

docs.title: Shape
docs.text: Field Rule Code, subject the document a mapping KB-RES-001, $ any mapping no field outside the schema KB-RES-022, the field's path schema the integer 1 (a number with no fraction) KB-RES-001 if missing or not an integer, KB-RES-021 if another integer image a name [a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,62} KB-RES-001, image kb_core.version, mcu.family strings KB-RES-001, the path mcu.target, mcu.port.version, rtos strings when present KB-RES-001, the path drivers[i] a name, or {name, version?} with strings KB-RES-001, drivers[i] or drivers[i].name buses.<name> name [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}; {model, devices, kind?}; devices are strings KB-RES-001, the path language {standard, compilers?}: 17, 20, 23 or 26; compilers: gcc, clang, msvc, arm_gcc, esp_idf KB-RES-001, KB-RES-022

docs.title: Semantics
docs.text:
1. kb-core: the version must be in the catalogue (KB-RES-002, kb_core.version). An rc warns (KB-RES-W01, kb-core); a dev revision warns (KB-RES-W03, kb-core).
  2. MCU: the family must exist (KB-RES-003) and be supported with a port (KB-RES-004), subject mcu.family. The target defaults to the family's first and must be one of its targets (KB-RES-005, mcu.target).
  3. RTOS: defaults to the family's. It must exist (KB-RES-006), be implemented (KB-RES-007: a backend that is planned, not yet available) and be allowed on the family (KB-RES-008: ESP-IDF needs FreeRTOS); subject rtos.
  4. Port: an extracted port takes the image's version or the default rule, which must exist (KB-RES-020, mcu.port.version; an rc warns KB-RES-W01, port-<family>). An in-tree port has kb-core's version; naming another is KB-RES-020.
  5. Drivers, subject the driver name: listed once (KB-RES-010); in the catalogue (KB-RES-009); a requested version is X.Y.Z or X.Y.Z-rc.N (KB-RES-012) and exists (KB-RES-011, also when a driver has no version at all). The default version is kb-core's pin when that tag is catalogued, else the newest release, else the newest rc. An rc warns (KB-RES-W01). The MCU gate: the version's mcus holds any or the family (KB-RES-013). kb_core_min, when set, is not above the selected kb-core (KB-RES-014).
  6. Buses (ADR-0009), in name order, subject <bus>/<device> unless noted: the model is owner or guarded (KB-RES-015, buses.<bus>.model); an explicit kind is a known bus kind (KB-RES-023, buses.<bus>.kind), otherwise the kind comes from a name like i2c0, spi1 or uart2, or stays unknown; a device appears once per bus (KB-RES-010) and is a listed driver (KB-RES-016); a requires_owner chip is not on a guarded bus (KB-RES-018); a known kind is one of the driver version's buses (KB-RES-019). A device on more than one bus is KB-RES-017, subject the device: one chip, one bus, one thread model.
  7. Language (Language floor), only when the image has a language block: kb-core's floor (standard above the image's is KB-RES-024, subject kb-core) and each driver version's floor (subject the driver name) are checked; a compiler the image names whose floor in the part is newer is KB-RES-025. Each such error carries alternative: the newest catalogued version (a release, else an rc; never dev) that fits, or null. A driver named without a version whose default does not fit takes that alternative instead and warns KB-RES-W04 (with the same alternative); only when nothing fits is it an error. A part with no language block is read as C++20 with the KB-CPP20 compiler floors. Compiler versions are quoted strings such as "12.2".

docs.title: Versions
docs.text: Tags are vX.Y.Z or vX.Y.Z-rc.N only. Order: by X, Y, Z, then a release after every rc of the same X.Y.Z, rcs by N. In a driver's catalogue entry the version is the tag without v (0.1.0-rc.1); its driver.yml carries the release it is a candidate for (0.1.0), which kb catalog build checks (PIN-006).

docs.title: Lock
docs.text: For a valid image: schema, image, kb_core (version, repository, tag, commit, kind, licence, authors), mcu (family, target), rtos, parts (utils, rtos, interfaces, and handlers when a driver is selected), ports (one entry), drivers (sorted by name), buses (sorted by name, devices sorted) and cmake (KB_MCU and KB_RTOS upper-case, KB_PARTS joined by ;, KB_ENABLE_<NAME> ON per driver). When the image has a language block, the lock also records it (language: standard and the sorted compilers, {} when none) and cmake gains KB_CPP_STANDARD; without one, both are absent, so the files of an image without the block do not change.

docs.title: Emitted files
docs.text:
Byte-for-byte the same from both implementations:

File Content kb-image.lock.yml One comment line, then the lock as canonical JSON (sorted keys, two-space indent, final newline); JSON is YAML, so any YAML or JSON parser reads it CMakePresets.json Presets version 6, one configure preset named after the image with the cmake values kb_image.cmake set() of KB_MCU, KB_RTOS, KB_PARTS, each KB_ENABLE_* in name order, then each KB_DRIVER_<NAME>_DIR as ${CMAKE_CURRENT_LIST_DIR}/external/drivers/<folder> (the file sits at the project root) kb-fetch.sh POSIX shell, run inside the user's git repository: adds kb-core, an extracted port and each driver as submodules under external/ (layout below), fetches each tag, refuses it when it no longer names the locked commit, checks out the commit (a dev kb-core: fetched by commit), removes any branch entry, stages the result; --verify only checks that every submodule is at its commit

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
One layout for every user project:

<project>/
├── kb-image.yml, kb-image.lock.yml, kb_image.cmake, CMakePresets.json, kb-fetch.sh
└── external/
    ├── kb-core/                 at its tag (an in-tree port is inside it: external/kb-core/components/ports/<family>)
    ├── port-<family>/           an extracted port, at its tag
    └── components/drivers/driver-<chip>/   each selected driver, at its tag

Drivers sit beside kb-core, not inside it: a submodule of the project cannot hold another submodule of the same project. The presets fragment carries the same KB_DRIVER_<NAME>_DIR values with ${sourceDir}.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text:
kb outdated, kb upgrade and the site's Open an existing project view plan an upgrade with one pure function of (catalogue, image, optional lock, targets, allow_rc). Neither front end reads a file, a clock or the network while planning; the result is the same rows, codes, new image, lock and report bytes from both.

  1. Current versions. With a lock, every version comes from it (kb-core, an extracted port, each driver): an image may leave versions out, and "today's default" moves as the catalogue grows. A lock that disagrees with the image, names a driver the image lacks, misses one it has, or is not a schema-1 lock is KB-UPG-002. Without a lock, unnamed versions are the resolver's defaults today. The current image must resolve (KB-UPG-001, followed by the resolver's own errors). Where the lock's commit (or kind) for a version differs from the catalogue's entry of that version (a kb-core development revision whose version has since been tagged, so the catalogue lists only the release; a moved tag; a lock from another catalogue), the row's from kind is the lock's, the row changes (lock_differs) and KB-UPG-W04 names both commits.
  2. Targets. to maps kb-core, port-<family> (an extracted port; an in-tree port moves with kb-core) or a driver name to a version. An unknown name is KB-UPG-003; a version not in the catalogue (or not a version) KB-UPG-004; one older than the current version KB-UPG-005. A named target may be a release candidate or a kb-core development revision; it must pass the driver gates below, else the gate's resolver code is the error.
  3. Order. kb-core first, then an extracted port, then each driver in name order, because the drivers' kb_core_min is checked against kb-core's new version.
  4. Candidates. Without a target: the catalogued versions above the current one (at or above it for a dev revision, so its release replaces it) of kind release, plus rc with allow_rc; never dev. A dev revision X.Y.Z is not offered its own X.Y.Z-rc.N, which sorts below it (a policy choice: a dev build is ahead of its candidates). Newest first, the first that passes the gates is taken; each newer one that fails is recorded as held back with the code of its first failing gate. No candidate: the current version stays.
  5. Driver gates, in this order, the resolver's own rules: MCU family (KB-RES-013), kb_core_min against the new kb-core (KB-RES-014), a requires_owner chip on a guarded bus (KB-RES-018), the bus kind in use (KB-RES-019), and, when the image has a language block, its standard and compilers (KB-RES-024, KB-RES-025; kb-core's candidates pass this gate too).
  6. New image. The image with every version explicit (kb-core, an extracted port, each driver, drivers sorted by name), everything else unchanged; it is resolved again and its lock and files are the plan's. Its warnings (KB-RES-W01, KB-RES-W03) join the plan's.
  7. Rows, one per component (kb-core, an extracted port, each driver): from and to with their kinds, change (none, major, minor, patch, prerelease when only the rc number or the kind changes, or commit when only the lock's commit differs), lock_differs, breaking, the newest release and a newer rc, the held-back versions, the known-vulnerability ids of both versions (null when not scanned), the ids the upgrade fixes, and the release page of the new tag.
  8. Breaking follows SemVer: a new major; before 1.0 a new minor, and before 0.1 a new patch. An rc moving to its own release is not breaking. Breaking rows warn KB-UPG-W01, held-back versions KB-UPG-W02, remaining known vulnerabilities KB-UPG-W03.

Both front ends read the same catalogue: the kb tool takes kb's catalog.json or the configurator's data/catalog.json, which it converts field for field as the site does (from_site in tools/kb/catalog.py, kbCatalog in configurator/js/shared.js, compared by a test on the shipped catalogue). Per-version facts (requires_owner, osv) are carried in both.

Emitted files of a successful plan, byte-for-byte the same from both implementations: kb-image.yml (one fixed style: block keys, flow values, every string double-quoted, so any YAML parser reads back the plan's image), the lock and the three files of Emitted files, and kb-upgrade.md (a table of the rows, breaking changes with their release pages, held-back versions, fixed and remaining vulnerabilities, warnings, next steps).

docs.title: Vectors
docs.text:
tests/resolver/vectors/NNN-<case>.json: a description, the catalogue (a file under catalogs/ or inline), the image, and the expectation (ok, the codes and subjects of errors and warnings with the alternative of those that name one, and for a valid image the lock and every emitted file). tools/kb/tests/test_vectors.py and tests/resolver/run_js_vectors.mjs run them all; CTest runs both (kb_cli_unit, kb_resolver_js_vectors). Every code above appears in at least one vector, which a test checks.

tests/resolver/vectors/upgrade/NNN-<case>.json: a description, the catalogue (../catalogs/upgrade.json and others, or inline), the image, an optional lock, options (to, allow_rc) and the expectation (ok, codes and subjects, the rows, the new image and lock, and every emitted file). tools/kb/tests/test_upgrade.py, tests/resolver/run_js_upgrade_vectors.mjs (run by run_js_vectors.mjs) and configurator/tests/project.test.mjs run them; every upgrade code appears in a vector, and a seeded test feeds the same mutated images, locks and targets to both planners.

docs.title: Assurance
docs.text: What kb-core claims, at which level, how each claim is verified, and what kb-core is not. Decision: ADR-0011. Records: Assurance records.

docs.title: Level and role
docs.text:
• kb-core is at the handbook's level high, like the drivers.
  • Drivers and handlers are not the safety layer. A product's safety functions must reach their safe state without any driver or handler call succeeding; kb-core provides bounded, documented building blocks (bounded waits, health states, liveness) that a safety layer may use as inputs.
  • safety is a later option per component, by a new decision record, once a MISRA checker accepted for that purpose is obtained and a product intends to qualify the component.

docs.title: Claim
docs.text:
kb-core's own code under components/lib/ complies with MISRA C++:2023 with one recorded library deviation above the boundary files (DEV-KBC-004, the *Ref adapters in kb/interfaces/refs.hpp, ADR-0011 amendment). Boundary files comply with the deviations recorded for them. Each MCU port makes the same claim for its own folder with its own records. The MCU SDKs, RTOS kernels and vendor HALs are SOUP and outside the claim. Drivers are covered by their own release evidence at their pinned tags.

The scan's paths are the library code: each part's public headers (components/lib/<part>/inc) and the RTOS boundary files. Test code (unit, compile-fail and fuzz tests, the host test port in components/lib/interfaces/host/ and the std::thread host backend in host/) is built with the same flags and analysed by clang-tidy and cppcheck, but is outside the MISRA claim.

MISRA C++:2023 scope Figure description and sources

Four zones, from strongest claim to none. kb-core's own code under components/lib/** is claimed compliant with zero repository deviations: kb::utils and kb::interfaces (the contracts and the host port) in phase 1, the kb::rtos public API in phase 2, and kb::handlers with the bindings in phase 4. Boundary files, the files that touch vendor code, are compliant with recorded deviations: the RTOS backends' (components/lib/rtos/backends/freertos/_boundary.cpp, DEV-KBC-) and the ports' (components/ports/esp32/src/_boundary.cpp, DEV-KBP-, in their own records); the claim for kb-core's own code includes them. Each driver- at its pinned tag is covered by its own evidence, its own ru-misra run at level high. SOUP (ESP-IDF, STM32 HAL, FreeRTOS, ThreadX, mbedTLS) is out of scope, listed with versions, included with -isystem and never reported.

Drawn from: docs/model/misra-scope.matrix.yml.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text: Phase Scope Target Gate P1 (M1, M3) components/lib/utils, components/lib/interfaces contracts, the host port Zero findings, zero repository deviations ru-misra at high, host and Cortex-M, from the first commit of each part P2 (M2) components/lib/rtos public API, none backend Zero deviations Same P3 (M2, M4) components/lib/rtos/backends/freertos/*_boundary.cpp, components/ports/esp32/src/*_boundary.cpp Findings only at SDK call sites, each a recorded deviation Same, plus a second review of every boundary diff P4 (M4, M5) components/lib/handlers bindings and handlers Zero deviations (driver headers compiled, not reported) Same P5 (M5) Compliance matrix for every guideline Complete per release Handbook misra_matrix.py

docs.title: The boundary-file method
docs.text:
• An SDK or RTOS header is included only by a .cpp listed in a boundary-files.yml; never by a header. The include checker and the symbol lint enforce it.
  • SDK include directories are passed with -isystem, and the MISRA scan's paths lists only kb-core's own folders, so findings inside SDK headers are never reported or deviated.
  • A boundary file holds only thin typed wrappers in an anonymous namespace: convert kb types to SDK types, call, convert the result to kb::Result with the vendor code in detail. No logic beyond a retry count.
  • Each remaining finding at an SDK call site gets one record (id, check: misra/Rule X.Y.Z, where, reason, mitigation, approved_by, date, review_by); a marker in code cites the id; a marker that deviates nothing fails the scan.
  • Each boundary file has a host test that links it against a fake of the SDK functions it calls (a link seam), so the conversion and error mapping are tested without the SDK.

docs.title: Bus access: non-blocking reads and held transactions
docs.text: Decision: ADR-0016. Every contract call is bounded; this page is about the two cases bounded is not enough for: a hot-path read that must not wait at all, and a sequence of transfers or calls that must not be interleaved.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text: Rule Detail Safety paths never wait on a bus A safety task cuts outputs first and reads only published snapshots (Latest(), Health(), the liveness verdict) Hot paths never block A read on the control path is started in one owner pass and collected in a later one (AsyncPoller); a poller over a port whose Start() waits does not compile unless it says AsyncUse::MayBlock One transfer in flight per port object Start...() returns Busy while one is in flight Deadlines bound everything A transfer not done by its deadline completes as Timeout; a completion after the deadline is Timeout too Buffers outlive the transfer AsyncPoller owns them; its destructor cancels a transfer in flight Sequences run held A multi-chunk range or several calls run under one hold: Guarded::Hold() or the owner's BusDomain::Hold() with OwnerAccess::Held() Never hold two buses Every wait is bounded, so a violation ends in Timeout, never a hang

docs.title: The asynchronous contract
docs.text:
kb/interfaces/async.hpp: I2cAsync (StartWrite, StartWriteRead, StartRead) and SpiAsync (StartTransfer) are the synchronous contracts plus Poll(now), Cancel() and kNonBlocking.

Call Returns Start...(..., kb::utils::Deadline) Ok (started), Busy, InvalidArgument, Timeout (deadline passed), NotReady; never waits Poll(now) AsyncPoll: Idle, Pending, or Done with Completion() as a kb::Result<std::size_t>; reported once Cancel() Ok; afterwards nothing touches the buffers, a racing completion is dropped, the next Poll() is Idle

AsyncFromSync<Bus, Clock> serves the contract from a synchronous port (Start() runs the transfer, the deadline rules still hold, kNonBlocking is false), so a binding builds on every port today and the remaining wait is visible in its type. What each port adds for a native form is listed in ADR-0016.

One asynchronous read Figure description and sources

The Owner task starts the transfer in one service pass and collects the result in a later one; no pass waits. In pass n the Owner task calls StartWriteRead on the AsyncPoller, which owns the buffers and asks the Port (I2cAsync or SpiAsync) to start with a deadline; the port answers Ok at once. A Step(now) in the same pass makes the poller call Poll(now), which reports Pending. The peripheral ISR then finishes the transfer and sets the owner's event flag. In pass n+1 the poll reports Done, Ok with the count, and Completion() is Ok with the bytes held. Past the deadline the result is Done with Timeout, late data included; Cancel() makes the poller Idle and releases the buffers.

Drawn from: docs/model/async-poll.seq.yml.

docs.title: In an owner-task access
docs.text:
struct PressureSampler {
  kb::handlers::AsyncPoller<Bus, 4U>& poller;
  kb::handlers::Seqlock<uint16_t>& out;

  [[nodiscard]] bool Service(const kb::handlers::ServiceKey& key, kb::Instant now) noexcept {
    static_cast<void>(key);
    if (!poller.InFlight()) {  // start the next read; returns at once
      static_cast<void>(poller.StartWriteRead(0x48U, kRegister, 2U, now, kb::Microseconds{800U}));
    }
    const kb::iface::AsyncPoll p = poller.Step(now);  // one poll, never a wait
    if (p.Completion().IsOk()) {
      out.Publish(Decode(poller.Received()));
    }
    return true;
  }
};
// The owner task: spi1.Service(now, sampler, other_handlers...) every step.

AsyncPoller counts starts, refusals, completions by outcome, cancels and the longest start-to-completion time (Stats()).

docs.title: Held transactions
docs.text:
BusDomain::Hold(timeout) returns a BusHold: [[nodiscard]], move-only, made only by the domain. On a guarded bus it is the bus mutex, taken within timeout; on an owner bus it is the service-pass flag, taken at once or not at all (a hold and a pass exclude each other, and a refused one is counted as a violation). Bus() is the bus while held and null after Release(); Bus() on a temporary hold does not compile, since the hold would be released before the bus is used.

Model Held calls Order and waits Guarded auto held = rom.Hold(timeout); then at25040b::Write(held, ...), held.Request(...), held.Sample(...) Handler mutex, then bus mutex, as every call; both bounded. Calls on a hold that was not had return Timeout, after Release() NotReady Owner On the owner task, between passes: auto bus = spi1.Hold(t); auto a = enc.Held(bus); auto b = rom.Held(bus); Never waits. Calls run inline; a hold of another bus type does not compile, of another domain object or released refuses with NotReady

A guarded handler has no Held(BusHold&): taking its handler lock while holding the bus would invert the lock order.

Held transactions Figure description and sources

Guarded bus, on the left: task X calls Guarded::Hold(timeout), takes the handler mutex first and then the bus mutex through BusDomain::Hold, both with a bounded wait, and holds the bus in GuardedHeld for several calls (Request, Sample and so on) with nothing in between; another task's plain Request waits (bounded) or returns Timeout. Owner bus, on the right: the owner task takes BusDomain::Hold() between passes, which never waits, and sets the pass flag while the hold is held; OwnerAccess::Held(hold) runs inline calls for several handlers, and Service(now, ...) reports Busy while the hold is held and the violation is counted.

Drawn from: docs/model/bus-hold.graph.yml.

What needs it: an at25040b range of several chunks (the integration test writes a record in three parts while another task writes the same range; the record lands whole), as5047u angle and velocity read as one pair, ads7952 mode programming followed by its frames, se05x T=1 block chains.

docs.title: Configurator
docs.text:
How a user gets exactly the kb-core configuration they need, pinned and with evidence: the image file, the kb command-line tool and the hosted configurator site. Decision: ADR-0013. Skeleton page: configurator/index.html.

Generators and the configurator Figure description and sources

From the top. Inputs are single sources published with each kb-core release: each pinned driver's driver.yml (bus, mcus, peripheral, kb_core_min, ports, binding), the release lock with the kb-core tag and SHA and every pin with its tag and SHA, the evidence (SBOM in SPDX and CycloneDX, CVE scan, licence report), the tested version sets kb YYYY.N and, later, board.yml with buses, pins and chips. One resolver specification has two front ends, the kb command line (Python standard library only, tools/kb) and the static configurator site on GitHub Pages, where the user picks MCU, RTOS, drivers and handlers. It resolves drivers, then handlers, interfaces and parts, and applies the MCU gates, kb_core_min and the thread model per bus. It produces byte-for-byte repeatable downloads: kb-image.yml (the selection), git commands (clone at the tag, check the SHA, init only the enabled submodules), a CMake presets fragment with kb_image.cmake, the evidence for the selection (SBOM, CVEs, licences, compatibility rows, tested set) and, later, a project archive.

Drawn from: docs/model/generator-flow.graph.yml.

docs.title: The image
docs.text:
An image is the selection one firmware build uses: MCU family and target, port version, RTOS backend, kb-core version, drivers (each at a catalogued version, by default kb-core's pin) and the thread model of each bus. It is one file (schema); the commits come from the catalogue into the lock, never from the image:

# kb-image.yml (in the board HAL or product repository)
image: example-board-a
schema: 1
kb_core: {version: 0.4.0}
mcu: {family: esp32, target: esp32s3}
rtos: freertos
drivers: [pf1550, bmp581, {name: tmc9660, version: 0.2.0-rc.1}]
buses:
  i2c0: {model: guarded, devices: [pf1550, bmp581]}
  spi1: {model: owner, devices: [tmc9660]}

docs.title: The site
docs.text:
A static site on GitHub Pages: no server, no account, no cookies, no analytics, no third-party script at run time.

Step What the user does What the site does 1 Picks MCU family and target Offers the kb-core versions and ports that support it 2 Picks the RTOS backend Checks it against the MCU (ESP-IDF needs FreeRTOS) 3 Picks a kb-core version or a tested set kb YYYY.N Loads that release's catalogue, lock and evidence 4 Picks drivers and handlers Resolves drivers to handlers to interfaces to parts; applies the MCU gates and kb_core_min 5 Declares the thread model of each bus Refuses a bus with both models, and kRequiresOwner chips on a guarded bus 6 Downloads kb-image.yml, the git commands, the CMake presets fragment, and the evidence

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
Every download is byte-for-byte repeatable: sorted keys, no timestamps (the CVE scan date is a separate field), every component named by version and commit SHA.

# In the project's git repository: every part as a submodule under external/ at its tag, each commit checked
sh kb-fetch.sh            # external/kb-core, external/drivers/driver-pf1550, ... (no branch, no --recursive)
sh kb-fetch.sh --verify   # in CI: every submodule still at its pinned commit

The layout is the same for the CLI and the site (Assembler and resolver).

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Evidence Format Source SBOM SPDX 2.3 JSON and CycloneDX 1.6 JSON The release's SBOM, filtered to the selection Known CVEs A report per component with scan date and database version Scanned in the release job, re-scanned on a schedule Licences A table of each component's SPDX licence and copyright holder The SBOM Compatibility The catalogue rows of the selection catalog/compat.yml of the release Tested set The tested version set the selection belongs to and the configurations that passed, or "untested combination" Tested version sets

The evidence is produced and signed by kb-core's release job; the site only filters and presents it.

docs.title: The kb tool
docs.text: One Python tool in tools/kb/ (the kb tool): kb catalog build, kb resolve (the lock, presets, kb_image.cmake, the fetch script) and kb sbom. The site and the tool implement one resolver specification (Assembler and resolver, ADR-0014) and pass the same golden test vectors (tests/resolver/vectors/). driver.yml may carry two optional fields the catalogue reads: license (else the LICENSE file decides) and requires_owner (kRequiresOwner).

docs.title: Phases
docs.text: Phase When Delivers P0 Now Skeleton page in configurator/, this design, ADR-0013 P1 M4 Catalogue as JSON, kb-image.yml, git commands, presets; kb image check in CI P2 M6 SBOM, CVE results, licence report and tested sets per release and per selection P3 M7 Project archive from kb-app-template, board.yml pin tables; move to kb-configurator

docs.title: Fault evidence: liveness and the fault journal
docs.text:
Fault evidence must survive the reset the fault causes, and a watchdog must only be kicked when the work, not just a loop, is alive. Two pieces serve that: the liveness verdict (kb::handlers::LivenessMonitor) and the fault journal (kb::utils::FaultJournal<Store, Slots>), joined by kb::handlers::HealthJournal on the supervisor task.

Fault evidence path Figure description and sources

Handler health is read lock-free and only its edges go to the HealthJournal. The LivenessMonitor's verdict goes there too, and the watchdog owner is kicked only when nothing is stale. The journal appends with one bounded store write into a FaultJournal ring of 32-byte CRC-32 records with a sequence number; at boot the port's reset reason is recorded with RecordReset. The store (RTC or no-init RAM, NVS, FRAM, flash) belongs to the port; after a reset Open() finds the newest record and skips a torn slot.

Drawn from: docs/model/fault-journal.graph.yml.

docs.title: Liveness
docs.text: Each handler beats when it is serviced or called (LivenessBeat). A monitor watches up to 32 beats, each with its own window (the stall budget). A context that stops on purpose declares it: Park() makes a beat never stale, and its window starts again when it beats or Resume()s. Verdict(now) gives the stale and parked bits and kick, true only when at least one beat is watched and none is stale; the watchdog owner (in the port) kicks only then. The monitor never calls a handler and never blocks.

docs.title: The fault journal
docs.text:
Property How Fixed size, no allocation Slots records of 32 bytes in the store (2 to 4096); the journal object holds four counters Integrity Magic, format version, CRC-32 (Crc32Ieee) over 28 bytes Torn write A reset in the middle of a write leaves a slot whose CRC fails: Open() counts it as torn and skips it; the next append overwrites it Wrap-around Appends go to the slot after the newest; the oldest is overwritten; sequences wrap and compare modulo 2^32 Bounded write Append() is one store write of 32 bytes, no scan After a reset Open() reads each slot once and continues after the newest valid sequence Reset reason RecordReset(reason, port_code, now) at boot: ResetReason in value, the port's raw code in detail

Record layout (little-endian): magic 0x4A4B (bytes 0-1), version 1 (2), kind (3), sequence (4-7), time in microseconds (8-15), source (16-17), kb::Status (18), reserved 0 (19), detail (20-23), value (24-27), CRC-32 of bytes 0-27 (28-31). ParseRecord() reports Empty (no magic: never written or erased), CrcMismatch (torn or corrupt) or Unsupported (another version, a reserved byte set, an unknown kind or status).

docs.title: The store
docs.text:
A JournalStore has Capacity(), Read(offset, span) and Write(offset, span), each bounded. kb-core ships RamJournalStore<Bytes> (host tests, and ports that place it in RAM kept across a reset). Ports add flash, NVS, FRAM or backup-register stores; a flash store hides erase units behind Write() or gives each slot its own write unit (ADR-0016 lists what each port adds).

kb::utils::RamJournalStore<16U * kb::utils::kFaultRecordBytes> store{};  // the port places it in no-init RAM
kb::utils::FaultJournal<decltype(store), 16U> journal{store};
static_cast<void>(journal.Open());
static_cast<void>(journal.RecordReset(port::ResetReason(), port::ResetCode(), kb::rtos::Now()));
const auto last_fault = journal.FindNewest(kb::utils::RecordKind::Fault);  // the evidence of the last run

docs.title: The health path
docs.text:
HealthJournal<Sink, N> writes edges only: a handler entering Faulted (Fault: its last status, the driver's code, failures in a row), a faulted handler serving again (Health), and a liveness watch going stale (Stall: the newly stale bits). A refused record is retried at the next observation. One context: the supervisor task that reads every handler's Health() and the verdict.

kb::handlers::HealthJournal<decltype(journal), 4U> evidence{journal};
// supervisor step:
static_cast<void>(evidence.Observe(0U, kImuId, imu.Health(), now));
const kb::handlers::LivenessVerdict v = monitor.Verdict(now);
static_cast<void>(evidence.ObserveLiveness(v, now));
if (v.kick) { port::KickWatchdog(); }

docs.text: What Where Record layout against a golden record, every parse refusal, store bounds, scans after a reset, torn writes, sequence wrap, reads by age, the reset record components/lib/utils/tests/test_fault_journal.cpp Parsing and scanning arbitrary bytes (fuzz) components/lib/utils/fuzz/fuzz_utils_journal.cpp Health and liveness edges, retries, records after a reset components/lib/handlers/tests/test_health_journal.cpp Parked beats and the verdict components/lib/handlers/tests/test_liveness.cpp

docs.title: Handlers
docs.text: What a handler is, how it starts, how it stays healthy, and how several tasks use it. Decisions: ADR-0009 (thread models) and ADR-0010 (start-up pipeline). Status: implemented in components/lib/handlers/ (the core in common/, one binding per driver in bindings/); every handler has its page under Handlers.

docs.title: What a handler is
docs.text:
A handler binds one driver instance to one device on a bus domain, one configuration and a health record, and exposes a typed API that returns kb::Result. It is the only object a HAL manager talks to for that chip.

Handler<Chip>   (kb::handlers::HandlerCore<Derived, Driver>, CRTP, ADR-0006)
├── Binding          satisfies the driver's port over kb contracts (hook bases or hand-written)
├── std::optional<Driver>   emplaced by the start-up pipeline, destroyed on failure or Deinitialize()
├── StartupPlan      constexpr list of declared stages (ADR-0010)
├── Config           driver config + handler config (address, deadlines, retry policy, health thresholds)
├── Health           state, consecutive failures, last error + detail + time, counters (seqlock snapshot)
└── Diagnostics      common header first, then chip counters

The core is single-threaded: it holds no lock. Thread safety comes from the access facade its bus declares (thread models).

Rules:

  • Construction stores references, does no I/O, touches no RTOS object and cannot fail; a handler works as a static object.
  • EnsureInitialized() is the one start (handbook ADR-0021). Reads and writes never start or restart the chip: before the start has succeeded they return NotInitialized and send nothing.
  • No board value inside kb-core: addresses, pins, deadlines and thresholds arrive in Config from the HAL.
  • A driver is never changed to suit a handler; the binding adapts.

docs.title: Start-up pipeline
docs.text:
EnsureInitialized() runs the chip's start-up plan: a constexpr list of declared stages, executed by one runner in HandlerCore. A plan lists only the stage kinds its chip needs, in a fixed order; one driver call may cover several kinds.

The handler start-up pipeline Figure description and sources

Two columns. Stages, in order: one runner and a declared plan of stages per chip, in a fixed order: Power (rail or enable pin), HostReset (reset pulse, hold, release), Boot (boot time, ready pin, advertisement), Link (transport session, T=1 or SHTP), Identify (ID, select, probe, capabilities), Secure (secure channel, platform SCP03), Configure (apply the configuration), Verify (read-back, lifecycle state), then Ready, when the handler serves calls. Plans of three chips: a plan lists only the stages its chip needs, and every stage is synchronous or polled and bounded by a deadline. Most drivers declare one step, Start, that calls the driver's EnsureInitialized(); Identify and Configure happen inside the driver. The bno08x resets with Begin(cfg), synchronous, boots and links by calling Poll() until Ready(), polled, and configures with SetFeature operations until OpDone, polled. The se05x sets platform keys with SetPlatformKeys() (no I/O), opens the link, identifies and secures with Open(), synchronous and bounded by the link, and optionally verifies the lifecycle state. An optional stage is skipped, not failed, when the HAL supplies no pin, rail or key for it.

Drawn from: docs/model/handler-startup.pipeline.yml.

Kind Does Power Enable a rail or an enable pin, wait its settle time HostReset Host-driven reset: pulse, hold, release Boot Wait the boot time or a ready condition (ready pin, advertisement) Link Bring up a transport session (T=1, SHTP) Identify Read the ID, select an applet, probe capabilities Secure Open a secure channel needed for normal use (platform SCP03) Configure Apply the configuration Verify Read back, check the lifecycle state

Each stage declares the driver call, sync (one call) or polled (repeated until done), its deadline (a Config field), and whether it is optional (skipped when the HAL supplies no pin, rail or key for it). The runner keeps a StartupReport: the stage reached, the kb::Status, the driver's own error in detail, and the time each stage took. On a failure it runs the plan's abort call, destroys the driver and stays Constructed, so the next EnsureInitialized() starts from the first stage again.

StartStep(now) runs at most one step of the current stage and returns Pending, Ok or the failure; an owner task calls it from Service(now) and never blocks. EnsureInitialized() is the loop over StartStep(), waiting with kb::rtos::SleepFor between polls and bounded by the sum of the stage deadlines.

docs.title: The plans
docs.text:
Chip Stages Calls Most drivers (21) Identify + Configure; optional Power, HostReset driver.EnsureInitialized() (sync); the optional stages only when the HAL supplies the pin and the driver does not drive it itself bno08x HostReset Begin(cfg) (sync): validates, brings the port up, pulses NRST when the port has SetReset Boot + Link Poll(now) until Ready() (polled): reset wait, advertisement, initialise handshake; deadline from startup_timeout_ms; fails when the driver enters Faulted Configure one SetFeature per configured sensor, polled until each OpDone; deadline from op_timeout_ms se05x Link + Identify + Secure SetPlatformKeys() first when the HAL supplies key handles (no I/O, never keys), then Open() (sync, every wait bounded by the link): link, card data, applet select, feature bits, capability probes, lifecycle state, platform SCP03 when required; skipped when IsOpen() Verify (optional) lifecycle state against what the HAL expects

A plan lists each kind once, in kind order (checked at compile time), so two calls that serve kinds of one stage are one stage: se05x sets its key handles at the start of its Open() stage, and bno08x without NRST declares Link = Begin(cfg), then Identify = Poll(now) until Ready(), then Configure.

What stays outside the pipeline, and the two driver-level waivers to handbook ADR-0021 (W-01 bno08x Begin/Poll, W-02 se05x Open/Close), are in ADR-0010. No handler-level waiver is needed. se05x applet sessions (UserID, AESKey, ECKey) are per transaction, opened by handler calls inside a held bus transaction.

docs.title: Lifecycle and health
docs.text:
Handler lifecycle and health Figure description and sources

Six states. A handler starts Unknown (constructed, no I/O). EnsureInitialized or StartStep moves it to Starting, which walks the declared stages, each bounded by its deadline; the last stage makes it Ready, a failing stage makes it Faulted, and a failed start leaves the driver destroyed so the next start begins again from the first stage. A failing call makes a Ready handler Degraded until the next call succeeds; fault_after failures in a row, or one fatal error (the chip reset or lost its state), make it Faulted. Recover() moves Faulted to Recovering with a backoff that doubles on each failure, and is refused after max_attempts; Recovering returns to Ready when the plan succeeds and to Faulted when it fails. Deinitialize() returns Ready or Faulted to Unknown. Only EnsureInitialized, StartStep, Deinitialize and Recover change the lifecycle: calls never start or restart the chip.

Drawn from: docs/model/handler-health.state.yml.

  • Health states: Unknown (not started); Starting; Ready; Degraded (failures below fault_after); Faulted (threshold reached, a start failed, or the binding calls the error fatal: the chip reset or lost its state); Recovering. When max_attempts recoveries in a row failed, Recover() refuses with Fault and the handler stays Faulted: the HAL decides on its safe state. A caller's own mistake (InvalidArgument) is recorded but not counted against the chip.
  • Recover() is explicit and never triggered by a read. It runs on the owner task (model O) or under the guarded locks (model G), at the HAL's chosen time, with backoff: bus recovery when the failure was a bus failure, then the plan's recovery (generic: Deinitialize() and the plan; se05x: the driver's Recover() ladder before Close() and the plan; bno08x: a hub restart is a Reset event and health Degraded, the plan runs again only after Faulted).
  • Health() is lock-free to read (a seqlock snapshot), so a supervisor can poll every handler without contending with its users.
  • A handler is not a safety function: a safety layer must reach its safe state without a handler call succeeding (ADR-0011).

docs.title: Thread models
docs.text:
Each bus declares one model; the handler's access facade must match it (compile error otherwise).

Handler thread models Figure description and sources

Two models, declared per bus, one above the other; callers on other tasks use one access API in both. Model O, the owner task, is the default for real-time buses: one real-time task, a kb::rtos::Thread, calls Service(now) at a fixed rate, steps the single-threaded cores of handlers A and B on BusDomain without a mutex (an owner check instead), publishes each step to a lock-free SeqlockSnapshot and drains a bounded command queue with completion. Other tasks read the latest snapshot with Latest() (a lock-free copy) or post a request with Request(cmd, timeout) and wait. Model G, the guarded facade, is for slow, sporadic devices: tasks X and Y each call Call(timeout, op) on a Guarded handler, C or D, which takes the handler lock and then, with a bounded wait (TryLockFor), the bus lock of BusDomain, which has a mutex, recovery and statistics. An interrupt service routine only sets event flags or notifies the owner task; it never calls a handler. Model O, owner task Model G, guarded facade For High-rate or timing-critical devices; buses whose devices one loop serves; chips that need continuous servicing (bno08x) Slow, sporadic devices used from several tasks (EEPROM, expander, power IC) Default Yes, for real-time buses No Bus type BusDomain<Bus, ThreadModel::Owner>: no mutex; debug-build owner check BusDomain<Bus, ThreadModel::Guarded>: mutex, recovery, statistics Who touches the handler Only the owner task, through Service(now) Only Guarded<H>, which owns it Other tasks OwnerAccess<H>: Latest() (lock-free snapshot with sequence and age), Request(cmd, timeout) (bounded queue, waits for the owner's completion) Guarded<H>::Call(timeout, op, args...): handler lock, then bus lock, both bounded TryLockFor; Timeout and nothing sent if either is not had in time Locks None on the bus Fixed order handler then bus; never held across another handler or a user callback Start-up StartStep(now) from Service EnsureInitialized() under the guarded locks, bounded

Both facades offer the same typed operations to callers, so HAL managers and applications do not change when a bus changes model. Interrupts never call handlers: an ISR sets an event flag or notifies the owner task. A chip that must be serviced continuously declares kRequiresOwner in its binding and cannot be wrapped in Guarded<H>.

A sequence of calls that must not be interleaved (an EEPROM range of several chunks, a pair of reads) runs held: Guarded<H>::Hold(timeout) keeps both locks in the same order, and on an owner bus the owner task takes BusDomain::Hold() between passes and calls through OwnerAccess<H>::Held(hold). A hot-path read that must not wait at all uses the asynchronous contract through AsyncPoller. Both are on Bus access (ADR-0016); the liveness verdict and the fault journal are on Fault evidence.

docs.title: Uniform API across driver shapes
docs.text: Driver shape Handler mapping EnsureInitialized() / Deinitialize() (21 drivers) direct, through the generic plan bno08x Begin(config), Poll(now), events, asynchronous OpId the plan above; Service(now) calls Poll and drains events into a bounded queue; typed calls complete when the OpDone arrives or the timeout expires se05x Open() / Close() / Recover(), transactions the plan above; Deinitialize() = Close(); Recover() drives the driver's ladder first; transactions run inside a BusHold

docs.title: How applications use kb-core
docs.text:
// Application code: only the HAL facade, kb::utils and kb::rtos.
class PressureLoop final : public kb::rtos::Thread<PressureLoop, 4096U> {
 public:
  explicit PressureLoop(board::Hal& hal) noexcept : hal_(hal) {}
  kb::Status Setup() noexcept { return hal_.Pressure().EnsureStarted(); }
  void Step() noexcept {
    const kb::Result<kb::Pascal> p = hal_.Pressure().Latest();  // manager -> owner snapshot
    if (p) { filter_.Push(p.value); }
  }
 private:
  board::Hal& hal_;
  kb::utils::MovingAverage<kb::Pascal, 8U> filter_{};
};
  • The composition root (the board facade) is one object, built statically, started explicitly from the first task in a fixed order; applications receive it by reference, never through a global Instance().
  • Applications use kb::utils and kb::rtos directly; they never include kb/interfaces or kb/handlers (include checker and symbol lint).
  • HAL-free application logic (control laws, protocol state machines) lives in libraries that link only kb::utils and are tested on the host with recorded-data replay.

The sketch is illustrative; the compiled version arrives in tests/docs/ with the first handler.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text: The design of kb-core in one page: what it is, the decisions taken, the phases and their exit criteria, and the risks. Detail is on the design pages (handlers, MCU ports and repositories, assurance, configurator, design rules) and in the decision records.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. Shape. One repository, four parts (kb::utils, kb::rtos, kb::interfaces, kb::handlers), one version, drivers as submodules pinned to release or release-candidate tags. The board HAL sits above; applications use the HAL, kb::utils and kb::rtos only (architecture).
  2. Contracts. C++20 concepts only, no virtual functions; a short register of CRTP bases that carry real shared behaviour; run-time choice through type-erased *Ref values (ADR-0006).
  3. MCU ports. A separate layer from the first commit: components/ports/esp32/ is its own CMake project inside kb-core until the contracts settle, then kokeb-labs-drivers/port-esp32 (ADR-0007, ADR-0008). RTOS backends and the host test port stay in kb-core.
  4. Handlers. One driver, one bus-domain device, one configuration, a health record. A single-threaded core with one of two access facades declared per bus: an owner task with snapshots (default for real-time buses) or a lock-guarded facade (ADR-0009). Start-up is a plan of declared stages that also fits bno08x and se05x (ADR-0010).
  5. Assurance. Level high: CodeQL MISRA C++:2023 plus the compliance matrix; zero repository deviations above the boundary files. Drivers and handlers are not the safety layer; safety is a later option (ADR-0011).
  6. Releases. Each release records its own SHA and every pin in a release lock, with SBOM, CVE scan and licence report (ADR-0012).
  7. Configurator. A static site (GitHub Pages) to pick MCU, RTOS, drivers and handlers and download a repeatable, pinned project with its evidence (ADR-0013).

docs.title: Phases
docs.text:
Each phase ends on its exit criteria, not a date.

Phase roadmap Figure description and sources

Eight phases, M0 to M7, in order; there are no calendar dates, each phase ends on its exit criteria. M0 fixes decisions and guardrails: ADR-0006 to ADR-0013 recorded, and the include checker, poison build, symbol lint, preflight and CI skeleton green on empty parts. M1 to M3 deliver kb::utils v0.1, kb::rtos v0.2 and kb::interfaces v0.3: MISRA at level high with zero findings and zero deviations, the coverage floor, the mutation gate and clean fuzzing; kb::rtos adds the none and FreeRTOS backends, at-least delays, bounded locks, CRTP threads with statistics, approved boundary deviations and a clean TSan run; kb::interfaces adds concepts, a host port with fault injection, BusDomain, and conformance and compile-fail tests. M4 (v0.4) adds the ESP32 port with reviewed boundary files and the first three simple drivers bound and handled, integration, compat.yml, kb image check, configurator P1 and a bench run. M5 (v0.9 to v1.0) rolls out handlers for all drivers, simplest to hardest (bno08x, se05x and tmc9660 last), with start-up plans, both thread models, and health and recovery tests. M6 adds breadth: port-stm32, the ThreadX backend, tested version sets, and SBOM, CVE and licence evidence in the configurator (P2). M7 adds the generators: pin tables from board.yml, a project archive and HIL in scheduled CI.

docs.title: Repository family
docs.text:
The kb repository family Figure description and sources

Consumers on top. A product organisation owns the product application and its board HAL, board-. The kokeb-labs organisation holds kb-core (utils, rtos, interfaces, handlers and the driver pins), kb-hal-common (shared HAL bases), the reference board HALs kb-board- and, planned, the configurator kb-configurator, an application template kb-app-template and the tested version sets kb-trains. The kokeb-labs-drivers organisation holds each driver- (one repository per chip) and each MCU port, port- (port-esp32, port-stm32). A board HAL builds on kb-hal-common and one port; both rest on kb-core, which pins the drivers. The configurator reads kb-core releases and fills the application template; the tested version sets list sets of kb-core. Only kb-core exists today; the other names are planned.

docs.title: Design rules and their reasons
docs.text:
Rules kb-core follows everywhere, each with the failure it prevents. They come from experience with embedded stacks of this kind and from the drivers' own review history; each becomes a test, a check or a review item.

Area Rule Prevents Ownership One composition root per image (the board facade), built statically and started explicitly, in a fixed order, after the scheduler runs. kb-core types have trivial or constexpr constructors that never touch the RTOS or hardware; no kb-core type is a singleton RTOS objects created in static constructors leaving the interrupt mask raised and wedging boot; singletons that block test injection Lifecycle [[nodiscard]] kb::Result<void> for every start; the ordered start fails closed and records which step failed A start whose result is ignored, and a failed chip showing up later as a null object Errors One kb::Result<T> with a detail field; ports put the vendor code there Several error styles side by side; losing the vendor status that bench debugging needs Bus sharing One thread model per bus, declared (ADR-0009) Priority inversion and lock traffic on real-time buses; a lock-free owner and a locking caller on one bus Blocking Every interface call takes or implies a timeout; hot paths use the asynchronous Start/Poll form (bus access); safety paths never wait on a bus A busy-polling bus wrapper eating a core; a safety task stuck in a vendor bus wait until the watchdog fires Time One 64-bit monotonic microsecond clock above the ports; delays wait at least the time asked; elapsed time by unsigned subtraction Round-down delays; a vendor tick that stalls under the RTOS; clock-wrap defects after 2^31 or 2^32 Threads The CRTP thread base carries Setup/Step/Cleanup, fixed-rate waiting with overrun counts, a fail-closed start, park and wake, step-time and stack statistics Instrumentation added by hand per thread, or not at all Liveness kb::handlers::LivenessMonitor: a beat per handler or thread with a stall budget; parked ones declare it (Park()); the watchdog owner reads the verdict (fault evidence) A watchdog kicked by a loop that is alive while the work is not Boundaries Include checks plus a symbol lint on linked objects; no allowlist files, only deviation records with a review date Leaks include checks miss (macros, inline SDK calls through a re-exported header); allowlists that only grow Configuration Presets emitted by the image generator; no product macro in kb-core; one source per fact (board.yml, the lock files) Product #if spread through shared code; two sources of pin data that drift apart Testing Host-first tests per part; HAL-free logic tested with recorded-data replay; bench evidence under docs/assurance/bench/ in a fixed form Code proven only on a bench run nobody can repeat Debt Every workaround cites an issue or a deviation id; a lint counts untracked workaround and errata comments Workarounds recorded as prose that nobody tracks Provenance Code written fresh under the pipeline (ADR-0005) Carrying unknown defects and an unclear licence into kb-core

docs.title: One asynchronous read
docs.text:
One asynchronous read Figure description and sources

The Owner task starts the transfer in one service pass and collects the result in a later one; no pass waits. In pass n the Owner task calls StartWriteRead on the AsyncPoller, which owns the buffers and asks the Port (I2cAsync or SpiAsync) to start with a deadline; the port answers Ok at once. A Step(now) in the same pass makes the poller call Poll(now), which reports Pending. The peripheral ISR then finishes the transfer and sets the owner's event flag. In pass n+1 the poll reports Done, Ok with the count, and Completion() is Ok with the bytes held. Past the deadline the result is Done with Timeout, late data included; Cancel() makes the poller Idle and releases the buffers.

docs.title: Held transactions
docs.text:
Held transactions Figure description and sources

Guarded bus, on the left: task X calls Guarded::Hold(timeout), takes the handler mutex first and then the bus mutex through BusDomain::Hold, both with a bounded wait, and holds the bus in GuardedHeld for several calls (Request, Sample and so on) with nothing in between; another task's plain Request waits (bounded) or returns Timeout. Owner bus, on the right: the owner task takes BusDomain::Hold() between passes, which never waits, and sets the pass flag while the hold is held; OwnerAccess::Held(hold) runs inline calls for several handlers, and Service(now, ...) reports Busy while the hold is held and the violation is counted.

docs.title: One call through the layers
docs.text:
One call through the layers Figure description and sources

A HAL reads a register of a PF1550 power IC; solid arrows are calls, going down, and dashed arrows are returns, going up. The HAL calls the guarded handler with Call(timeout, ReadRegister) (its bus is declared guarded), which takes the handler lock and then the bus lock, both bounded, and calls the driver. The driver calls its own WriteRead hook, WriteRead(addr, tx, n, rx, m), implemented by the kb binding (Pf1550Port), which calls WriteRead(addr, span, span) on the ESP32 I2cDevice of the port. The port answers ok or an I2cFailure (AddressNack, DataNack, Bus, Timeout, BusStuck); the binding returns a bool and keeps the failure for GetLastFailure; the driver returns its Result; the handler returns a kb::Result carrying the driver's error in detail. Only the last step knows it runs on an ESP32.

docs.title: The CI flow
docs.text:
The CI flow Figure description and sources

From the top. Every change first passes tools/preflight.sh on a workstation, then reaches CI as a pull request or push. Always run: repository checks (DCO, lint, handbook, drift), layering (include checker, CMake DAG, poison build, symbol lint), layout and examples (root allowlist, retired locations, example index), own parts (host build and tests on GCC and Clang, clang-tidy, cppcheck), MISRA at level high (CodeQL pack plus kokeb-cpp20, host and Cortex-M) and pin hygiene (gitlink, lock and a release or rc tag with a green gate, never a branch). Run when the paths under components/drivers, handlers, interfaces, ports or cmake match, and on main and tags: quality (coverage, sanitizers, fuzz, mutation kill-rate gate), integration (the binding, port, MCU and RTOS matrix from catalog/compat.yml), the ESP-IDF v5.5 build of the port and the catalogue (regenerate compat.yml, fail on drift). Never re-run for components/drivers: the drivers' own tests, fuzz, mutation, MISRA, tidy and docs, which each driver runs in its own repository and which are trusted through pin hygiene. Everything ends in one required gate, ru-ci-gate; a tag vX.Y.Z adds the release assets (per-part packages, SHA256SUMS, compat.yml, release lock, SBOM, CVE scan, licence report, provenance), and a schedule re-scans releases for known vulnerabilities and records the tested version set kb YYYY.N.

docs.title: Ownership of a DMA buffer
docs.text:
Ownership of a DMA buffer Figure description and sources

Three states. A buffer is constructed in Cpu: static, line-aligned and padded. Lend moves it from Cpu to Device after the owned cache lines are cleaned or invalidated and a barrier ran. Complete moves it from Device back to Cpu after a receive is invalidated and a barrier ran; Abort with proof that the bus master stopped also returns it to Cpu. Abort without proof, or a lease destroyed while the device owns the buffer, moves it from Device to Quarantined. Recover with proof, after the peripheral was re-initialised, moves it from Quarantined to Cpu. In Quarantined a Lend is refused with a Fault and the CPU view is empty. Only the port holds the key that moves a buffer between states (ADR-0030).

docs.title: The DMA copy-out stream
docs.text:
The DMA copy-out stream Figure description and sources

From the top. The DMA ring in the buffer holds two halves or N frames. A half or complete interrupt makes PublishFromDevice invalidate the lines, copy the finished frame out and stamp a sequence number, a time and a torn flag. It copies into a slot of a ring of at least two slots; when every slot is held the frame is dropped, counted as Full, and the next frame carries Gap(). The task takes a slot with TryTake and reads it through a move-only FrameView that releases on its end. Judge checks the content, and Supervise answers None, Restart, BackOff or UseFallback. EnterFallback switches to the declared fallback producer, whose frames carry Fallback(). The ring is never lent to the task (ADR-0031).

docs.title: Fault evidence path
docs.text:
Fault evidence path Figure description and sources

Handler health is read lock-free and only its edges go to the HealthJournal. The LivenessMonitor's verdict goes there too, and the watchdog owner is kicked only when nothing is stale. The journal appends with one bounded store write into a FaultJournal ring of 32-byte CRC-32 records with a sequence number; at boot the port's reset reason is recorded with RecordReset. The store (RTC or no-init RAM, NVS, FRAM, flash) belongs to the port; after a reset Open() finds the newest record and skips a torn slot.

docs.title: Handler lifecycle and health
docs.text:
Handler lifecycle and health Figure description and sources

Six states. A handler starts Unknown (constructed, no I/O). EnsureInitialized or StartStep moves it to Starting, which walks the declared stages, each bounded by its deadline; the last stage makes it Ready, a failing stage makes it Faulted, and a failed start leaves the driver destroyed so the next start begins again from the first stage. A failing call makes a Ready handler Degraded until the next call succeeds; fault_after failures in a row, or one fatal error (the chip reset or lost its state), make it Faulted. Recover() moves Faulted to Recovering with a backoff that doubles on each failure, and is refused after max_attempts; Recovering returns to Ready when the plan succeeds and to Faulted when it fails. Deinitialize() returns Ready or Faulted to Unknown. Only EnsureInitialized, StartStep, Deinitialize and Recover change the lifecycle: calls never start or restart the chip.

docs.title: The pieces of a handler
docs.text:
The pieces of a handler Figure description and sources

From the top. A HAL manager or application task calls an access facade with EnsureStarted, Request, Sample, Latest or Health; there is one facade per handler, chosen by the bus's thread model: OwnerAccess (request queue and a lock-free snapshot) or Guarded (handler lock, then bus lock). Only a facade can make the ServiceKey that the handler core needs, and the facade also owns the BusDomain of its bus, which holds one bus and its declared thread model. The core, HandlerCore of the handler, the driver, the snapshot, the command and the reply, holds the start-up plan runner (kStartupPlan), the health record and the snapshot (both seqlocks) and a liveness beat. It builds the driver in a std::optional; the driver reaches the bus through the binding's Port, driver hooks (I2cHooks, SpiHooks, UartHooks, AdcHooks, GpioHooks) over the kb::iface contract through which the HAL supplies its bus, pins and clock.

docs.title: The handler start-up pipeline
docs.text:
The handler start-up pipeline Figure description and sources

Two columns. Stages, in order: one runner and a declared plan of stages per chip, in a fixed order: Power (rail or enable pin), HostReset (reset pulse, hold, release), Boot (boot time, ready pin, advertisement), Link (transport session, T=1 or SHTP), Identify (ID, select, probe, capabilities), Secure (secure channel, platform SCP03), Configure (apply the configuration), Verify (read-back, lifecycle state), then Ready, when the handler serves calls. Plans of three chips: a plan lists only the stages its chip needs, and every stage is synchronous or polled and bounded by a deadline. Most drivers declare one step, Start, that calls the driver's EnsureInitialized(); Identify and Configure happen inside the driver. The bno08x resets with Begin(cfg), synchronous, boots and links by calling Poll() until Ready(), polled, and configures with SetFeature operations until OpDone, polled. The se05x sets platform keys with SetPlatformKeys() (no I/O), opens the link, identifies and secures with Open(), synchronous and bounded by the link, and optionally verifies the lifecycle state. An optional stage is skipped, not failed, when the HAL supplies no pin, rail or key for it.

docs.title: Handler thread models
docs.text:
Handler thread models Figure description and sources

Two models, declared per bus, one above the other; callers on other tasks use one access API in both. Model O, the owner task, is the default for real-time buses: one real-time task, a kb::rtos::Thread, calls Service(now) at a fixed rate, steps the single-threaded cores of handlers A and B on BusDomain without a mutex (an owner check instead), publishes each step to a lock-free SeqlockSnapshot and drains a bounded command queue with completion. Other tasks read the latest snapshot with Latest() (a lock-free copy) or post a request with Request(cmd, timeout) and wait. Model G, the guarded facade, is for slow, sporadic devices: tasks X and Y each call Call(timeout, op) on a Guarded handler, C or D, which takes the handler lock and then, with a bounded wait (TryLockFor), the bus lock of BusDomain, which has a mutex, recovery and statistics. An interrupt service routine only sets event flags or notifies the owner task; it never calls a handler.

Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/handler-threading.py

docs.title: The layer stack
docs.text:
The layer stack Figure description and sources

From top to bottom. The product application (control, protocols, safety layer) calls the board HAL: its facade and managers built on kb-hal-common, the board config (bus table, thread model per bus, chip list, pins) and the platform bind, which builds the port objects and sets the start-up order. The board HAL uses kb::handlers and picks one MCU port. In kb-core, kb::handlers (bindings, handler core, start-up pipeline, owner and guarded access) uses the driver of each chip and the interface contracts; kb::interfaces (C++20 concepts only, plus the host test port) rests on kb::rtos (the API, with the backends none, FreeRTOS and ThreadX), and kb::rtos rests on kb::utils (Status/Result, units, containers, CRC, seqlock). Each driver- is brand-free, has its own CI at level high and is pinned at release tags. The MCU port (port-esp32 in components/ports/esp32, its own CMake project; port-stm32 planned in its own repository) satisfies the interface contracts and touches the vendor SDK in its boundary files only; the RTOS backends touch the kernel in theirs. The vendor SDK, kernels and mbedTLS (ESP-IDF, STM32 HAL, FreeRTOS, ThreadX, mbedTLS) are SOUP: never analysed, never edited.

docs.title: Phase roadmap
docs.text:
Phase roadmap Figure description and sources

Eight phases, M0 to M7, in order; there are no calendar dates, each phase ends on its exit criteria. M0 fixes decisions and guardrails: ADR-0006 to ADR-0013 recorded, and the include checker, poison build, symbol lint, preflight and CI skeleton green on empty parts. M1 to M3 deliver kb::utils v0.1, kb::rtos v0.2 and kb::interfaces v0.3: MISRA at level high with zero findings and zero deviations, the coverage floor, the mutation gate and clean fuzzing; kb::rtos adds the none and FreeRTOS backends, at-least delays, bounded locks, CRTP threads with statistics, approved boundary deviations and a clean TSan run; kb::interfaces adds concepts, a host port with fault injection, BusDomain, and conformance and compile-fail tests. M4 (v0.4) adds the ESP32 port with reviewed boundary files and the first three simple drivers bound and handled, integration, compat.yml, kb image check, configurator P1 and a bench run. M5 (v0.9 to v1.0) rolls out handlers for all drivers, simplest to hardest (bno08x, se05x and tmc9660 last), with start-up plans, both thread models, and health and recovery tests. M6 adds breadth: port-stm32, the ThreadX backend, tested version sets, and SBOM, CVE and licence evidence in the configurator (P2). M7 adds the generators: pin tables from board.yml, a project archive and HIL in scheduled CI.

docs.title: kb::rtos backends

kb::rtos backends Figure description and sources

One API, one seam, four backends. The kb::rtos API (Mutex, RecursiveMutex, Semaphore, Queue, EventFlags, Timer, Thread, CriticalSection in components/lib/rtos/inc) reaches a backend through kb::rtos::backend (backend.hpp), where each native object lives in opaque storage sized there and every backend static_asserts that it fits. FreeRTOS (the ESP32 default, any FreeRTOS target, static API only) and ThreadX (Eclipse ThreadX targets, one boundary file) reach their kernel through boundary files; the kernel is SOUP, from ESP-IDF or KB_FREERTOS_INCLUDE_DIRS for FreeRTOS, and from KB_THREADX_INCLUDE_DIRS or third_party/threadx for ThreadX. docs.title: The ThreadX backend
docs.text:
The ThreadX backend Figure description and sources

The kb::rtos API (Mutex, RecursiveMutex, Semaphore, Queue, EventFlags, Timer, Thread, CriticalSection) reaches the seam, kb::rtos::backend in backend.hpp. The ThreadX backend is two files: threadx_isr.cpp, where every FromIsr call is the same call with TX_NO_WAIT, and threadx_boundary.cpp, the only boundary file, which creates ThreadX objects (tx_*_create) on kb-owned control blocks and stacks. A call refused for the caller's own mistake (InvalidArgument) is recorded as the last error and counted in refused_calls, but does not change the state. A binding may say which failures are fatal (IsFatal) and which do not count (CountsAgainstHealth). On an owner bus, a successful periodic read clears the failures in a row, so failing commands alone reach fault_after only between reads; bindings whose commands matter more than their reads document a longer sample_period.

docs.text:
• components/lib/handlers/tests/: the core on the deterministic none backend, both facades, and real threads on the host backend (contention, lock timeouts, recovery storms, seqlock readers); compile-fail tests for a wrong facade, a wrong bus kind, Guarded over a chip that requires an owner, a missing ServiceKey and a plan out of order.

docs.text: ADS7950, ADS7951, ADS7952 and ADS7953 4- to 16-channel, 12-bit SPI SAR ADCs, through kb::handlers::ads7952::Handler<Dev> (kb/handlers/bindings/ads7952.hpp, driver driver-ads7952 at the pin in components/drivers/drivers.lock.yml). docs.title: What it gives the application
docs.text:
Kind Name What Snapshot Snapshot One Auto-1 scan: code[16] (channel n at index n), mask (the channels scanned), range Command ReadChannel(io, ch, timeout) The code of one channel, converted now (Manual mode) Command ScanAuto1(io, timeout) One Auto-1 pass now, as a Snapshot Command SetRange(io, range, timeout) 0 to VREF or 0 to 2 x VREF Command SetGpioOutputs(io, levels, timeout, verify) / ReadGpio(io, timeout) The GPIO pins Command CheckScale(io, timeout) The scale monitor's code, checked against its window Command Command{Op::...} with Request() ScanAuto2, SetAuto1Channels, SetAuto2LastChannel, SetAlarmThresholds

Codes convert to microvolts with ads7952::CodeToMicrovolts(code, range, vref_mv).

docs.title: Thread model
docs.text:
kRequiresOwner = false; either model works, and the choice depends on use:

  • Owner (the usual choice for control loops and monitoring): the owner task scans the Auto-1 sequence every sample_period and publishes it, so any task reads the newest scan lock-free with Latest() (sequence and age included), and on-demand reads go through the owner's queue.
  • Guarded: a task reads single channels on demand (ReadChannel()), for slow or occasional measurements on a bus shared with other slow devices.

docs.title: Start-up
docs.text:
Stage Kinds Mode Driver call Deadline 0 Identify + Configure sync EnsureInitialized(): register reset, power-up wait, every program register written, channel-address identity check, optional scale monitor Config::start_deadline

The chip has no reset or enable pin (the driver resets it by command), so there is no Power or HostReset stage. Every reply 0xFFFF fails stage 0 with NoDevice; replies without the channel addresses with Fault (DeviceIdMismatch).

docs.title: Health
docs.text:
Driver error kb::Status Effect DeviceReset, NotInitialized NotReady Faulted at once (a brown-out reset the registers) Bus, ChannelMismatch, SequenceMismatch BusError Counts toward fault_after NoDevice NoDevice Counts toward fault_after; at start-up the start fails DeviceIdMismatch, WriteMismatch, RangeMismatch, ScaleMismatch, DeviceFault Fault Counts toward fault_after InvalidArgument, Unsupported, Timeout, Crc, Busy the same name InvalidArgument is refused (recorded, not counted); the others count toward fault_after

Recovery is the generic plan: Deinitialize() (power-down frame), then the start-up again, which programs the chip in full.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
using Dev = board::AdcCs;                                         // a kb::iface::SpiDevice
using Io = kb::handlers::ads7952::Handler<Dev>;
kb::handlers::BusDomain<Dev, kb::handlers::ThreadModel::Owner> spi1{dev};
kb::handlers::OwnerAccess<Io, decltype(spi1)> adc{spi1, dev, timing, config};

static_cast<void>(adc.Create());
// The owner task: spi1.Service(kb::rtos::Now(), adc) every step.
if (adc.EnsureStarted(kb::Milliseconds{20U}).IsOk()) {
  const auto scan = adc.Latest();                                  // the newest Auto-1 scan
  const kb::Result<uint16_t> ch3 = kb::handlers::ads7952::ReadChannel(adc, 3U, kb::Milliseconds{5U});
}

Tests: tests/integration/ads7952/ (the driver's chip model behind a kb::iface::SpiDevice, both thread models, the owner one sampling Auto-1 scans).

docs.title: ads9324 handler
docs.text: ADS9324 16-channel simultaneous-sampling ADC on SPI, through kb::handlers::ads9324::Handler<Dev> (kb/handlers/bindings/ads9324.hpp, driver driver-ads9324 at the pin in components/drivers/drivers.lock.yml).

docs.title: What it gives the application
docs.text:
Kind Name What Snapshot Snapshot microvolts[16], codes[16], present_mask, clipped_mask, window_alert, standby Command Identify(io, timeout) DEVICE_ID, read now (0x0004) Command ReadWindowFlags(io, timeout) The latched window comparator flags of both banks Command ClearWindowFlags(io, group, timeout) Clears the flags of group 0 (AIN1 to AIN8) or 1 (AIN9 to AIN16) Command SetStandby(io, standby, timeout) Power down, or wake and check the registers Command RunCalibration(io, timeout) The ADC calibration configured in chip.calibration Command RunSelfTest(io, timeout) Test patterns on every channel; the configuration is restored Command Command{Op::...} with Request() Reset (software or RESET pin), CONVST pulse, alarm pin, calibration off, raw register

io is either facade; the calls are the same on an owner bus and on a guarded bus.

Pins. Config::outputs holds RESET (kPinReset, wire it active low) and CONVST (kPinConvst, active high); Config::inputs holds DRDY/ALARM (kPinAlarm) at its electrical level: leave active_low false, the driver applies Alarm::active_low itself. An absent pin makes the driver's pin calls fail (Bus): wire CONVST, or set host_convst = false when the board drives CONVST and Measure() should wait for data ready and read the frame. CaptureLanes has no kb contract, so data comes on SDOUT (one lane).

Samples. Measure() is MeasureOnce() (CONVST pulse, data-ready wait, frame read) or, with host_convst = false, WaitDataReady() then ReadFrame(). While the chip is powered down it sends nothing and republishes the last frame with standby set, so an owner task does not count standby as failures.

The port's DelayUs goes through the hook timing: a spin on the HAL's busy-wait below 1 ms, a kb::rtos::SleepFor (at least the time asked) from 1 ms.

docs.title: Thread model
docs.text: kRequiresOwner = false. A converter sampled at the control period is the owner model's case: the owner task converts every sample_period and every other task reads Latest() without a lock, with the sequence and age of the frame. A guarded bus works for occasional reads from several tasks.

docs.title: Start-up
docs.text:
Stage Kinds Mode Driver call Deadline 0 Identify + Configure sync EnsureInitialized(): 30 ms power-up wait, reset (RESET pin with chip.hardware_reset, else SW_RST), DEVICE_ID and BANK_SEL, calibration idle, configuration written, optional calibration Config::start_deadline

The driver drives RESET itself, so there is no HostReset stage. On a failure the report names stage 0 with the driver's error in detail; the next EnsureStarted() starts again.

docs.title: Health
docs.text:
Driver error kb::Status Effect UnexpectedReset, NotInitialized NotReady Faulted at once (RESET_DETECT_FLAG: the registers were lost) Refused NotReady Counts toward fault_after (a call the powered-down chip refuses) Bus, DataMismatch BusError Counts toward fault_after (a failed transfer, or a stuck or floating SDOUT frame) DeviceIdMismatch, DeviceFault, VerifyFailed Fault Counts toward fault_after InvalidArgument, Timeout, Busy, Unsupported the same name InvalidArgument is refused (recorded, not counted); the others count toward fault_after Crc CrcMismatch Not returned by the driver

Recovery is the generic plan: Deinitialize() (standby), then the start-up again, which resets the chip and writes the whole configuration.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
using Dev = board::Spi2Adc;                                       // a kb::iface::SpiDevice, mode 0
using Adc = kb::handlers::ads9324::Handler<Dev>;
kb::handlers::BusDomain<Dev, kb::handlers::ThreadModel::Owner> spi2{dev};
kb::handlers::ads9324::Config config{};
config.outputs[kb::handlers::ads9324::kPinConvst].pin.emplace(convst_pin);
config.handler.sample_period = kb::Milliseconds{10U};
kb::handlers::OwnerAccess<Adc, decltype(spi2)> adc{spi2, dev, timing, config};

static_cast<void>(adc.Create());
adc.RequestStart();                                              // the owner task runs the plan
// owner task, every step: static_cast<void>(spi2.Service(kb::rtos::Now(), adc));
const auto frame = adc.Latest();                                 // any task, lock-free

docs.title: alicat_basis2 handler
docs.text: BASIS 2 mass flow meters and controllers on a serial line (ASCII protocol or Modbus RTU), through kb::handlers::alicat_basis2::Handler<Uart> (kb/handlers/bindings/alicat_basis2.hpp, driver driver-alicat-basis2 at the pin in components/drivers/drivers.lock.yml).

docs.title: What it gives the application
docs.text:
Kind Name What Snapshot Snapshot frame: flow, setpoint, temperature, valve drive, total, gas and status flags of the last poll Command ReadFrame(io, timeout) The data frame, polled now Command SetSetpoint(io, flow, timeout) The setpoint in the instrument's flow unit (controllers) Command ReadSetpoint(io, timeout) The current setpoint Command CloseValve(io, timeout) The valve held closed: the switch-off, never refused for an unknown state Command HoldValve(io, percent, timeout), ResumeControl(io, timeout) Hold the valve, then closed-loop control again Command Tare(io, duration_ms, timeout), SetGas(io, gas, timeout) Tare at true zero flow; select the gas Command Command{Op::...} with Request() Setpoint source, totalizer reset

io is either facade; the calls are the same on an owner bus and on a guarded bus. The commands that can strand the instrument (unit ID, Modbus address, baud rate, protocol switch, factory restore) need the driver's guard tokens and are not in the command set.

docs.title: Thread model
docs.text: kRequiresOwner = false. The instrument answers only when asked, and a transaction blocks for at most one reply wait (processing_ms plus the line time, slow_command_ms for a command that writes non-volatile memory). A guarded line (BusDomain<Uart, ThreadModel::Guarded> with Guarded<Handler>) suits the usual use: a setpoint now and then, reads from several tasks. On an owner line the owner task polls the frame every sample_period and other tasks read Latest(). One handler serves one instrument; it owns the driver's line machine (Bus<Port>).

docs.title: Start-up
docs.text:
Stage Kinds Mode Driver call Deadline 0 Link sync EnsureInitialized(): port up, configuration checked, no instrument traffic Config::link_deadline 1 Identify sync Begin(): poll, firmware, serial number, full scale, gas, controller settings; read only Config::identify_deadline

The instrument has no reset or enable pin the driver could use, so there is no Power or HostReset stage. On a failure the report names the stage with the driver's error in detail; the next EnsureStarted() starts again at stage 0.

docs.title: Health
docs.text:
Driver error kb::Status Effect StateUnknown, NotInitialized NotReady Faulted at once (a guarded command left the line settings in doubt) Bus BusError Counts toward fault_after Timeout Timeout Counts toward fault_after; at start-up the start fails Rejected, BadReply, DeviceIdMismatch, DeviceFault, VerifyMismatch Fault Counts toward fault_after Busy, RateLimited Busy Counts toward fault_after Unsupported, FirmwareTooOld Unsupported Counts toward fault_after InvalidArgument, GuardNotConfirmed InvalidArgument Refused: recorded as the last error, not counted against the chip (a caller's mistake) Crc, OutOfRange, Overflow CrcMismatch, OutOfRange, Overflow Counts toward fault_after

Recovery runs the driver's own Recover() first: it polls the configured ID and, with one instrument on the line, scans for the one that answers and checks it is the same instrument. The ID, address or baud rate it adopted is kept in the handler's configuration, then the plan runs again from stage 0.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
using Uart = board::Rs485;                                        // a kb::iface::UartPort
using Mfc = kb::handlers::alicat_basis2::Handler<Uart>;
kb::handlers::BusDomain<Uart, kb::handlers::ThreadModel::Guarded> line{uart};
kb::handlers::Guarded<Mfc, decltype(line)> mfc{line, uart, timing, config};

static_cast<void>(line.Create());
static_cast<void>(mfc.Create());
if (mfc.EnsureStarted(kb::Milliseconds{3000U}).IsOk()) {
  static_cast<void>(kb::handlers::alicat_basis2::SetSetpoint(mfc, 12.5, kb::Milliseconds{500U}));
  const kb::Result<alicat_basis2::Frame> f = kb::handlers::alicat_basis2::ReadFrame(mfc, kb::Milliseconds{500U});
}
