docs.title: tmc9660 handler
docs.text: TMC9660 servo controllers and gate drivers, on SPI or UART, in parameter, register or bootloader mode, through kb::handlers::tmc9660::Handler<Bus, kControlPins> (kb/handlers/bindings/tmc9660.hpp, driver driver-tmc9660 at the pin in components/drivers/drivers.lock.yml).

docs.title: What it gives the application
docs.text:
Kind Name What Snapshot Snapshot mode, last_status; in parameter mode also velocity, position and general_errors (after a good Service()) Command EnableDrive(io, commutation_mode, timeout) Energise the gate driver in parameter mode, after the driver's guards Command DisableDrive(io, timeout) Switch the gate driver off (never refused) Command SetTargetVelocity(io, velocity, timeout) TARGET_VELOCITY Command SetTargetPosition(io, position, timeout) TARGET_POSITION Command GetParam(io, param, timeout) An axis parameter, read now Command SetParam(io, param, value, timeout) An axis parameter, checked against the driver's table Command Command{Op::...} with Request() Motor stop, target torque, clear flags, register read and write (register mode), chip ID, Service()

io is either facade; the calls are the same on an owner bus and on a guarded bus. A call that belongs to another mode returns Unsupported with WrongMode in the detail and sends nothing.

The bus type picks the transport: a kb::iface::SpiDevice gives the SPI link, a kb::iface::UartPort the UART link (the port must not return the echo of its own bytes; a driver exchange with no bytes to send only drains the line). With kControlPins = false (the default) the driver gets no pin hooks: no hardware reset, DRV_EN wired high, and the stop is made with parameters. With kControlPins = true the HAL gives RSTN, DRV_EN and WAKE outputs and the FAULTN input in Config::pins (RSTN and FAULTN are usually active_low); DRV_EN must then be wired, because a missing output fails its hook (the driver still sends every stop frame and reports Bus).

docs.title: Thread model
docs.text: kRequiresOwner = false. Set points and parameter access are sporadic and the control loops run in the chip, so a guarded bus is the usual choice. On an owner bus the owner task runs Service() (FAULTN, the error flags and the heartbeat) and the parameter reads every sample_period; other tasks read Latest().

docs.title: Start-up
docs.text:
Stage Kinds Mode Driver call Deadline 0 Identify + Configure sync EnsureInitialized(): bus up, RSTN pulse when chip.hardware_reset (the driver drives the pin), chip ID in chip.mode Config::start_deadline (above chip.boot_timeout_ms)

The driver drives RSTN itself, so there is no HostReset stage. On a failure the report names stage 0 with the driver's error in detail; the next EnsureStarted() starts again.

docs.title: Health
docs.text:
Driver error kb::Status Effect UnexpectedReset, NotInitialized NotReady Faulted at once (the chip restarted) Bus BusError Counts toward fault_after DeviceIdMismatch NoDevice Counts toward fault_after; at start-up the start fails InvalidArgument, Refused InvalidArgument Refused: recorded as the last error, not counted against the chip (a caller's mistake) Crc, BadReply CrcMismatch Counts toward fault_after Nack Nack Counts toward fault_after Unsupported, WrongMode Unsupported Counts toward fault_after DeviceFault, VerifyFailed Fault Counts toward fault_after Timeout, Busy the same name Counts toward fault_after

Recovery is the generic plan: Deinitialize() (the gate driver off, also after a reported reset), then the start-up again, which adopts the chip in chip.mode.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
using Dev = board::Spi2Servo;                                     // a kb::iface::SpiDevice
using Servo = kb::handlers::tmc9660::Handler<Dev>;
kb::handlers::BusDomain<Dev, kb::handlers::ThreadModel::Guarded> spi2{dev};
kb::handlers::Guarded<Servo, decltype(spi2)> servo{spi2, dev, timing, config};

static_cast<void>(spi2.Create());
static_cast<void>(servo.Create());
if (servo.EnsureStarted(kb::Milliseconds{600U}).IsOk()) {
  static_cast<void>(kb::handlers::tmc9660::EnableDrive(servo, 2U, kb::Milliseconds{50U}));
  static_cast<void>(kb::handlers::tmc9660::SetTargetVelocity(servo, 1000, kb::Milliseconds{20U}));
}

docs.title: ws2812_rmt handler
docs.text:
WS2812, SK6812 and compatible single-wire addressable LEDs, driven by a timed pulse peripheral (the ESP32 RMT transmitter), through kb::handlers::ws2812_rmt::Handler<Hw, Pixels> (kb/handlers/bindings/ws2812_rmt.hpp, driver driver-ws2812-rmt at the pin in components/drivers/drivers.lock.yml).

kb has no contract for a pulse peripheral (BusKind::Pio). Hw is the driver's own port type, supplied by the MCU port: a class with EnsureInitialized(), ResolutionHz(), Transmit(), DelayUs() and optionally GpioSet() (the strip supply) and Log(). The binding's Port<Hw> passes every hook through. The driver is MCU-gated to ESP32 in kb's build switch (cmake/kb_mcu_gates.cmake); the header still compiles anywhere, so the host tests run it over the driver's own model of the channel.

docs.title: What it gives the application
docs.text:
Kind Name What Snapshot none An actuator: Latest() and Sample() return NotReady and Unsupported Command SetPixel(io, index, colour, timeout, show) One pixel; with show the frame is sent too Command FillStrip(io, colour, timeout, show) Every pixel; sends the frame by default Command ClearStrip(io, timeout, show) Every pixel black; sends the frame by default Command SetStripBrightness(io, brightness, timeout) Linear dimming of the next frames Command Show(io, timeout) Send the frame Command SetPower(io, on, timeout) The strip supply (needs Hw::GpioSet) Command Command{Op::...} with Request() A range of pixels, read a pixel back; every reply carries the frame time

io is either facade; the calls are the same on an owner bus and on a guarded bus.

docs.title: Thread model
docs.text: kRequiresOwner = false, guarded by preference. A strip is updated sporadically by an application task, and its channel is its own bus, so a guarded domain costs one uncontended lock per frame. An animation loop that sends frames at a fixed rate can own the channel on an owner bus instead. Show() blocks for the frame time plus the port's slack (Config::chip.transmit_slack_ms); request timeouts must cover it.

docs.title: Start-up
docs.text:
Stage Kinds Mode Driver call Deadline 0 Link sync EnsureInitialized(): configuration check, open the channel, resolve the waveform at its tick rate Config::link_deadline 1 Configure (optional) sync PowerOn() when Hw has the pin, then a black frame (Clear(), Show()) Config::blank_deadline

Stage 1 runs when Config::blank_on_start is true, so the pixels hold a known state after a start. The supply pin is the driver's own hook, so there is no separate Power stage. The pixels are write-only: there is no Identify.

docs.title: Health
docs.text:
Driver error kb::Status Effect NotInitialized NotReady Faulted at once NotPowered NotReady Counts toward fault_after (a frame between PowerOff and PowerOn) Bus BusError Counts toward fault_after (a hook failed, a frame was cut or timed out) TimingUnreachable, Unsupported Unsupported Counts toward fault_after; at start-up the start fails InvalidArgument InvalidArgument Refused: recorded as the last error, not counted against the chip (a caller's mistake) Timeout, DeviceIdMismatch, Crc, Busy, DeviceFault Timeout, Fault, CrcMismatch, Busy, Fault Not returned by this driver

Deinitialize() and recovery switch the supply off (PowerOff()) when Hw has the pin; recovery then runs both stages again.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
using Strip = kb::handlers::ws2812_rmt::Handler<board::RmtPort, 60U>;    // board::RmtPort: the MCU port's channel
kb::handlers::BusDomain<board::RmtPort, kb::handlers::ThreadModel::Guarded> rmt0{rmt_port};
kb::handlers::Guarded<Strip, decltype(rmt0)> leds{rmt0, rmt_port, config};

static_cast<void>(rmt0.Create());
static_cast<void>(leds.Create());
if (leds.EnsureStarted(kb::Milliseconds{20U}).IsOk()) {
  const auto green = ws2812_rmt::Colour::FromPacked(0x002000U);
  static_cast<void>(kb::handlers::ws2812_rmt::FillStrip(leds, green, kb::Milliseconds{20U}));
}

docs.title: kb::dma
docs.text:
Buffers that a DMA master reads or writes, and the streams built on them, with the cache rules, the ownership rules and the failure rules written once. Header-only; depends on kb::utils. A port supplies the cache hooks and the register code; a driver or handler gets a buffer it cannot misuse. Decisions: ADR-0030, ADR-0031, ADR-0032.

#include "kb/dma/dma.hpp"
Header Gives Contract in one line region.hpp Region concept, CachePolicy, Direction, MasterSet, RoundUp, RequireFrameFits, RequireReachable, RequireWholeUnits, RequireElementBytes A region states its cache policy, line size, alignment unit and the masters that reach it; a mismatch is a build error cache.hpp CacheOps concept, NoCacheOps The port's Clean, Invalidate, Barrier; called only over lines the buffer owns buffer.hpp Buffer<Region, Bytes>, Lease<Region>, PortKey<Tag>, BufferState, BufferStats Static, line-aligned and padded; the CPU has a view only while it owns the buffer; a lease is move-only completion.hpp CompletionLatch, Outcome, StopEvidence, CancelClaim A transfer completes once and is reported once, whatever races a cancel stream.hpp Stream<Frame, Frames, Region>, FrameView, StreamConfig, StreamStats, SupervisorAction Copy-out ring of at least two frames with sequence numbers, timestamps, overrun checks, a signed stall check and a restart policy capabilities.hpp Capabilities, DmaHealth, TransferMode A port says which path serves (DMA, interrupt or polled) and its ceiling; a fallback is never silent

docs.title: Ownership: a buffer is either the CPU's or the device's
Streams: copy out, never lend the ring
docs.text:
The DMA copy-out stream Figure description and sources

From the top. The DMA ring in the buffer holds two halves or N frames. A half or complete interrupt makes PublishFromDevice invalidate the lines, copy the finished frame out and stamp a sequence number, a time and a torn flag. It copies into a slot of a ring of at least two slots; when every slot is held the frame is dropped, counted as Full, and the next frame carries Gap(). The task takes a slot with TryTake and reads it through a move-only FrameView that releases on its end. Judge checks the content, and Supervise answers None, Restart, BackOff or UseFallback. EnterFallback switches to the declared fallback producer, whose frames carry Fallback(). The ring is never lent to the task (ADR-0031).

Drawn from: docs/model/dma-stream.graph.yml.

Stream<Frame, Frames, Region> has at least two slots. The interrupt copies each finished hardware frame (PublishFromDevice, which invalidates the frame's lines first) into a slot with a sequence number and the time of the completion; the task takes the oldest frame (TryTake) and holds it while it reads (FrameView, released on Give or when the view ends). Zero-copy is available only through a Lease.

Situation What happens All slots held when a frame arrives The frame is dropped and counted (overruns); the next delivered frame has Gap() and a larger sequence number The peripheral overruns, or the pool overflows OnOverrun: counted, never a frame, flags the next frame The hardware lapped the copy (both flags pending, counter inside the half) The frame is published Torn No frame for stall_periods periods CheckStall: signed elapsed time, so a frame stamped after the task read its clock is not a stall The content check rejects bad_frames_to_restart frames in a row Supervise returns Restart A restart came too recently BackOff Restarts keep failing UseFallback; frames from the declared fallback producer carry Fallback() and a new epoch

One context publishes (the interrupt) and one context consumes (the owner task); the counters are atomics, the ring indices are single-writer.

docs.title: What a port implements
docs.text: Piece Rule CacheOps Clean(range), Invalidate(range), Barrier(); ranges are whole lines of the buffer, never a caller's memory Start Check Buffer::Verify once; Lend; program the transfer from DeviceView(key); round a receive length up to the unit inside the padding Completion One interrupt path reads and clears the flags; TryComplete on a CompletionLatch, Complete the lease Errors Clear each flag by its own bit; report an error as an error; the first fault ends the transfer Cancel Disable the stream, wait for the enable bit to read 0 within a bound, then Abort(Confirmed); otherwise Abort(NotConfirmed) and return Fault Timeout A timed-out transfer is cancelled the same way before the buffer is returned Capabilities Capabilities() says the mode, the ceiling and the staging size; DmaHealth carries the mode and a fault flag Fallback Interrupt or polled service up to a published ceiling, reported in Capabilities() and in the health record

docs.title: Host model and conformance suite
docs.text:
components/lib/dma/host is a model of the hardware side: memory with a write-back cache (with speculative refills), a DMA engine with bursts, a stuck mode and receive-length rounding, and a reference port with injectable defects. The conformance suite T1 to T18 (kb/dma/host/conformance.hpp) runs against any rig with the same member functions; each case passes on the good model and is shown to fail on a model with the defect it targets.

Case Defect it catches T1 transmit without a clean T2 receive without an invalidate (before or after) T3 an invalidate after a CPU-copy transfer T4 a receive target that shares a cache line with a neighbour T5 CPU access during a lease T6 a DMA write after a timeout returned the buffer T7 an abort that does not wait for the enable bit T8 receive-length rounding past an unpadded buffer T9 a held frame overwritten, an overrun not counted T10 a lapped copy published as clean T11 a half delivered twice by two drainers T12 an unsigned stall check T13 a pool overflow delivered as a frame T14 an error reported as success; the other pending flag lost to a global clear T15 a cancel racing a completion reporting twice T16 an unconfirmed stop returning the buffer to the CPU T17 an unreported fallback T18 a synchronous transfer making the caller's memory a DMA target

docs.title: Compile-time checks
docs.text: Helper Fails the build when RequireFrameFits<Driver, Port> the driver's largest frame exceeds the port's DMA limit RequireReachable<Masters, Region> a named DMA master cannot reach the region (tightly coupled memory) RequireWholeUnits<Bytes, Region> a size is not a multiple of the alignment unit RequireElementBytes<Element, Bytes> a stream element differs in size from the board declaration Region concept line or unit is not a power of two, the unit is smaller than a line, or a cached region has no line Stream<Frame, 1, ...> fewer than two frames RequireInterruptTier<Stream, Rtos> a stream that notifies a task runs above the RTOS syscall limit, or its priority is outside the implemented bits RequireSamePriority<S1, S2> the streams of one peripheral run at different interrupt priorities RequireBusCarries<Bus, Bytes> the driver's largest frame exceeds what the bus carries in the mode the board gave it RequireShape<Decl, Frame, Frames> the handler's frame size or ring length differs from the board's stream declaration

docs.title: Board declarations
docs.text: kb/dma/assignment.hpp holds the values the board generator writes into board_dma.hpp from board.yml: a StreamAssignment per DMA stream (engine, stream, request line, arbitration priority, interrupt priority, how the interrupt notifies the owner, which interrupts are on, normal or circular), the InterruptLimits of the RTOS, the BusLimits of each bus (DMA or not, the largest frame each way, the receive-length multiple, the alignment unit) and the StreamShape of each stream. A port receives a resolved assignment and only checks it with the helpers above; it never looks for a free stream at run time. What engine, stream and request number is the port's to define (its docs/dma.md).

docs.title: kb::handlers
docs.text:
Platform-free glue between drivers and kb contracts. Used only by the HAL. Each driver has a binding (its port over kb contracts, the one map of its errors to kb::Status, its start-up plan and thread-model needs) and a handler on the shared single-threaded core (HandlerCore), reached through the access facade its bus declares (owner task or guarded).

Piece Names Hook bases I2cHooks, SpiHooks, UartHooks, AdcHooks, GpioHooks (CRTP), HookTiming Bindings kb/handlers/bindings/<name>.hpp: Port, ToStatus(), Config, Snapshot, Command, Handler, app calls Core HandlerCore<Derived, Driver, Snapshot, Command, Reply>, Stage, StartupReport, HealthRecord, ServiceKey Bus and access BusDomain<Bus, ThreadModel>, BusHold (Hold()), OwnerAccess<H, Domain> (Held()), RequestChannel, Guarded<H, Domain> (Hold()), GuardedHeld, OwnerHeld Non-blocking reads AsyncPoller<Op, Bytes, Use>, AsyncUse, AsyncStats Supervision LivenessBeat (Park(), Resume()), LivenessMonitor<N> (Verdict()), Seqlock<T>, HealthJournal<Sink, N>

Build: -DKB_ENABLE_<NAME>=ON links a driver into kb::handlers; -DKB_BUILD_TESTS=ON -DKB_BUILD_INTEGRATION=ON compiles and tests every binding whose driver is checked out.

Pages: Handlers (overview and one page per handler); design: Handlers, Bus access, Fault evidence.

docs.title: kb::interfaces
docs.text:
The contracts of buses, pins, clocks and logs, as C++20 concepts in kb::iface and only concepts (ADR-0006), the vocabulary types they use, a type-erased *Ref for each, and the host test port. Used only by the HAL, kb::handlers and the MCU ports; applications never include it.

#include "kb/interfaces/interfaces.hpp"

docs.title: The contracts
docs.text:

Every *Ref is in refs.hpp (or the umbrella interfaces.hpp).

Vocabulary (types.hpp): Level, Edge, I2cFailure (None, AddressNack, DataNack, Bus, Timeout, BusStuck), CanFrame, LogLevel, Duty (0.01 % steps). Results are kb::Status or kb::Result<T>; a port puts its vendor code in Detail().

docs.title: Run-time choice without virtual functions
docs.text:
A *Ref is a context pointer and a pointer to a constant table of function pointers, made from any type that satisfies the concept and itself checked against it. It costs one indirect call per operation:

kb::iface::GpioOutputRef reset_line = board.UsesExpander() ? kb::iface::GpioOutputRef{expander_pin3}
                                                           : kb::iface::GpioOutputRef{mcu_pin12};

docs.title: Serving the drivers' ports
docs.text:
Every driver keeps its own CRTP port base and concept. A binding derives from the driver's base and forwards each hook to a kb contract in a line or two; the tests prove it for three drivers over the host fakes and over the *Ref values (components/lib/interfaces/tests/driver_ports/):

class Tmc5160Spi : public tmc5160::SpiInterface<Tmc5160Spi<Dev>> {

docs.title: The host port
docs.text: components/lib/interfaces/host/ (kb::interfaces_host, header-only, test code outside the MISRA claim): FakeI2cBus (register-file devices, failure injection per kind), FakeSpiDevice (scripted replies, transmit log), FakeUart (receive script, responder, transmit log), FakeGpioPin (output, input and edge interrupts), FakeAdc, FakePwm, FakeCanBus (bus-off), FakeClock (jumps across 2^32 microseconds), FakeBusyWait, FakeLogSink, and FakeAsyncI2c, FakeAsyncSpi (the asynchronous contract over the I2C and SPI fakes: latency in polls, a hang, a late completion, the cancel race). Each is static_asserted against its concept.

docs.title: MISRA C++:2023 notes
docs.text:
• The contract headers: zero findings and zero deviations (level high). The *Ref values live in refs.hpp, kb-core's one library deviation, DEV-KBC-004 (Rule 8.2.6): one helper, detail::ContextAs<T>, turns the void* context back into the type its table was built for (ADR-0011 amendment).
  • Concepts only, no virtual function (ADR-0006); the function tables are namespace-scope structs and variable templates, so no type is nested in a class template; comparison operators are non-members.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
examples/host/interfaces_fakes/ runs a function written to the I2cBus concept against the host port's fake bus; the same function takes a target port's bus unchanged. It is built and run by CI.

constexpr uint8_t kAddress = 0x48U;
constexpr uint8_t kRegister = 0x10U;

// Any type that satisfies kb::iface::I2cBus can be passed here: the fake on a PC, a port's bus on a
// target.
template <kb::iface::I2cBus Bus>
bool RunChecks(Bus& bus) {
  bool ok = bus.EnsureReady() == kb::Status::Ok;
  // Write register 0x10 (the first byte is the register, the rest are data), then read it back.
  const std::array<uint8_t, 3> tx{kRegister, 0xABU, 0xCDU};
  ok = ok && (bus.Write(kAddress, tx) == kb::Status::Ok);
  const std::array<uint8_t, 1> pointer{kRegister};
  std::array<uint8_t, 2> rx{};
  ok = ok && (bus.WriteRead(kAddress, pointer, rx) == kb::Status::Ok);
  ok = ok && (rx[0] == 0xABU) && (rx[1] == 0xCDU);
  // A device that is not on the bus is reported, not ignored.
  ok = ok && (bus.Read(0x50U, rx) == kb::Status::NoDevice);
  // An injected fault shows up as the Status the contract documents, and clears after its count.
  bus.FailNext(kb::iface::I2cFailure::Timeout, 1U);
  ok = ok && (bus.Read(kAddress, rx) == kb::Status::Timeout);
  ok = ok && (bus.Read(kAddress, rx) == kb::Status::Ok);
  return ok;
}

docs.title: ThreadX backend
docs.text:
KB_RTOS=THREADX runs the whole kb::rtos API on Eclipse ThreadX: the same classes, the same contract (static allocation, waits of at least the time asked, bounded locks, fail-closed creation), the same tests as the FreeRTOS backend. Why ThreadX is supported, with the evidence: ADR-0015.

The ThreadX backend Figure description and sources

The kb::rtos API (Mutex, RecursiveMutex, Semaphore, Queue, EventFlags, Timer, Thread, CriticalSection) reaches the seam, kb::rtos::backend in backend.hpp. The ThreadX backend is two files: threadx_isr.cpp, where every FromIsr call is the same call with TX_NO_WAIT, and threadx_boundary.cpp, the only boundary file, which creates ThreadX objects (tx_*_create) on kb-owned control blocks and stacks. The kernel is SOUP and never edited; it comes from a product's copy (KB_THREADX_INCLUDE_DIRS, for STM32Cube or a vendor SDK) or from the pinned submodule third_party/threadx at a release tag, with KB_THREADX_PORT choosing cortex_m0, cortex_m4, cortex_m7 or linux. Tests run the boundary on a fake kernel in tests/fakes/threadx (contract and seam, exact ticks, kb_rtos_tests_threadx) and, on the pinned kernel's Linux port, as a threaded suite with priority inheritance (kb_rtos_tests_threadx_linux).

Drawn from: docs/model/rtos-threadx.graph.yml.

docs.title: Getting the kernel
docs.text:
ThreadX is SOUP: never copied into kb-core, never edited. The backend builds against one of two kernels, and the configure stops when neither is given.

You have Configure with Who links the kernel A kernel from your vendor tooling (STM32Cube, an SDK) -DKB_RTOS=THREADX -DKB_THREADX_INCLUDE_DIRS="<common/inc>;<port inc>;<tx_user.h dir>", -DKB_THREADX_DEFINITIONS="<every TX_* define the kernel is compiled with>" (at least TX_INCLUDE_USER_DEFINE_FILE when it uses tx_user.h) and -DKB_THREADX_TICK_HZ=<its TX_TIMER_TICKS_PER_SECOND> (required) Your image, as before Nothing yet -DKB_RTOS=THREADX -DKB_THREADX_PORT=cortex_m4 (any GNU port directory of the ThreadX kernel) and git submodule update --init third_party/threadx; KB_THREADX_TICK_HZ defaults to 1000 Your image links the threadx target this builds

third_party/threadx is the official eclipse-threadx/threadx repository at a release tag (the SOUP list records which). KB_THREADX_USER_FILE picks the tx_user.h it is built with (default components/lib/rtos/threadx-config/kb_tx_user.h, which takes the tick from KB_THREADX_TICK_HZ; any other user file needs KB_THREADX_TICK_HZ given explicitly).

The backend must see the kernel as the kernel was compiled. It reads ThreadX control blocks (TX_THREAD, TX_MUTEX, ...) whose layout depends on options such as TX_ENABLE_STACK_CHECKING, TX_DISABLE_NOTIFY_CALLBACKS or the TX_*_USER_EXTENSION macros. With the pinned kernel the backend takes the kernel target's own include directories and defines, so they always agree. With a product kernel, pass the same tx_user.h and the same TX_* defines in KB_THREADX_DEFINITIONS; to have the build check it, also pass KB_THREADX_THREAD_BYTES (the sizeof(TX_THREAD) your kernel build sees), and the backend fails to compile when its own differs.

docs.title: Kernel configuration
docs.text: Option Required Why TX_NO_TIMER not defined Yes (a compile error otherwise) Timeouts, sleeps and kb::rtos::Timer need the timer component TX_TIMER_TICKS_PER_SECOND set on purpose, equal to the real tick Yes (a compile error when it differs from KB_THREADX_TICK_HZ) kb-core converts milliseconds with it, and tx_api.h silently defaults it to 100 when tx_user.h is not included. On Cortex-M the SysTick reload in the port's tx_initialize_low_level.S sets the real rate. kb-core's tests run at 1000 and, on the Linux port, also at 100 ULONG of 32 bits or more Yes (a compile error otherwise) Ticks and flags are 32-bit in kb-core TX_ENABLE_STACK_CHECKING Recommended Thread::StackFreeBytes() and ThreadX's own overflow detection; without it StackFreeBytes() is Unsupported TX_DISABLE_ERROR_CHECKING Either kb-core checks its own arguments before every call; the kernel's checks are a second line TX_TIMER_PROCESS_IN_ISR Either A Timer callback runs in "timer context" either way and must not block TX_MAX_PRIORITIES Any (32 by default) kb priorities are clamped to it KB_THREADX_QUEUE_WORD_BYTES (kb-core) When sizeof(ULONG) is not 4 The word queue slots are rounded to; a wrong value is a compile error. Only the ThreadX build rounds slots; other backends keep them at the item size

docs.title: How the kb API maps
docs.text: kb-core ThreadX Note Mutex tx_mutex_create(..., TX_INHERIT) Priority inheritance. A ThreadX mutex nests; kb::Mutex does not: a second take by the holder fails after its timeout (at once for an unbounded wait) RecursiveMutex the same mutex Nests; each take needs its unlock Semaphore tx_semaphore_create, tx_semaphore_ceiling_put ThreadX has no maximum count: the ceiling put keeps kb's Queue<T, N> tx_queue_create on the kb buffer ThreadX moves whole words: an item is copied through a word buffer, so any T up to 16 words (64 bytes on a 32-bit MCU) works; a larger one is Unsupported at Create() EventFlags tx_event_flags_* Clear is a set with TX_AND; a wait returns the flags before any clear, or the flags now on a timeout Timer tx_timer_create, deactivated until Start() The period in ticks (rounded up); Start() restarts the whole period. 32 timers at most (the expiry finds its timer in a table) Thread tx_thread_create on the kb stack, auto start, no time slice kb priority p (higher first) is ThreadX TX_MAX_PRIORITIES - 1 - p, but never more urgent than TX_TIMER_THREAD_PRIORITY + 1, so no kb thread delays timeouts and timer callbacks (with 32 priorities: kb 0 to 30 are distinct, 30 and above share ThreadX 1); the name is copied (15 characters) Periodic, the thread grid tx_thread_sleep of the rest of the period ThreadX has no delay-until; an overrun returns at once and is counted, and so is a wake-up after the grid point (a preemption between reading the tick and sleeping). The arithmetic is platform-free (kb/rtos/backend_rules.hpp) SleepFor(0), Yield() tx_thread_relinquish CriticalSection tx_interrupt_control Nests; the outermost restores the posture it found Thread::StackFreeBytes() the kernel's highest stack pointer and the 0xEF fill pattern The lower of the two; needs TX_ENABLE_STACK_CHECKING ...FromIsr() the same call with TX_NO_WAIT ThreadX allows these from an interrupt; the port's interrupt exit reschedules, so there is no yield request. Queue::SendFromIsr puts one message buffer (16 words: 64 bytes on a 32-bit MCU) on the interrupt stack; size the ISR stack for it

docs.title: Differences from FreeRTOS that a user can see
docs.text:
• Object lifetime. ThreadX keeps every created object on a kernel list. A kb object's destructor deletes its kernel object (tx_*_delete, ADR-0017), and a deleted timer frees its slot of the backend's timer table, so a kb object on a stack frame leaves no dangling entry. Static storage is still the rule for objects that live for the whole program; an object must not be ended while a thread holds or waits on it.
  • A holder's unbounded retake. Mutex::TryLockFor(kb::kMaxMilliseconds) by the thread that holds the mutex fails at once on ThreadX; on FreeRTOS it never returns. Both are a bug in the caller.
  • Mutexes from an interrupt are not allowed on any backend. On ThreadX tx_thread_identify() in an interrupt returns the interrupted thread, so a misuse may look like the holder's retake; with a zero timeout it only fails.
  • Queue item size. At most 16 native words per item (FreeRTOS has no limit).
  • Timers. At most 32 at once; the callback may run in the tick interrupt when the kernel is built with TX_TIMER_PROCESS_IN_ISR.
  • Interrupt calls. No portYIELD_FROM_ISR: the port's interrupt exit does it.
  • Priorities. ThreadX numbers urgency the other way round; kb-core maps it, so ThreadConfig::priority means the same on both.

docs.title: What a port needs
docs.text: An MCU port that runs ThreadX (port-stm32 first) provides what the kernel needs and kb-core does not: the kernel's low-level start-up (tx_initialize_low_level, the vector table entries for SysTick and PendSV, the tick at TX_TIMER_TICKS_PER_SECOND), the call to tx_kernel_enter() and a tx_application_define() that runs the image's composition root (where kb::rtos objects are created), and the configure options above. kb-core's own kb::MonotonicUs() clock still comes from the port (handbook), not from the ThreadX tick.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Test Kernel What it proves kb_rtos_tests_threadx fake (tests/fakes/threadx) The single-context contract suite with exact tick counts, as on none and FreeRTOS, and the seam: creation failures, thread parameters and priority mapping, the non-recursive rule, semaphore maximum, odd-sized queue items, timer restart and table bound, critical-section posture, the tick wrap, delay-until, the stack high-water mark kb_rtos_tests_threadx_linux the pinned kernel, Linux port (-DKB_THREADX_HOST_TESTS=ON, Linux; the pre-flight runs it at KB_THREADX_TICK_HZ 1000 and 100) The threaded suite of the host backend on real ThreadX threads (including a verified start and a join that end within two ticks of their timeout), plus priority inheritance resolving an inversion (the test fails with TX_NO_INHERIT), preemption by priority, and stack measurement test_backend_rules.cpp (in kb_rtos_tests_none) none The platform-free delay-until, late wake-up, holder retake and tick-extension rules Cortex-M cross-compile the pinned kernel, cortex_m0, cortex_m4, cortex_m7 ports The backend and the kernel build for M0+, M4F and M7F with Arm GCC and kb-core's strict flags (tools/preflight/threadx_cross.sh)

The Linux port runs each ThreadX thread on its own pthread stack, so on it the stack measurement is only checked to be in range; the depth logic is checked on the fake kernel.

docs.title: kb::rtos
docs.text:
The only place a scheduler is touched. A small typed API (header-only, no RTOS type in any signature) over one backend chosen by KB_RTOS. Depends on kb::utils; applications, the HAL, handlers and ports may all use it.

#include "kb/rtos/rtos.hpp"
Header Gives Contract in one line time.hpp SleepFor, Periodic, Now, TickRateHz, ToTicksAtLeast, Yield A sleep or timeout is never shorter than asked: ticks rounded up, plus one mutex.hpp Mutex, LockGuard, RecursiveMutex, RecursiveLockGuard Every lock is bounded; a failed TryLockFor waited at least its timeout; priority inheriting where the RTOS has it semaphore.hpp Semaphore Counting, bounded by its maximum; GiveFromIsr is ISR-safe queue.hpp Queue<T, N> N copies of a trivially copyable T, storage inside the object (on ThreadX each slot is whole kernel words); SendFromIsr is ISR-safe event_flags.hpp EventFlags 24 flags; WaitAny/WaitAll return the flags seen; SetFromIsr is ISR-safe timer.hpp Timer Periodic or one-shot callback in the timer context; never blocks critical_section.hpp CriticalSection RAII mask of interrupts and preemption; nests thread.hpp Thread<Derived, StackBytes>, ThreadConfig, ThreadStats, ThreadState CRTP base (ADR-0006 register): static stack, fixed-rate loop, verified start, stop, park and resume, statistics, stack high-water

docs.title: Life cycle: construct inert, create explicitly
docs.text:
Every kb-core RTOS object has a constexpr constructor that does nothing an RTOS could notice, so it can be a static object without the static-initialisation hazards of RTOS calls before the scheduler runs. It becomes usable with Create() (Start() for a thread), which returns kb::Result<void> and fails closed: AlreadyStarted on a second call, InvalidArgument for a bad count or period, the backend's status otherwise. Every call on an object that was never created fails harmlessly (returns false or 0).

kb::rtos::Queue<Sample, 16> g_samples{};      // static, no RTOS call
kb::rtos::Mutex g_bus{};

kb::Status StartAll() noexcept {
  if (!g_samples.Create().IsOk() || !g_bus.Create().IsOk()) { return kb::Status::Fault; }
  return kb::Status::Ok;
}

docs.title: Threads
docs.text:
class Sampler : public kb::rtos::Thread<Sampler, 4096U> {
public:
  bool Setup() noexcept { return sensor_.Start().IsOk(); }        // false: the thread ends Failed
  bool Step() noexcept {                                          // false: the loop ends
    return g_samples.SendFor(sensor_.Read(), kb::Milliseconds{2U});
  }
  void Cleanup() noexcept { sensor_.Stop(); }                     // always runs last
};

Sampler g_sampler{};
kb::rtos::ThreadConfig cfg{};
cfg.name = "sampler";
cfg.priority = 5U;
cfg.period = kb::Milliseconds{10U};                               // a 10 ms grid; 0 runs back to back
const auto started = g_sampler.Start(cfg);
...
g_sampler.RequestStop();
const bool ended = g_sampler.Join(kb::Milliseconds{100U});
const kb::rtos::ThreadStats stats = g_sampler.Stats();           // steps, overruns, max_step_us

The loop wakes on a fixed grid from its first step: a late step does not shift later ones, and every wake-up that had already passed is counted as an overrun.

Call Does StartAndWaitToVerify(cfg, timeout) Start(), then waits for Setup() to return: Ok, Fault (Setup failed, Cleanup ran) or Timeout RequestPark() / Resume() / ResumeFromIsr() Parks the loop after the current step until resumed; the grid restarts on resume, so a park is not counted as overruns; RequestStop() also ends a park; IsParked() StackFreeBytes() The fewest free stack bytes seen, while the thread is starting or running; Unsupported where the backend cannot measure (none, host, ThreadX without stack checking)

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
kb::rtos backends Figure description and sources

One API, one seam, four backends. The kb::rtos API (Mutex, RecursiveMutex, Semaphore, Queue, EventFlags, Timer, Thread, CriticalSection in components/lib/rtos/inc) reaches a backend through kb::rtos::backend (backend.hpp), where each native object lives in opaque storage sized there and every backend static_asserts that it fits. The none backend is for host tests and bare-metal bring-up, with one context and a deterministic fake clock; the host backend (std::thread) runs PC tests with real threads and is never built for a target. FreeRTOS (the ESP32 default, any FreeRTOS target, static API only) and ThreadX (Eclipse ThreadX targets, one boundary file) reach their kernel through boundary files; the kernel is SOUP, from ESP-IDF or KB_FREERTOS_INCLUDE_DIRS for FreeRTOS, and from KB_THREADX_INCLUDE_DIRS or third_party/threadx for ThreadX. FreeRTOS and ThreadX also run their tests on fake kernels (tests/fakes) with exact ticks.

Drawn from: docs/model/rtos-backends.graph.yml.

KB_RTOS Folder Use Notes NONE components/lib/rtos/backends/none/ Host tests, bare-metal bring-up One context, deterministic fake clock (kb/rtos/none/control.hpp); timers fire as time advances; threads Unsupported FREERTOS components/lib/rtos/backends/freertos/ ESP32 (default), any FreeRTOS target Static API only; 32-bit ticks; ESP-IDF builds it into the component kb HOST components/ports/host/ PC tests with real threads std::thread; outside the MISRA claim; never built for a target THREADX components/lib/rtos/backends/threadx/ Eclipse ThreadX targets (STM32 next) One boundary file; a product's kernel or the pinned third_party/threadx; ThreadX backend

Each native object lives in opaque storage inside the kb object (detail::OpaqueStorage), sized and aligned in backend.hpp; every backend static_asserts that its object fits. A wait without a limit is kb::kMaxMilliseconds. A kb object's destructor deletes its native object (ADR-0017): vQueueDelete and vEventGroupDelete on FreeRTOS, tx_*_delete on ThreadX, the standard-library destructors on the host backend, nothing on none (a timer leaves its table). A FreeRTOS timer is not deleted: xTimerDelete only queues the delete for the timer task, which may still use the control block after the storage has ended. Objects that live for the whole program still take static storage; never end an object while a thread holds or waits on it (the host backend then leaves the object in place rather than destroy it under that thread).

docs.title: MISRA C++:2023 notes
docs.text:
• The API headers and the none backend: zero findings, zero deviations (level high).
  • The FreeRTOS backend is two boundary files (deviations/boundary-files.yml). FreeRTOS headers are SOUP, reached with -isystem; a finding at a FreeRTOS call site (a macro of the kernel API, a cast of the opaque storage to the static buffer type) is a recorded deviation in deviations/deviations.yml, cited at the line.
  • The ThreadX backend is one boundary file (threadx_boundary.cpp) under the same records; threadx_isr.cpp includes no ThreadX header. The ThreadX sources are SOUP: listed, pinned, never scanned.
  • The host backend and the test fakes are test code, outside the claim.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
examples/host/rtos_thread/ runs on the host backend on a PC and is built and run by CI; the ESP32 port's kb_rtos_smoke is the same program over FreeRTOS. Its source is shown by snippet includes.

// A thread is a class: Setup runs once, Step runs on the period until it returns false, Cleanup
// runs last. It gets the queue and the flags it works with by pointer, so the example needs no
// global.
class Ticker : public kb::rtos::Thread<Ticker, 4096U> {
public:
  Ticker(kb::rtos::Queue<uint32_t, 8>& queue, kb::rtos::EventFlags& flags) noexcept
      : queue_{&queue}, flags_{&flags} {}
  bool Setup() noexcept {
    count_ = 0U;
    return true;
  }
  bool Step() noexcept {
    const bool sent = queue_->SendFor(count_, kb::Milliseconds{10U});
    ++count_;
    return sent && (count_ < 5U);
  }
  void Cleanup() noexcept {
    flags_->Set(0x1U);
  }

private:
  kb::rtos::Queue<uint32_t, 8>* queue_;
  kb::rtos::EventFlags* flags_;
  uint32_t count_{0U};
};

void OnTimer(void* context) noexcept {
  static_cast<kb::rtos::EventFlags*>(context)->Set(0x2U);
}

bool RunChecks() {
  kb::rtos::Queue<uint32_t, 8> queue{};
  kb::rtos::Mutex mutex{};
  kb::rtos::EventFlags flags{};
  kb::rtos::Timer timer{};
  Ticker ticker{queue, flags};
  bool ok = queue.Create().IsOk() && mutex.Create().IsOk() && flags.Create().IsOk();
  ok = ok && timer.Create(&OnTimer, &flags, kb::Milliseconds{20U}, false).IsOk() && timer.Start();
  kb::rtos::ThreadConfig config{};
  config.name = "kb_ticker";
  config.priority = 5U;
  config.period = kb::Milliseconds{10U};
  ok = ok && ticker.Start(config).IsOk();
  uint32_t value = 0U;
  for (uint32_t expected = 0U; ok && (expected < 5U); ++expected) {
    ok = queue.ReceiveFor(value, kb::Milliseconds{100U}) && (value == expected);
  }
  ok = ok && ((flags.WaitAll(0x3U, kb::Milliseconds{200U}) & 0x3U) == 0x3U);
  ok = ok && ticker.Join(kb::Milliseconds{100U});
  const kb::Instant before = kb::rtos::Now();
  kb::rtos::SleepFor(kb::Milliseconds{5U});
  ok = ok && (kb::utils::ElapsedUs(kb::rtos::Now(), before) >= 5000U);
  ok = ok && mutex.TryLockFor(kb::Milliseconds{1U});
  mutex.Unlock();
  return ok;
}

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• kb_rtos_tests_none, kb_rtos_tests_freertos and kb_rtos_tests_threadx: one contract suite (test_rtos_single.cpp) run over the none backend and over the FreeRTOS and ThreadX boundaries with their fake kernels, with exact tick counts.
  • test_threadx_seam.cpp: the ThreadX seam (ThreadX backend); with -DKB_THREADX_HOST_TESTS=ON on Linux, kb_rtos_tests_threadx_linux runs the threaded suite on the real kernel.
  • test_freertos_seam.cpp: creation failures, task parameters (stack depth, clamped priority), the whole thread life cycle, ISR context switches, critical sections, the 64-bit clock across a tick wrap.
  • kb_rtos_tests_host: real threads and contention (producer and consumer, bounded lock refused for at least its timeout, timers, periodic thread, recursive mutex, verified start, park and resume); the same file is the threaded suite on ThreadX.
  • compile_fail/: non-copyable items, bare-integer sleeps, a thread without Step, copied RTOS objects.
  • ESP32-C6: components/ports/esp32/examples app kb_rtos_smoke, built in CI with ESP-IDF v5.5.

docs.title: kb::utils
docs.text:
Vocabulary types and algorithms with no OS, no MCU and no I/O: the one error model, typed time, fixed-capacity containers, CRCs, byte packing, checked arithmetic and heap-free text. Header-only, constexpr where it can be, depends on nothing. Applications, the HAL, handlers and ports may all use it.

#include "kb/utils/utils.hpp"   // or one header per area, below
Header Gives Contract in one line status.hpp kb::Status, kb::ToString() Ok is the only success; every name is a literal, never null result.hpp kb::Result<T>, kb::Result<void> A value or a failure with a vendor Detail(); a default result is a failure time.hpp kb::Microseconds, kb::Milliseconds, kb::Instant, ElapsedSince(), Deadline Distinct duration types; elapsed time by unsigned subtraction; instants are never ordered numeric.hpp CheckedAdd/Sub/Mul, SaturatingAdd/Sub/Mul, InRangeCast, Saturate, Clamp, DivCeil Exact or refused, never undefined; no bool or character types crc.hpp Crc<T, Poly, Init, Reflected, XorOut> and 11 presets Table built at compile time; each preset proven on its catalogue check value endian.hpp LoadBe16 ... StoreLe64, ByteReader, ByteWriter Fixed-extent spans; a cursor fails sticky at the first overrun static_vector.hpp StaticVector<T, N> Inline storage; a call that does not fit returns false and changes nothing ring_buffer.hpp RingBuffer<T, N>, SpscRing<T, N> One-context FIFO; wait-free single-producer single-consumer FIFO (N a power of two) span.hpp CheckedSubspan, CopyInto, Fill, Equal, ConstantTimeEqual, ObjectBytes No offset arithmetic can wrap; secret comparison in constant time fixed_string.hpp FixedString<N> NUL-terminated, truncation flagged, numbers formatted without printf fault_journal.hpp FaultJournal<Store, Slots>, RamJournalStore<Bytes>, JournalStore, FaultRecord, ResetReason 32-byte CRC-checked records in a ring that survives a reset; torn writes detected; one bounded write per append (fault evidence)

docs.title: The error model
docs.text:
Every kb-core call that can fail returns kb::Status or kb::Result<T>. A result has no public data: it is made by Success(value) or Failure(status, detail) and read by IsOk(), Value(), ValueOr(), Error() and Detail(). Ports put the vendor error code in detail, so bench debugging keeps it.

kb::Result<uint16_t> ReadId(Bus& bus) noexcept {
  uint16_t raw = 0U;
  if (!bus.Read(raw)) {
    return kb::Result<uint16_t>::Failure(kb::Status::BusError, bus.VendorCode());
  }
  return kb::Result<uint16_t>::Success(raw);
}

const auto id = ReadId(bus);
if (!id.IsOk()) {
  log.Write(kb::ToString(id.Error()));
}

Failure(Status::Ok) is a programming error and is recorded as Status::Fault, so a failure never reads as a success.

docs.title: Time without wrap defects
docs.text:
const kb::Instant start = clock.Now();                       // 64-bit microseconds
const auto limit = kb::utils::Deadline::After(start, kb::Milliseconds{20U});
while (!limit.Expired(clock.Now())) { ... }

// A driver hook with a 32-bit millisecond clock:
const uint32_t now_ms = kb::utils::NarrowMs(clock.Now());
if (kb::utils::HasElapsed(now_ms, since_ms, 100U)) { ... }   // right across the 2^32 wrap
  • Milliseconds and Microseconds do not convert into each other implicitly, and a bare integer is not a duration (compile-fail tests prove both).
  • ToMicroseconds saturates, ToMillisecondsCeil and MillisecondsToTicksCeil round up: a wait converted with them is never shorter than asked.
  • There is no operator< on Instant. Comparing two timestamps is the half-range defect; compare the elapsed time with the timeout instead.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
kb::utils::RingBuffer<Sample, 16> history{};
static_cast<void>(history.PushOverwrite(sample));   // keeps the newest 16

kb::utils::SpscRing<uint8_t, 64> rx{};              // ISR produces, task consumes
// ISR:  if (!rx.TryPush(byte)) { ++overruns; }
// task: uint8_t b = 0U; while (rx.TryPop(b)) { Parse(b); }

Elements are trivially copyable value types; storage is inline, so a container is as large as its capacity and never allocates.

docs.title: MISRA C++:2023 notes
docs.text:
• Zero findings and zero deviations is the target for every header here (level high, ADR-0011).
  • Factories build a value-initialised object and set its fields (Result r{}; r.error_ = e; return r;), the form the scan accepts under Rule 0.2.2.
  • Comparison operators are non-member functions (Rule 16.6.1); there are no user-defined literals (Rule 6.9.2) and no types nested in class templates.
  • Every if ... else if ends in else; operands of && and || are parenthesised (Rule 8.0.1); arithmetic on narrow types is done after an explicit cast to uint32_t or the widest type (Rules 7.0.4 to 7.0.6).
  • Digits are looked up in a table, never computed from a character (Rule 7.0.3); no printf, so no PRId64 on newlib.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
examples/host/utils_checks/ runs on a PC and is built and run by CI; its source is shown here by a snippet include, so this page cannot drift from code that compiles.

constexpr std::array<uint8_t, 9> kCheck{0x31U, 0x32U, 0x33U, 0x34U, 0x35U,
                                        0x36U, 0x37U, 0x38U, 0x39U};

bool RunChecks() {
  // The CRC catalogue check value is the CRC of the ASCII digits "123456789".
  bool ok = kb::utils::Crc32Ieee::Compute(kCheck) == 0xCBF43926UL;
  ok = ok && (kb::utils::Crc16Modbus::Compute(kCheck) == 0x4B37U);
  // Byte packing into a caller-owned buffer, read back little-endian.
  std::array<uint8_t, 4> buffer{};
  kb::utils::ByteWriter writer{buffer};
  ok = ok && writer.WriteBe32(0x01020304UL);
  ok = ok && (kb::utils::LoadLe32(std::span<const uint8_t, 4>{buffer}) == 0x04030201UL);
  // Saturating arithmetic and a time comparison that survives the 32-bit counter wrapping.
  ok = ok && (kb::utils::SaturatingAdd<uint8_t>(250U, 10U) == 255U);
  ok = ok && kb::utils::HasElapsed(5U, 0xFFFFFFFBU, 10U);
  return ok;
}
